The components of the field are polynomials, so their partial derivatives, again polynomials, are continuous at every point of space (corollary 1.70), and we may take the whole space for \(D\).

The left side. The partial derivatives are \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = 2a\,(L - x)\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\), so the divergence is \(2a\,(L - x) - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) = 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\). It does not depend on \(y\) and \(z\), so it does not change over the cross-section with the side \(2c\), and by definition 4.8 and by lemma 3.54, item 3, the inner integral in \(z\) equals \(2c \cdot 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\), and the middle one in \(y\) equals \(4c^2 \cdot 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\). The function \(Lx - x^2/2\) has the derivative \(L - x\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus along the length of the bar \(\int_0^L (L - x)\,\mathrm{d}x = L^2/2\), and

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \Big( \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = 4c^2 \cdot 0{,}8\,a \cdot \frac{L^2}{2} = 1{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2 = 0{,}2811\ \text{mm}^3 .\]

The right side. The box has six faces (figure 4.50).

  1. The bottom face \(x = L\) with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integrand is \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, y, z) = a L^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\). The inner integral in \(z\) is \(\int_{-\mathrm{c}}^{c} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}z = 2c\,y^2 + \tfrac23 c^3\), the outer one in \(y\) is \(2c \cdot \tfrac23 c^3 + \tfrac23 c^3 \cdot 2c = \tfrac83 c^4\). The integral over the face is therefore \(4c^2\,a L^2 - 0{,}3\,a \cdot \tfrac83 c^4 = 4\,a\,c^2 L^2 - 0{,}8\,a\,c^4\).
  2. The top face \(x = 0\) with the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{x}}(0, y, z) = 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\), the integral over the face \(0{,}8\,a\,c^4\).
  3. The face \(y = c\) with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The integrand is \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, c, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,c\). The integral in \(z\) gives the factor \(2c\), the integral in \(x\) the factor \(L^2/2\), together \(-0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\).
  4. The face \(y = -c\) with the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, -c, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,c\), the same as in item 3, and the integral is again \(-0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\).
  5. The faces \(z = \pm c\) with the normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) lie in front of the plane of the figure and behind it. They give the same as the faces \(y = \pm c\), each \(-0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\), because \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) differs from \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) only by \(z\) in place of \(y\).

The sum is \(4\,a\,c^2 L^2 - 0{,}8\,a\,c^4\) \(+\) \(0{,}8\,a\,c^4\) \(-\) \(4 \cdot 0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\) \(= 1{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\), the same as the left side.

What do the numbers mean (figure 4.50)? The box is drawn blackwhite before the loading and orange after it. Its origin is \(O\) at the top, the length \(L\) and the half width \(c\) are marked along the edge, and the axes \(x\) and \(y\) are at the top left. The bottom face, of area \(4c^2 = 36\ \text{mm}^2\), moves down by \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, 0, 0) = a L^2 = 19{,}52\) µm and sweeps \(36\ \text{mm}^2 \cdot 0{,}01952\ \text{mm} = 0{,}7027\ \text{mm}^3\), when we neglect the very small term \(0{,}8\,a\,c^4\). The four side faces move toward the axis, at the top by \(0{,}6\,aLc = 3{,}5\) nm, because the bar gets thinner, and each sweeps \(0{,}1054\ \text{mm}^3\) inward, together \(0{,}4216\ \text{mm}^3\). The top face stays in place at its centre, while its rim rises by about \(10^{-12}\) m, too little to show in the figure, and it sweeps only \(0{,}8\,a\,c^4 = 1{,}3 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{mm}^3\). The volume of the box grows by \(0{,}7027 - 0{,}4216 = 0{,}2811\ \text{mm}^3\). The box has the volume \(36\ \text{mm}^2 \cdot 10\,000\ \text{mm} = 360\,000\ \text{mm}^3\), so the relative change is \(0{,}2811/360\,000 = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\). This is exactly the sum \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) at the point \(P\) at the depth of 5 m, which we computed in section 1.17.4.

Why exactly at \(P\)? The relative change is the left side divided by the volume of the box, that is, the average of the divergence over the box. The divergence \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\) depends only on the depth, so this is also its average over the length of the bar. Let us draw it (figure 4.51). Horizontally is the depth \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L = 10\) m, vertically the divergence. The line falls from \(0{,}8\,aL = 1{,}562 \cdot 10^{-6}\) at the top to zero at the bottom. The integral along the length is the area under the line, and the average is the height of the rectangle with the same area over the same length. The triangle that the line adds above the height at the middle over the upper half of the bar is congruent to the triangle that the line takes from this height over the lower half, since both have half the length and half the fall of the line as their legs. So the area under the line equals the area of the rectangle with the height of the value at the middle, \(7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\), and the average is this value, at \(x = L/2 = 5\) m, where \(P\) lies.

What does the theorem demand of the field? Continuous differentiability on an open set that contains the body. This assumption entered in step 4 of the first part of the proof: we used the fundamental theorem of calculus on every segment, and it needs a continuous derivative along the whole segment. Let us look at a field that does not meet it. On the cube \(K = [0, 1]^3\) let \(v_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) for \(x < \tfrac12\) and \(v_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) for \(x \ge \tfrac12\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}} = v_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The field jumps on the plane \(x = \tfrac12\), where it is not even continuous, so we cannot differentiate it there (figure 4.52, the hidden edges of the cube are dashed). Everywhere that the derivatives exist, \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) is constant, so \(\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = 0\) and the divergence is zero. The left side would be zero. The right side: the normal is \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) on the faces \(x = 1\) and \(x = 0\) and perpendicular to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) on the other four, where \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\). Through the face \(x = 1\) we have \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} = 1 \cdot 1\), so the integral over the area \(1\) is \(1\). Through the face \(x = 0\) we have \(v_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), so the integral is zero. The right side is \(1 \neq 0\).

The theorem fails because the field is not continuously differentiable on the plane \(x = \tfrac12\). Every segment parallel to the axis \(x\) crosses the jump. The left graph of figure 4.53 shows the value \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) along one such segment. The horizontal axis runs along the segment from \(0\) to \(1\), and the value of the field is drawn upward. The graph is at the height \(0\) for \(x < \tfrac12\) and at the height \(1\) for \(x \ge \tfrac12\). On both halves it is horizontal, so the derivative is zero there, and the integral of the derivative along the segment, where the derivative exists, is \(0\). The difference of the values at the ends of the segment, however, is \(1\). All of this difference is made by the jump at \(x = \tfrac12\), which the divergence computed from the derivatives does not capture. A continuously differentiable field has no jump, so the divergence overlooks nothing in it.

In mechanics we meet a related case in a body made of two glued materials, where the displacement field has no continuous derivatives at the interface (section 1.15.6). The field itself does not jump here, because the materials are glued. The displacement \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) along a segment that crosses the interface is the right graph of figure 4.53. In the first material it grows with the slope \(0{,}4\), in the second with the slope \(1{,}6\), so the graph has a kink at the interface, not a jump. We then use the theorem on each material separately, provided the field in each material can be written by a formula that stays continuously differentiable a little beyond the interface, for example by a polynomial. The interface then contributes one surface integral for each side. Since the displacement field is continuous across the interface, these two integrals have the same \(\vek u\) and opposite normals, so they cancel as in step 2 of the second part of the proof. On the segment this is the value \(0{,}2\) at the interface, which is the end of the first piece and the start of the second, so the increments \(0{,}2\) and \(0{,}8\) add up to the whole difference \(1\). The equality (4.9) therefore holds for the whole body, with the divergence computed in each material separately. A term at the interface remains only when the field itself jumps, as in the cube example or at a crack.

4.2.6 Bodies with a curved surface

Even for an arbitrary smooth body the outward normal depends on the point (figure 4.54, left). The round hanging bar is not a body made of boxes. Its side face, the mantle of a cylinder, is curved, and the outward normal on it changes from point to point. At the point \((x, y, z)\) of the mantle, where \(y^2 + z^2 = r^2\) and \(r = 5\) mm is the radius of the cross section, the outward normal is \(\vek n = (0, y/r, z/r)\) (figure 4.54, right). The axis \(x\) points down from the centre \(O\) of the top face. This vector is a unit vector, because \((y/r)^2 + (z/r)^2 = 1\), it has no component along the axis of the bar, and it points away from the axis. On the top face the outward normal is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), on the bottom face \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The top and bottom faces are not rectangles either, but discs.

The divergence theorem holds for such bodies too. Precisely: let \(V\) be a closed and bounded set of points bounded by a surface made of finitely many smooth pieces, and let the components of the field \(\vek v\) be continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(V\). Then (4.9) holds, where \(\vek n\) is the outward normal of the surface (KREYSZIG §10.7, Theorem 1, PDF p. 479, CM (2.4.46), PDF p. 82, SADD (1.8.6), PDF p. 28). KREYSZIG proves the theorem first for a body bounded above and below by the graph of a function, and then for a body that can be cut into finitely many such pieces, so that the contributions of the inner cuts cancel as with our cells (PDF pp. 480-482). For the most general bodies he says that a limit process is still needed (PDF p. 482). We will take the same route, for a class of bodies that includes the round hanging bar, and in section 4.3.7 also for bodies that we get by bending a box continuously, such as the pieces of a ball. We will not develop the limit process, because all the bodies of our examples can be cut into such pieces.

The route is as follows. In this subsection we define a body bounded above and below by a graph, and show how to cut the round bar into three such bodies. The integral over such a body will again be an iterated integral, except that the limits of the inner integral will not be constant but will depend on the outer variables. So in section 4.2.7 we show that such an integral changes continuously, and how to differentiate it with respect to a variable on which the limits depend. Then we define the integral over such a body (section 4.2.8) and over its curved surface (section 4.2.11). Finally we prove the theorem and test it on the round bar (section 4.2.12). The bodies that we cannot cut into such pieces, such as a ball, and two questions about the independence of the integral, which we will name when they come up, are treated in sections 4.2.10, 4.3.6 and 4.3.7.

Let us start with a body that is a box with a curved top and bottom lid (figure 4.55). Below it, in the plane \(z = 0\), lies the rectangle \([a, b] \times [c, d]\), which we call the shadow of the body. Above every point \((x, y)\) of the shadow the body occupies a vertical segment that starts at the height \(g(x, y)\) and ends at the height \(h(x, y)\). The bottom lid of the body is the graph of the function \(g\), the top lid the graph of the function \(h\), and the four side faces are flat, in the planes \(x = a\), \(x = b\), \(y = c\) and \(y = d\). The figure also shows the outward unit normals, \(\vek n\) on the top lid, \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) on the front face and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) on the right face. The axis \(x\) points toward the viewer, the axis \(y\) to the right and the axis \(z\) up. In this section the letter \(g\) is not the gravitational acceleration but a function.

Definition 4.15 Body between two graphs (telo med dvema grafoma)

Let \(a < b\) and \(c < d\) be numbers and \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) a rectangle in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), that is, the set of points \((x, y)\) with \(a \le x \le b\) and \(c \le y \le d\). Let \(U\) be an open set of points of the plane that contains \(R\), that is, a set that contains, together with each of its points, a disc of some positive radius around it. Let \(g\) and \(h\) be functions whose input is a point \((x, y)\) of \(U\) and whose output is a number, and which are continuously differentiable on \(U\): at every point of \(U\) they have the partial derivatives with respect to \(x\) and to \(y\) (definition 1.26), which are continuous at every point of \(U\). Let \(g(x, y) \le h(x, y)\) for every point \((x, y) \in R\). The set of points of space

\[V = \{ (x, y, z) : (x, y) \in R,\ g(x, y) \le z \le h(x, y) \} \tag{4.10}\]

is a body between two graphs (telo med dvema grafoma), of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R\). The graph of the function \(h\) over \(R\) is its top lid, the graph of the function \(g\) its bottom lid. We use the same name for the set obtained when the roles of the coordinates are exchanged, for example the set of points with \(a \le x \le b\), \(c \le z \le d\) and \(g(x, z) \le y \le h(x, z)\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7, (6) (PDF p. 480), where the shadow of the body is a more general region, not only a rectangle. The restriction to a rectangle is not from the source.

The definition says what goes in. The rectangle \(R\) is the shadow of the body. The functions \(g\) and \(h\) take a point of the shadow as input, and their output is the height of the bottom and of the top lid above it. Why must they be continuously differentiable, and on an open set containing \(R\)? From their partial derivatives we will compute the normal of a lid in section 4.2.11, and in the proof of the theorem we will need them also on the edge of the shadow. A partial derivative at a point needs values of the function on both sides of the point (definition 1.26), so the functions must be defined a little beyond the edge. The inequality \(g \le h\) says that the bottom lid is not above the top lid. Equality is allowed: for the bar, the lids will meet at the edge of the shadow. The simplest body between graphs is the box \([a, b] \times [c, d] \times [g_0, h_0]\), for which \(g\) and \(h\) are constant functions with the values \(g_0 < h_0\), with zero partial derivatives.

A body over a rectangle is a special case. KREYSZIG allows the shadow, the set of points \((x, y)\) below the body, to be a more general region of the plane (KREYSZIG §10.7, (6), PDF p. 480). We will need the rectangle in the proof of the theorem, where we will exchange the order of integration in \(x\) and in \(y\). On a rectangle we may do so by theorem 4.9 on the order of integration. On more general regions we do not have this theorem. KREYSZIG avoids it by requiring the body to have this shape in the direction of all three axes, and obtains the terms with \(x\) and \(y\) from the term with \(z\) by renaming the axes (PDF pp. 480-481). How severe is our restriction? Less than it seems, because we may exchange the roles of the coordinates and cut a body into several pieces. Let us show this on the round bar.

The round hanging bar of length \(L = 10\) m, with a cross section of radius \(r = 5\) mm and the axis \(x\) down from the centre \(O\) of the top face, is the set of points with \(0 \le x \le L\) and \(y^2 + z^2 \le r^2\). Let

\[q(t) = \sqrt{r^2 - t^2} , \qquad -r \le t \le r ,\]

be the upper half of the circle of radius \(r\). At every \(y\) between \(-r\) and \(r\) the cross section of the bar occupies a vertical chord from \(z = -q(y)\) to \(z = q(y)\). Is the bar a body between the graphs of the functions \(-q(y)\) and \(q(y)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-r, r]\)? It is not, because \(q\) has no derivative at \(t = r\). For \(k > 0\) we have \(q(r - k) = \sqrt{2rk - k^2}\), so the slope of the segment from the point of the graph above \(r - k\) to the point above \(r\) is

\[\frac{q(r) - q(r - k)}{k} = -\frac{\sqrt{2rk - k^2}}{k} = -\sqrt{\frac{2r}{k} - 1} .\]

For \(r = 5\) mm and \(k = 1\) mm this is the segment from the point \((4, 3)\) to the point \((5, 0)\) with slope \(-\sqrt{10 - 1} = -3\). At \(k = 0{,}01\) mm the slope is \(-31{,}61\), and at \(k = 0{,}0001\) mm it is \(-316{,}2\): the smaller \(k\) is, the more upright the segment stands. As \(k\) goes to zero, \(2r/k\) grows beyond every bound, and with it the absolute value of the slope, so there is no limit. The tangent at the point \((r, 0)\) is vertical (figure 4.57, left, with the axes \(t\) and \(q\)). For \(t > r\) the function \(q\) is not even defined, because \(r^2 - t^2 < 0\).

So we cut the bar with the planes \(y = 3\) mm and \(y = -3\) mm into three pieces (figure 4.57, right). We chose the number \(3\) because \(3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2\). The points \((y, z) = (\pm 3, \pm 4)\) in millimetres therefore lie on the circle, and \(q(\pm 3) = 4\) and \(q(\pm 4) = 3\). Let us write the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) in millimetres.

  1. The middle piece \(C\) consists of the points of the bar with \(-3 \le y \le 3\). For such \(y\), \(z\) lies between \(-q(y)\) and \(q(y)\), so \(C\) is a body between the graphs of the functions \(-q(y)\) and \(q(y)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-3, 3]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(y\).
  2. The right piece \(D\) consists of the points of the bar with \(y \ge 3\). For such a point \(z^2 \le 25 - y^2 \le 16\), so \(-4 \le z \le 4\) (lemma 1.29, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square). From \(y^2 \le 25 - z^2 = q(z)^2\) it follows by the same lemma that \(y \le q(z)\). Conversely, every point with \(-4 \le z \le 4\) and \(3 \le y \le q(z)\) satisfies \(y^2 + z^2 \le q(z)^2 + z^2 = 25\). The piece \(D\) is therefore a body between the graphs of the constant function \(3\) and the function \(q(z)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-4, 4]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(z\). Here \(y\) is the coordinate that runs between the graphs. The condition \(3 \le q(z)\) holds because \(q(z)^2 = 25 - z^2 \ge 9\).
  3. The left piece \(E\) consists of the points of the bar with \(y \le -3\). Like \(D\), it is a body between the graphs of the functions \(-q(z)\) and \(-3\) over the same rectangle.

For the pieces to be bodies between graphs, we still have to show that \(q\) is continuously differentiable on an open interval containing \([-4, 4]\). What must come out can be seen in the figure before any computation. The radius from the centre to the point \((3, 4)\) has slope \(4/3\). The tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius, and a quarter turn sends the direction \((3, 4)\) to the direction \((4, -3)\), so the tangent has slope \(-3/4\). At the point \((t, q(t))\) the same reasoning gives the slope \(-t/q(t)\). This view tells where the formula comes from and why it fails at \(t = \pm r\): there the radius is horizontal and the tangent vertical. It does not tell that the tangent of geometry really is the limit of the slopes of segments between two points of the graph, as the definition of the derivative demands, and it does not give the continuity of the derivative. The computation in the lemma gives both. In it we get rid of the root by writing the difference of two roots through the difference of their squares.

Lemma 4.16 Derivative of the upper half of a circle (odvod zgornje polovice krožnice)

Let \(r > 0\) and \(q(t) = \sqrt{r^2 - t^2}\) for \(-r < t < r\). Then \(q(t) > 0\), the function \(q\) is differentiable at every point of the open interval \((-r, r)\),

\[q'(t) = -\frac{t}{q(t)} , \tag{4.11}\]

and \(q'\) is continuous at every point of \((-r, r)\). The function \(q\) is thus continuously differentiable on \((-r, r)\).

Proof

We must show that the difference quotient of the function \(q\) converges to \(-t/q(t)\) and that this number changes continuously with \(t\).

  1. Let \(-r < t < r\). Then \(|t| < r\) and by lemma 1.29 \(t^2 < r^2\), so \(r^2 - t^2 > 0\). The square root of a positive number is positive, because its square is positive, while the square of the number \(0\) is \(0\) (theorem 1.37). Thus \(q(t) > 0\): between its end points the graph lies above the axis \(t\).
  2. Let \(s, t \in (-r, r)\), and let the points of the graph above them be the ends of a segment like the one drawn. We have \(\big(q(s) - q(t)\big)\big(q(s) + q(t)\big) = q(s)^2 - q(t)^2 = (r^2 - s^2) - (r^2 - t^2) = t^2 - s^2\). Since \(q(s) + q(t) > 0\), we may divide by it:
    \[q(s) - q(t) = -\frac{(s - t)(s + t)}{q(s) + q(t)} .\]
  3. Continuity. The denominator in step 2 is not smaller than the height \(q(t)\), because \(q(s) \ge 0\). The numerator equals \(|s - t|\,|s + t|\) in absolute value and is at most \(2r\,|s - t|\), because \(|s + t| \le |s| + |t| < 2r\) (lemma 1.6, items 2 and 1). Hence
    \[|q(s) - q(t)| \le \frac{2r}{q(t)}\,|s - t| ,\]
    so the graph lies in the wedge between the lines through the point \((t, q(t))\) with slopes \(\pm 2r/q(t)\), for \(r = 5\) and \(t = 3\) with slopes \(\pm 2{,}5\). The difference \(|q(s) - q(t)|\) is less than \(\eta\) when \(|s - t| < \eta\,q(t)/(2r)\), for \(\eta = 0{,}5\) on the interval \(|s - 3| < 0{,}2\), where the wedge stays in the band \(4 \pm 0{,}5\). The graph of \(q\) thus has no jump at \(t\) (definition 1.59).
  4. The difference quotient. Let \(k \neq 0\) and \(|k| < r - |t|\), so that \(t + k\) lies in \((-r, r)\). By step 2 with \(s = t + k\),
    \[\frac{q(t + k) - q(t)}{k} = -\frac{2t + k}{q(t + k) + q(t)} .\]
    This is the slope of the segment between the points of the graph above \(t\) and above \(t + k\), which at \(t = 3\) for \(k = 1\), \(0{,}5\) and \(-1\) is \(-1\), \(-0{,}859\) and \(-0{,}583\) respectively. The drawn segment from \((4, 3)\) to \((5, 0)\) reaches the end point \(t + k = r\), which the lemma does not cover, but the formula of step 2 still holds there, because \(q(4) + q(5) = 3 > 0\), and gives \(-(2 \cdot 4 + 1)/(0 + 3) = -3\).
  5. We compare the slope of the segment with the slope of the tangent, the number \(-t/q(t)\). We write the two fractions with a common denominator and simplify the numerator:
    \[-\frac{2t + k}{q(t + k) + q(t)} + \frac{t}{q(t)} = \frac{t\,\big(q(t + k) - q(t)\big) - k\,q(t)}{\big(q(t + k) + q(t)\big)\,q(t)} .\]
    In the numerator, \(-(2t + k)\,q(t) + t\,\big(q(t + k) + q(t)\big) = t\,q(t + k) - t\,q(t) - k\,q(t)\).
  6. The denominator is not smaller than \(q(t)^2\), because \(q(t + k) \ge 0\). By step 3, \(|q(t + k) - q(t)| \le 2r\,|k|/q(t)\), and \(|t| < r\). By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, items 1 and 2) the absolute value of the difference in step 5, the difference of the slopes of the segment and the tangent, is therefore at most
    \[\frac{r \cdot 2r\,|k|/q(t) + |k|\,q(t)}{q(t)^2} = C_{\mathrm{t}}\,|k| , \qquad C_{\mathrm{t}} = \frac{2r^2 + q(t)^2}{q(t)^3} .\]
    As a function of \(k\), the difference thus lies in the wedge between the lines \(\pm C_{\mathrm{t}}\,k\), at \(t = 3\) with slopes \(\pm 1{,}031\).
  7. For \(\eta > 0\) we take as the band \(\delta\) the smaller of the numbers \(\eta/C_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(r - |t|\). For every \(k\) with \(0 < |k| < \delta\) the difference in step 5 is less than \(\eta\): at \(t = 3\) and \(\eta = 0{,}2\), \(\delta = 0{,}194\), and there the wedge does not leave the band \(\pm 0{,}2\). By the definition of the derivative 1.9 and of the limit 1.5, \(q'(t) = -t/q(t)\). For \(r = 5\) and \(t = 3\) this is the slope \(-3/4\) of the drawn tangent, and \(C_{\mathrm{t}} = (50 + 16)/64 = 1{,}031\). The slope of the segment with \(k = 0{,}01\) therefore differs from \(-3/4\) by at most \(0{,}0103\). The computation gives \(-0{,}75196\), a difference of \(0{,}00196\).
  8. Continuity of the derivative. We compare the slopes of the tangents at \(s\) and \(t\). For \(s \in (-r, r)\), as in step 5,
    \[-\frac{s}{q(s)} + \frac{t}{q(t)} = \frac{t\,\big(q(s) - q(t)\big) - (s - t)\,q(t)}{q(s)\,q(t)} .\]
    By step 3, \(|q(s) - q(t)| < q(t)/2\) when \(|s - t| < q(t)^2/(4r)\), and then \(q(s) > q(t)/2\) and the denominator is greater than \(q(t)^2/2\). As in step 6, the numerator is at most \((2r^2/q(t) + q(t))\,|s - t|\). The difference is therefore at most \(2C_{\mathrm{t}}\,|s - t|\), which is less than \(\eta\) when \(|s - t|\) is smaller than \(\eta/(2C_{\mathrm{t}})\) and than \(q(t)^2/(4r)\). The derivative is continuous at \(t\).

Source: LEBL1 Example 4.1.4 (PDF p. 156) computes the derivative of the function \(\sqrt x\) with the same device of a difference of squares, and Proposition 4.1.10 (PDF p. 159) is the chain rule, from which the formula would follow. The proof is not from the sources.

For the bar \(r = 5\) mm, and the interval \([-4, 4]\) lies in \((-5, 5)\), away from the end points with a vertical tangent. The function \(q(y)\), taken as a function of the point \((x, y)\) on the open set of points of the plane with \(-5 < y < 5\), has the partial derivative zero with respect to \(x\) and the partial derivative \(q'(y)\) with respect to \(y\). Both are continuous, because two points of the plane differ in the coordinate \(y\) by at most their distance. The same holds for \(-q(y)\), for \(\pm q(z)\) and for the constant functions \(\pm 3\). All three pieces are therefore bodies between graphs. The tangent at the point \(t = 3\) has the slope \(q'(3) = -3/4\). The cut at \(y = \pm 3\) makes sure that each piece uses the function \(q\) only on the interval \([-4, 4]\), where its derivative is at most \(4/3\) in absolute value, at \(t = \pm 4\), at the point \((4, 3)\) and its mirror image. Without the cut the slope would grow beyond every bound near the edge, as with the segment to the end point. In the piece \(D\) the lids \(y = 3\) and \(y = q(z)\) meet at \(z = \pm 4\) at the corners of the cuts, because \(q(\pm 4) = 3\), which the definition allows.

The pieces touch only at the cuts. A point that lies in \(C\) and in \(D\) has \(y \le 3\) and \(y \ge 3\), so \(y = 3\), and lies on the rectangle \(0 \le x \le L\), \(-4 \le z \le 4\) in the plane \(y = 3\). An interior point of the piece \(C\), however, has \(y < 3\). A ball around it lies in \(C\), where \(y \le 3\) (section 1.15.6), and if the point had \(y = 3\), the ball would contain points with \(y > 3\). So no interior point of the piece \(C\) lies in \(D\), and likewise no interior point of the piece \(D\) lies in \(C\). The same holds for the pieces \(C\) and \(E\), while the pieces \(D\) and \(E\) have no common points.

Finally let us show that a body between graphs is closed and bounded. We will need this, because we will use the theorem on uniform continuity 4.6 on it. Closed means that the body contains its surface: the inequalities in (4.10) are not strict, so the lids and the side faces belong to the body. What would go wrong without it? With strict inequalities \(g < z < h\) the lids do not belong to the set. The points at the heights \(h - 1/n\) above one point of the shadow, for every \(n\) with \(1/n < h - g\), would lie in the set, but their limit on the top lid would not, and the continuous function \(1/(h - z)\), which has the values \(1, 2, 3, \dots\) at them, would grow beyond every bound on such a set. On a closed and bounded set this cannot happen to a continuous function.

Lemma 4.17 A body between two graphs is closed and bounded (telo med grafoma je zaprto in omejeno)

The body between graphs \(V\) of definition 4.15 is a closed and bounded set of points (definition 1.75).

Proof

We must show that the limit of a convergent sequence of points of \(V\) lies in \(V\) and that all points of \(V\) are at most some number away from the origin.

  1. The functions \(g\) and \(h\) are continuous at every point of \(U\) by lemma 1.92, that a continuously differentiable function is continuous. The lemma speaks of functions of three variables, but its proof with theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step holds likewise for functions of two variables.
  2. Let the sequence of points \(P_{\mathrm{n}} = (x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}, z_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(V\) converge to the point \(P = (x, y, z)\). By lemma 1.67 on convergence coordinate by coordinate, \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \to x\), \(y_{\mathrm{n}} \to y\) and \(z_{\mathrm{n}} \to z\).
  3. From \(a \le x_{\mathrm{n}} \le b\) and \(c \le y_{\mathrm{n}} \le d\), by lemma 1.49 that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 2, it follows that \(a \le x \le b\) and \(c \le y \le d\). The point \((x, y)\) lies in the shadow \(R\).
  4. We view the point \((x, y)\) of the plane as the point \((x, y, 0)\) of space, which leaves the distances between points unchanged. From \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \to x\) and \(y_{\mathrm{n}} \to y\), by lemma 1.67 in the other direction, the points \((x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge to \((x, y)\), and \(g\) is continuous at \((x, y)\). By lemma 1.69 on continuity through sequences of points, applied on the set of points \((x, y, 0)\) with \((x, y) \in U\), therefore, \(g(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}) \to g(x, y)\). Likewise \(h(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}) \to h(x, y)\).
  5. From \(g(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}) \le z_{\mathrm{n}} \le h(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}})\), by lemma 1.49, item 1, it follows that \(g(x, y) \le z \le h(x, y)\). The point \(P\) lies on the vertical segment above \((x, y)\), between the lids or on one of them, hence in \(V\), which is therefore closed.
  6. Boundedness. The rectangle \(R\), seen as the set of points \((x, y, 0)\) of space, is closed and bounded (section 4.2.2). The functions \(g\) and \(h\) are continuous on it, so by theorem 1.79, the extreme value theorem in space, there are numbers \(m\) and \(M\) with \(m \le g\) and \(h \le M\) on \(R\): the lids lie between two horizontal planes. For every point of \(V\) we therefore have \(|z| \le |m| + |M|\), and also \(|x| \le |a| + |b|\) and \(|y| \le |c| + |d|\). As for the box in section 1.13.4, \(|\overrightarrow{OP}|\) is at most the root of the sum of the squares of these three bounds.

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. The proof follows the examples of the box and the bar in section 1.13.4.

4.2.7 Differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter

Let us recall the proof of the divergence theorem for a box (theorem 4.14). We wrote the integral of the term \(\partial f/\partial x\) as an iterated integral whose inner integral is over \(x\), which we were allowed to do by theorem 4.9. The fundamental theorem of calculus then turned the integral along every segment parallel to the axis \(x\) into the difference of the values on the faces \(x = a_1\) and \(x = b_1\). For a body between graphs we can treat the term \(\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) in this way, because the segments parallel to the axis \(z\) are exactly the chords from the bottom to the top lid. The terms \(\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\) and \(\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y\), however, are inside the inner integral over \(z\), whose limits \(g(x, y)\) and \(h(x, y)\) depend on \(x\) and \(y\). So we must bring the derivative with respect to \(x\) or \(y\) out of the integral. In doing so both the integrand and the limits change, and the motion of the limits will give terms on the lids. This section says how such an integral changes: first, that it changes continuously, which we need for the iterated integral to exist at all, and then how to differentiate it.

The inner integral of a body between graphs is the function

\[F(x, y) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z ,\]

whose input is a point \((x, y)\) of the shadow and whose output is a number. When the point moves a little, the integrand changes a little, and the two limits move a little. The uniform continuity of the function \(f\) bounds the change of the integrand, as in lemma 4.7. The motion of the limits adds or removes a short piece of the interval, on which \(f\) is bounded, so its contribution is small too.

Let us draw this (figure 4.60, left) with the axis \(z\) vertical, the shadow \(R\) is the horizontal line below it. Above the point \(P\) of the shadow we integrate along the blackwhite segment from \(g\) to \(h\), above the nearby point \(P'\) along the blue one from \(g'\) to \(h'\). On the common part from \(z_1\) to \(z_2\) we integrate both times, and only the integrands differ. What remains are the pieces at the ends, here the bottom piece of the blackwhite segment and the top piece of the blue one. Each is as long as the limit has moved. If the limits move by more than the length of the segment, there is no common part (figure 4.60, right): the blackwhite segment lies wholly below the blue one. The segments themselves are then shorter than the motions of the limits, the blackwhite one than the motion of the lower limit \(g' - g\), the blue one than the motion of the upper limit \(h' - h\).

The lemma that follows rests on two hypotheses, and the figure says where they enter. The first is the continuity of the limits \(g\) and \(h\), which definition 4.15 requires: because of it the pieces at the ends are short when \(P'\) is close to \(P\). If the top lid had a step \(1\) mm high, then for \(f = 1\) the top piece would be \(1\) mm long however close \(P'\) is, and \(F\) would jump by \(1\) mm. The second is the boundedness of the function \(f\), which follows from continuity on a closed and bounded body: the contribution of a piece is at most the bound \(M\) times its length. On a body without its lids this conclusion fails, because there a continuous function can be unbounded (section 4.2.6).

Lemma 4.18 Continuity of an integral with variable limits (zveznost integrala s spremenljivima mejama)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15) and \(f\) a function that is continuous on \(V\). Then for every point \((x, y) \in R\) the integral

\[F(x, y) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\]

exists, and for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|F(x', y') - F(x, y)| < \eta\) for all points \((x, y), (x', y') \in R\) with \((x' - x)^2 + (y' - y)^2 < \delta^2\).

Proof

We must show that the integral exists and that it changes little when the point moves a little. We split the intervals of integration at two nearby points into a common part and pieces at the ends.

  1. Existence. For fixed \(x\) and \(y\) the function \(z \mapsto f(x, y, z)\) is continuous on \([g(x, y), h(x, y)]\), the segment over the point \(P = (x, y)\), because the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x, y, z')\) is \(|z - z'|\). By theorem 3.53 it is integrable. If \(g(x, y) = h(x, y)\), the integral is zero by the convention of definition 3.49.
  2. Bounds. The body \(V\) is closed and bounded by lemma 4.17, so by theorem 1.79 there is a number \(M > 0\) with \(|f| \le M\) on \(V\). By the same theorem, applied to the continuous function \(h - g\) on \(R\), there is a number \(H > 0\) with \(h - g \le H\) on \(R\): no segment is longer than \(H\).
  3. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|f(Q) - f(Q')| < \eta/(2H)\) for any two points \(Q, Q' \in V\) with \(|QQ'| < \delta_1\). By the same theorem on \(R\) there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|g(P') - g(P)| < \eta/(4M)\) and \(|h(P') - h(P)| < \eta/(4M)\) for any two points \(P, P' \in R\) with \(|PP'| < \delta_2\), so that each piece at an end is shorter than \(\eta/(4M)\). For \(\delta\) we take the smaller of the numbers \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\).
  4. Let \(P = (x, y)\) and \(P' = (x', y')\) be points of \(R\) with \(|PP'| < \delta\). We write \(g = g(P)\), \(h = h(P)\), \(g' = g(P')\) and \(h' = h(P')\), and \(z_1 = \max\{g, g'\}\) and \(z_2 = \min\{h, h'\}\). In figure 4.60 these are the segment above \(P\), the segment above \(P'\) and the ends of the common part. For short we also write \(f(P, z)\) for \(f(x, y, z)\).
  5. The case \(z_1 \le z_2\), when the intervals \([g, h]\) and \([g', h']\) overlap (figure 4.60, left). The interval \([g, h]\) splits into \([g, z_1]\), \([z_1, z_2]\) and \([z_2, h]\), and by additivity (lemma 3.54, item 2, with the convention for pieces of length zero) \(F(P)\) is the sum of the integrals over these three pieces. Likewise \(F(P')\) splits over \([g', z_1]\), \([z_1, z_2]\) and \([z_2, h']\). Hence
    \[\begin{aligned} F(P') - F(P) = {} & \int_{\mathrm{z}_1}^{z_2} \big(f(P', z) - f(P, z)\big)\,\mathrm{d}z \\ & + \int_{\mathrm{g}'}^{z_1} f(P', z)\,\mathrm{d}z + \int_{\mathrm{z}_2}^{h'} f(P', z)\,\mathrm{d}z \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{z_1} f(P, z)\,\mathrm{d}z - \int_{\mathrm{z}_2}^{h} f(P, z)\,\mathrm{d}z . \end{aligned}\]
  6. The points \((P, z)\) and \((P', z)\) with \(z_1 \le z \le z_2\) lie in \(V\) and are a distance \(|PP'| < \delta_1\) apart, so the first integrand, the one on the common part, is less than \(\eta/(2H)\) in absolute value. By the bound (lemma 3.54, item 3) the first integral is at most \(\eta\,(z_2 - z_1)/(2H) \le \eta/2\) in absolute value, because \(z_2 - z_1 \le h - g \le H\).
  7. By the bound, the other four integrals, over the pieces at the ends, are at most \(M\) times the length of the interval in absolute value. Of the lengths \(z_1 - g\) and \(z_1 - g'\) one is zero and the other \(|g' - g|\), because \(z_1\) is the larger of the numbers \(g\) and \(g'\). In the figure \(z_1 = g'\), so the piece \([g', z_1]\) has length zero and the piece \([g, z_1]\) has length \(g' - g\). Likewise, of the lengths \(h - z_2\) and \(h' - z_2\) one is zero and the other \(|h' - h|\). The sum of the four is therefore at most \(M\,(|g' - g| + |h' - h|) < M \cdot 2\eta/(4M) = \eta/2\).
  8. The case \(z_1 > z_2\), when the intervals do not overlap (figure 4.60, right). Since \(g \le h\) and \(g' \le h'\), then \(g' > h\) or \(g > h'\). Let \(g' > h\), the other case is the same with the two points exchanged. Then \(h - g < g' - g\) and \(h' - g' < h' - h\). By the bound \(|F(P)| \le M\,(h - g)\) and \(|F(P')| \le M\,(h' - g')\), so \(|F(P') - F(P)| \le |F(P')| + |F(P)| < M\,(|g' - g| + |h' - h|) < \eta/2\).
  9. In both cases, when the segments overlap and when they do not, by the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|F(P') - F(P)| < \eta/2 + \eta/2 = \eta\).

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. For constant limits it is LEBL1 Proposition 7.5.12 (PDF p. 292), as lemma 4.7.

The lemma has extended item 1 of lemma 4.7 to variable limits. With it the iterated integral of the function \(f\) in the order \(z\), \(y\), \(x\) will exist in section 4.2.8. Two devices were the key: uniform continuity, which bounded the change of the integrand for all \(z\) of the common part at once, and the boundedness of the function \(f\), which bounded the contribution of the pieces at the ends.

Now the derivative. Take a function of two variables \(f(t, s)\) and its integral over \(t\) whose limits depend on \(s\):

\[G(s) = \int_{\varphi(\mathrm{s})}^{\psi(s)} f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t .\]

We chose the letters \(t\) and \(s\) so that they do not get mixed up with the coordinates. In the proof of the theorem, \(t\) will be the coordinate \(z\), and \(s\) will be \(y\) or \(x\). When \(s\) increases by \(k\), \(G\) changes for three reasons (figure 4.61, left). The integrand changes over the whole interval, by about \(k\,\partial f/\partial s\). The upper limit moves by about \(\psi'(s)\,k\), and the interval gains a piece of this length, on which the integrand is about \(f(\psi(s), s)\). The lower limit moves by about \(\varphi'(s)\,k\), and the interval loses a piece with the integrand about \(f(\varphi(s), s)\). Divided by \(k\), this gives the three terms of the derivative. The same happens on the cross section of the bar (figure 4.61, right, with the axes \(y\) and \(z\)): the chord at \(y = 3\) mm runs from \(z = -4\) to \(z = 4\), the chord at a larger \(y\) is shorter and loses a piece at each end, because the limits \(\pm q(y)\) approach the axis \(y\).

The proof will do this precisely, in two parts (figure 4.62). On the left is the part with constant limits. The function \(f\) is given on the rectangle with sides from \(\alpha\) to \(\beta\) and from \(c\) to \(d\) in the plane of the variables \(t\) and \(s\). At \(s\) we integrate along the blackwhite segment, at \(s + k\) along the blue one. Above every \(t\) the integrand changes from its value at the blackwhite dot to its value at the blue one. By the mean value theorem this change equals \(k\) times the derivative \(\partial f/\partial s\) at some intermediate point \(\sigma_{\mathrm{t}}\). We want the derivative on the blackwhite segment, but the intermediate point is somewhere else for every \(t\). What helps is the band around the blackwhite segment with half height \(\delta_1\): in it the derivative \(\partial f/\partial s\) differs from its value on the blackwhite segment by less than the chosen error, and it does so for all \(t\) at once. On the right one end of the segment is magnified, for variable limits. The limit \(\chi\), which is \(\varphi\) or \(\psi\), passes through the point \((w, s)\) and, when \(s\) increases by \(k\), through the point \((w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k)\). The segment at \(s + k\) therefore gains the piece from \(w\) to \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\). Every point \((t, s + k)\) of this piece lies in the disc of radius \(\delta_2\) around \((w, s)\), in which \(f\) differs from \(f(w, s)\) by less than the chosen error. The integral over the piece is therefore about \(f(w, s)\) times the length of the piece \(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w\).

The lemma has three hypotheses, and each enters at its own place. The first is the continuity of the functions \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\) on the whole closed rectangle. It gives uniform continuity, that is one band for all \(t\) at once. Without it every \(t\) would have its own band, the bands could be arbitrarily narrow, and we could not bound the error along the whole segment by one number.

What happens when the derivative \(\partial f/\partial s\) is not continuous is shown by the function

\[f(t, s) = \frac{t\,s^2}{(s + t^2)^2} \ \text{for}\ s > 0 , \qquad f(t, s) = 0 \ \text{for}\ s \le 0\]

on the rectangle \([0, 1] \times [-1, 1]\) (figure 4.63). The function \(f\) is continuous also at \(s = 0\), because \(0 \le f(t, s) \le t\,s/(s + t^2) \le \sqrt{s}/2\) for \(s > 0\), since \(s + t^2 \ge s\) and \(s + t^2 - 2t\sqrt{s} = (t - \sqrt{s})^2 \ge 0\). For every \(t\) it is differentiable with respect to \(s\), at \(s = 0\) with the derivative \(0\), because \(0 \le f(t, s)/s \le s/t^3\) for \(t > 0\) and \(f(0, s) = 0\). At \(s = 0\) the derivative \(\partial f/\partial s\) is therefore zero for all \(t\), and the integral of the derivative is \(0\). For \(s > 0\), however, the derivative \(\partial f/\partial s = 2t^3 s/(s + t^2)^3\) is a narrow spike with its peak at \(t = \sqrt{s}\), of height \(1/(4\sqrt{s})\). At \(s = 0{,}04\) the peak is \(1{,}25\) high, at \(s = 0{,}01\) it is \(2{,}5\) high and at \(s = 0{,}0025\) it is \(5\) high. As \(s\) goes to zero, the spike gets narrower and moves toward \(t = 0\), while the area under it approaches \(1/2\), for these three spikes it measures \(0{,}46\), \(0{,}49\) and \(0{,}50\) (SymPy). So the derivative is not continuous near \((0, 0)\), and the band around \(s = 0\) would narrow without end toward \(t = 0\). The integral is \(G(s) = s/(2(1 + s))\) for \(s > 0\) and \(G(s) = 0\) for \(s \le 0\) (SymPy). The graph of \(G\) has at \(0\) the slope \(1/2\) on the right and the slope \(0\) on the left. So \(G'(0)\) does not exist, while the integral of the derivative would give \(0\).

The second is the differentiability of the limits at the point \(s_0\), which says how fast the end of the segment moves. Where a limit does not have it, \(G\) in general has none either (figure 4.64). With \(f = 1\), \(\varphi(s) = 0\) and \(\psi(s) = 1 + |s - 3|\) \(G(s)\) is just the length of the segment, \(G(s) = 1 + |s - 3|\). The difference quotient at \(s_0 = 3\) is \(+1\) for \(k > 0\) and \(-1\) for \(k < 0\), so there is no limit. A kink in a limit can, however, cancel, for example when the integrand is zero at the limit. With \(f(t, s) = t\), \(\varphi(s) = 0\) and \(\psi(s) = |s - 3|\) the segment at \(s\) near \(3\) gains or loses a piece where the integrand \(t\) is almost zero. Then \(G(s) = (s - 3)^2/2\), the difference quotients at \(k = 0{,}1\) and \(k = -0{,}1\) are \(0{,}05\) and \(-0{,}05\), and \(G'(3) = 0\), although \(\psi\) has no derivative at \(3\). For the round bar the limit \(q(y)\) has no derivative at the edge of the cross section, at \(y = \pm 5\) mm, because the tangent is vertical there, and this is why the piece \(C\) reaches only to \(y = \pm 3\) mm.

The third is that the limits stay between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), because \(f\) is given only on the rectangle. This is why for the round bar at the end of the section we will take the rectangle \([-5, 5] \times [2, 4]\) in millimetres. With \([-4, 4] \times [2, 4]\) the chord of the cross section at \(y = 2\) mm would reach to \(z = \pm q(2) = \pm 4{,}58\) mm, beyond the edge of the rectangle, where \(f\) is not given, and the lemma would say nothing about the integral along it.

Lemma 4.19 Differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter (odvod integrala po parametru)

Let \(\alpha < \beta\) and \(c < d\) be numbers, and let \(f\) be a function whose input is two numbers \(t\) and \(s\) from the rectangle \([\alpha, \beta] \times [c, d]\) and whose output is a number \(f(t, s)\). For every \(t \in [\alpha, \beta]\) let the function \(\sigma \mapsto f(t, \sigma)\) be differentiable at every point of the interval \([c, d]\), at the endpoints \(c\) and \(d\) with a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9). We denote its derivative at the point \(s\) by \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\), like the partial derivative (definition 1.26), which is the derivative with the other variable held fixed. Let the functions \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\) be continuous on this rectangle.

  1. The function
    \[G(s) = \int_\alpha^\beta f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\]
    is differentiable at every point \(s \in (c, d)\), its derivative is
    \[G'(s) = \int_\alpha^\beta \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{4.12}\]
    and \(G'\) is continuous on \((c, d)\).
  2. Let \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) be functions on \([c, d]\) with \(\alpha \le \varphi(s) \le \psi(s) \le \beta\) for every \(s \in [c, d]\), which are differentiable at the point \(s_0 \in (c, d)\). Then the function
    \[G(s) = \int_{\varphi(\mathrm{s})}^{\psi(s)} f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\]
    is differentiable at \(s_0\), and
    \[\begin{aligned} G'(s_0) = {} & \int_{\varphi(\mathrm{s}_0)}^{\psi(s_0)} \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s_0)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & + f\big(\psi(s_0), s_0\big)\,\psi'(s_0) - f\big(\varphi(s_0), s_0\big)\,\varphi'(s_0) . \end{aligned} \tag{4.13}\]
Proof

We must show both items. For the first we write the change of the integrand with the mean value theorem, with the derivative at an intermediate point, and bound it uniformly for all \(t\), with one band. For the second we split the change of the function \(G\) into the change of the integrand, which the first item handles, and the pieces at the ends.

1. Constant limits.

  1. For every \(s \in [c, d]\) the functions \(t \mapsto f(t, s)\) and \(t \mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\) are continuous on \([\alpha, \beta]\), the horizontal segment of the rectangle at height \(s\), because the distance between the points \((t, s)\) and \((t', s)\) is \(|t - t'|\). By theorem 3.53 they are integrable, so the numbers \(G(s)\) and \(I(s) = \int_\alpha^\beta \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\) exist.
  2. The rectangle is closed and bounded (section 4.2.2). We choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(\big|\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t', s') - \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\big| < \eta/(2(\beta - \alpha))\) for any two points of the rectangle less than \(\delta_1\) apart (in figure 4.62, left, the band of this half height around \(s\)).
  3. Let \(s \in (c, d)\) and let \(\delta\) be the smallest of the numbers \(\delta_1\), \(s - c\) and \(d - s\). Let \(0 < |k| < \delta\), so that \(s + k\) lies in \((c, d)\).
  4. Let \(t \in [\alpha, \beta]\). The function \(\sigma \mapsto f(t, \sigma)\) is continuous on \([c, d]\), because \(f\) is continuous on the rectangle and the distance between the points \((t, \sigma)\) and \((t, \sigma')\) is \(|\sigma - \sigma'|\), as in step 1. By hypothesis it is differentiable at every point of \([c, d]\), with the derivative \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, \sigma)\). By step 3 the closed interval between \(s\) and \(s + k\) lies in \((c, d)\). By the mean value theorem 1.85 there is a number \(\sigma_{\mathrm{t}}\) between \(s\) and \(s + k\) such that
    \[f(t, s + k) - f(t, s) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, \sigma_{\mathrm{t}})\,k .\]
  5. The point \((t, \sigma_{\mathrm{t}})\) is less than \(|k| < \delta_1\) away from \((t, s)\), so it lies in the band, so by step 2
    \[\begin{aligned} & \Big| f(t, s + k) - f(t, s) - k\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s) \Big| \\ & \quad = |k|\,\Big| \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, \sigma_{\mathrm{t}}) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s) \Big| \le \frac{\eta\,|k|}{2(\beta - \alpha)} \end{aligned}\]
    for every \(t \in [\alpha, \beta]\).
  6. The function inside the absolute value on the left is a continuous function of \(t\) (step 1 and corollary 1.65). By linearity (lemma 3.54, item 1) its integral is \(G(s + k) - G(s) - k\,I(s)\), where \(G(s + k)\) is the integral over the blue segment and \(G(s)\) the one over the blackwhite segment, and by the bound (item 3 of the same lemma) this is at most \(\eta\,|k|/2\) in absolute value. We divide by \(|k|\):
    \[\Big| \frac{G(s + k) - G(s)}{k} - I(s) \Big| \le \frac{\eta}{2} < \eta .\]
  7. The error \(\eta\) was arbitrary, so the band can be arbitrarily narrow, and by the definition of the derivative 1.9 and of the limit 1.5, \(G'(s) = I(s)\).
  8. Continuity of the derivative. For \(s, s' \in (c, d)\) with \(|s' - s| < \delta_1\), when the segment at height \(s'\) lies in the band around \(s\), by step 2 and the bound, \(|I(s') - I(s)| \le (\beta - \alpha) \cdot \eta/(2(\beta - \alpha)) < \eta\). The function \(G' = I\) is therefore continuous at every point of \((c, d)\).

2. Variable limits.

  1. For \(w \in [\alpha, \beta]\) and \(\sigma \in [c, d]\) let \(K(w, \sigma) = \int_\alpha^w f(t, \sigma)\,\mathrm{d}t\), which for \(w = \alpha\) is zero by the convention of definition 3.49. This is the integral from the left edge of the rectangle to the point \(w\), and the segment between the limits is the difference of two such pieces. By additivity (lemma 3.54, item 2, with the same convention for pieces of length zero), for every \(\sigma \in [c, d]\)
    \[G(\sigma) = K\big(\psi(\sigma), \sigma\big) - K\big(\varphi(\sigma), \sigma\big) .\]
  2. We write \(s = s_0\) and let \(0 < |k|\), where \(|k|\) is smaller than the numbers \(s - c\) and \(d - s\). We also write \(\varphi = \varphi(s)\), \(\psi = \psi(s)\), \(\varphi_{\mathrm{k}} = \varphi(s + k)\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}} = \psi(s + k)\). By step 1, adding and subtracting \(K(\psi, s + k) - K(\varphi, s + k)\),
    \[\begin{aligned} G(s + k) - G(s) = {} & \big[K(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(\psi, s + k)\big] \\ & - \big[K(\varphi_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(\varphi, s + k)\big] \\ & + \int_{\varphi}^{\psi} \big(f(t, s + k) - f(t, s)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t . \end{aligned}\]
    The first bracket is the integral over the piece that the segment gains at the upper limit, the second over the piece it loses at the lower one, and the last term is the change of the integrand above the original segment. By additivity and linearity the last term equals \(K(\psi, s + k) - K(\varphi, s + k) - K(\psi, s) + K(\varphi, s)\).
  3. The last term, the change of the integrand over the original segment, divided by \(k\) approaches \(\int_\varphi^\psi \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\). If \(\varphi < \psi\), this is the first item, applied on the rectangle \([\varphi, \psi] \times [c, d]\), which lies in \([\alpha, \beta] \times [c, d]\). If \(\varphi = \psi\), both sides are zero.
  4. The pieces at the ends. Let \(\chi\) be one of the functions \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\), \(w = \chi(s)\) and \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \chi(s + k)\) (figure 4.62, right). We must show that \(\big(K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k)\big)/k\) approaches \(f(w, s)\,\chi'(s)\). We choose an error \(\eta\) with \(0 < \eta \le 1\). Larger errors need not be considered, because the band that fits the error \(1\) fits them. Let \(\eta' = \eta/\big(|\chi'(s)| + 1 + |f(w, s)|\big)\), which is not larger than \(1\). The function \(f\) is continuous at the point \((w, s)\), so there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|f(t, \sigma) - f(w, s)| < \eta'\) for the points \((t, \sigma)\) of the rectangle less than \(\delta_2\) away from \((w, s)\). The function \(\chi\) is differentiable at \(s\), hence continuous there (lemma 1.80), and there is a \(\delta_3 > 0\) such that \(|w_{\mathrm{k}} - w| < \delta_2/2\) for \(|k| < \delta_3\).
  5. Let \(|k|\) also be smaller than \(\delta_3\) and than \(\delta_2/2\). For every \(t\) between \(w\) and \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\) the distance between the points \((t, s + k)\) and \((w, s)\) is \(\sqrt{(t - w)^2 + k^2}\). It is not larger than \(|t - w| + |k|\), because the square of this sum is \((t - w)^2 + 2\,|t - w|\,|k| + k^2\) (lemma 1.29), so it is smaller than \(\delta_2/2 + \delta_2/2 = \delta_2\). Hence \(f(w, s) - \eta' < f(t, s + k) < f(w, s) + \eta'\).
  6. If \(w_{\mathrm{k}} > w\), then by additivity \(K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k) = \int_{\mathrm{w}}^{w_{\mathrm{k}}} f(t, s + k)\,\mathrm{d}t\), the integral over the gained piece. By the bound and step 5 this number lies between \((f(w, s) - \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\) and \((f(w, s) + \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\). If \(w_{\mathrm{k}} < w\), the difference is \(-\int_{\mathrm{w}_\mathrm{k}}^{w} f(t, s + k)\,\mathrm{d}t\) and lies between \((f(w, s) + \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\) and \((f(w, s) - \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\). If \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = w\), it is zero. In all three cases
    \[\big| K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k) - f(w, s)\,(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w) \big| \le \eta'\,|w_{\mathrm{k}} - w| .\]
  7. The difference quotient \((w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)/k\) of the function \(\chi\) at \(s\) converges to \(\chi'(s)\). By the definition of the limit 1.5 with the error \(\eta'\), for small enough \(|k|\) the difference \(|(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)/k - \chi'(s)|\) is therefore smaller than \(\eta'\), and since \(\eta' \le 1\), \(|w_{\mathrm{k}} - w|/|k| < |\chi'(s)| + 1\). We divide the inequality of step 6 by \(|k|\) and use the triangle inequality for numbers:
    \[\begin{aligned} \Big| \frac{K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k)}{k} - f(w, s)\,\chi'(s) \Big| &< \eta'\,\big(|\chi'(s)| + 1\big) \\ &\quad + |f(w, s)|\,\eta' . \end{aligned}\]
    By the choice of the number \(\eta'\) in step 4 the right side equals \(\eta\). The quotient therefore approaches \(f(w, s)\,\chi'(s)\).
  8. By step 2, \((G(s + k) - G(s))/k\) is a sum of three quotients. By step 7 the first, from the piece gained, approaches \(f(\psi, s)\,\psi'(s)\), the second, from the piece lost, with the minus sign \(-f(\varphi, s)\,\varphi'(s)\), and by step 3 the third, from the change of the integrand, \(\int_\varphi^\psi \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\,\mathrm{d}t\). For the error \(\eta\) we take \(|k|\) so small that each of the three quotients is less than \(\eta/3\) away from its limit. By the triangle inequality, \((G(s + k) - G(s))/k\) is then less than \(\eta\) away from the sum of the limits, which is the right side of (4.13).

Source: LEBL2 Theorem 9.1.1 (PDF pp. 65-66) for item 1, where \(f\) is given only on the rectangle. The source does not have item 2, and its proof is not from the sources.

The lemma says what the figure predicted. The first item says that with constant limits we may differentiate under the integral sign: the segment keeps its length, only the integrand on it changes. The second adds two terms contributed by the moving limits: the value of the integrand at the limit, times the speed at which the limit moves. The proof used devices we know: the mean value theorem, as in the first item of the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55, uniform continuity, as in theorem 3.53, and the bound of the integral over a short piece, as in the second item of the fundamental theorem of calculus. In the interior points of the interval the derivative in this second item even follows from the second item of the lemma. With the integrand \(f(t, s) = f(t)\), which does not depend on \(s\), the constant lower limit \(\varphi(s) = \alpha\) and the upper limit \(\psi(s) = s\) on \([c, d] = [\alpha, \beta]\), the second item gives \(G'(s) = 0 + f(s) \cdot 1 - f(\alpha) \cdot 0 = f(s)\) for every \(s \in (\alpha, \beta)\). The first term is zero because \(\partial f/\partial s = 0\), the one is the derivative \(\psi'(s)\), and the zero is the derivative \(\varphi'(s)\) of the constant limit. At the endpoints \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) the lemma says nothing, because it requires \(s_0 \in (c, d)\), and the one-sided derivatives at the endpoints come only from the fundamental theorem of calculus.

Let us test the second item on the cross section of the round bar (figure 4.61, right). The square of the distance of the point \((y, z)\) of the cross section from the axis of the bar is \(y^2 + z^2\). At every \(y\) we integrate it along the chord from \(z = -q(y)\) to \(z = q(y)\):

\[\Theta(y) = \int_{-\mathrm{q}(\mathrm{y})}^{q(y)} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}z .\]

We will meet such an integral in section 4.2.12, because the downward displacement of the hanging bar has the term \(-0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\). Here \(t = z\), \(s = y\), \(f(z, y) = y^2 + z^2\), \(\varphi = -q\) and \(\psi = q\). For the rectangle we take \([-5, 5] \times [2, 4]\) in millimetres. On it \(f\) is a polynomial with the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial y = 2y\), and the limits \(\pm q(y)\) lie in \([-5, 5]\). At \(y = 3\) mm we have \(q(3) = 4\) mm and by (4.11) \(q'(3) = -3/4\), so \(\varphi'(3) = 3/4\). By (4.13)

\[\begin{aligned} \Theta'(3) &= \int_{-4}^{4} 2 \cdot 3\,\mathrm{d}z + (9 + 16) \cdot \Big(-\frac34\Big) - (9 + 16) \cdot \frac34 \\ &= 48 - 18{,}75 - 18{,}75 = 10{,}5\ \text{mm}^2 . \end{aligned}\]

The first term says that the integrand grows, because \(y^2\) grows with \(y\). The other two say that the chord gets shorter. When \(y\) increases by a small step, say \(0{,}01\) mm, each end of the chord moves toward the axis \(y\) by about \(0{,}75\) times as much, \(0{,}0075\) mm, at a place where the integrand is \(y^2 + q(y)^2 = r^2 = 25\ \text{mm}^2\), because the end of the chord lies on the circle. In the figure the step is enlarged to \(0{,}8\) mm, so that the lost pieces can be seen. Let us magnify the upper end of the chord (figure 4.65, left). The end of the chord at \(y = 3\) mm is the point \((3, 4)\) on the circle, the chord at \(y = 3{,}8\) mm is the step \(0{,}8\) mm to the right of it. The tangent to the circle at the point \((3, 4)\) has the slope \(q'(3) = -3/4\). Along the tangent the end of the chord would drop by \(0{,}75 \cdot 0{,}8 = 0{,}6\) mm, along the circle it drops by \(0{,}75\) mm, because the circle lies below the tangent and moves ever further away from it. At so large a step the curvature of the circle already shows. The same holds for the lower end. At the step \(0{,}01\) mm (figure 4.65, right) the piece is \(0{,}00752\) mm long and differs from the prediction \(0{,}0075\) mm by only \(0{,}00002\) mm, so the tangent and the circle cannot be told apart in the figure. Let us check without the lemma. By the fundamental theorem of calculus with the function \(y^2 z + z^3/3\), whose derivative with respect to \(z\) is \(y^2 + z^2\), we get \(\Theta(y) = 2\,q(y)\,y^2 + \tfrac23\,q(y)^3\), and \(\Theta(3) = 72 + 42{,}667 = 114{,}667\ \text{mm}^3\). With SymPy we computed \(\Theta(3{,}01) = 114{,}771\ \text{mm}^3\) and the difference quotient \((\Theta(3{,}01) - \Theta(3))/0{,}01 = 10{,}44\) mm², and with the step \(0{,}001\) mm \(10{,}49\) mm². The quotients approach \(10{,}5\) mm².

4.2.8 Integral over a body between two graphs

Now we can define the integral of a function over a body between graphs as the integral over a box, with iterated integrals in the order \(z\), \(y\), \(x\): first along the chord above a point of the shadow, then over the shadow \(R\). The inner integral over \(z\) exists by lemma 4.18 and has the property of item 1 of lemma 4.7. By item 2 of that lemma the middle integral over \(y\) therefore exists and is a continuous function of \(x\), and the outer integral exists by theorem 3.53. For a body with exchanged roles of the coordinates, as for the piece \(D\) of the round bar, where \(y\) runs between the graphs, the argument is the same, because the proofs of both lemmas use only which coordinate runs between the graphs, not its name.

Definition 4.20 Integral over a body between two graphs (integral po telesu med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15) and \(f\) a function that is continuous on \(V\). The integral of the function \(f\) over the body \(V\) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z \bigg) \mathrm{d}y \bigg) \mathrm{d}x . \tag{4.14}\]

For a body with exchanged roles of the coordinates the inner integral is over the coordinate that runs between the graphs, and the middle and the outer one are over the coordinates of the rectangle, in the order given by the description of the body.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.3, (3) (PDF p. 453), for the double integral over a region between two curves, and §10.7 (PDF pp. 478-479), where the triple integral is defined by a subdivision into small boxes and computed by three successive integrations. LEBL2 Proposition 10.5.8 (PDF p. 126) states that the integral of the general theory over a region between two graphs in the plane equals the iterated integral, and leaves the proof to the reader. The definition by the iterated integral is not from the sources.

The round bar is not described by a single body between graphs but by three pieces. We define the integral over it as the sum of the integrals over the pieces.

Definition 4.21 Body cut into pieces (telo, razrezano na kose)

Let \(V\) be a set of points that is the union of the bodies between graphs \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\) (definition 4.15), each with its own naming of the axes, and let no interior point of any of them lie in another one. We then say that \(V\) is cut into pieces (razrezano na kose) \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\). The integral of a continuous function \(f\) over a body cut in this way is the sum of the integrals over the pieces (definition 4.20),

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \int_{\mathrm{V}_\mathrm{k}} f\,\mathrm{d}V .\]

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF p. 482) cuts a body by auxiliary surfaces into pieces, for which it proves the divergence theorem separately. The definition of the integral as a sum over the pieces is not from the sources.

Why do we require that no interior point of a piece lies in another piece? So that no part of the body is counted twice. Take the cube \(K = [0, 1] \times [0, 1] \times [0, 1]\), with lengths in millimetres, and look at it in figure 4.66 along the axis \(y\), with the axis \(x\) to the right and the axis \(z\) upward. On the left the plane \(x = 1/2\) cuts it into the boxes \(V_1\) and \(V_2\), each with volume \(1/2\ \text{mm}^3\) (lemma 4.10, item 2). They share only the points of the plane of the cut. Such a point is an interior point of neither box, because every ball around it contains points with \(x > 1/2\), which are not in \(V_1\), and points with \(x < 1/2\), which are not in \(V_2\). The condition holds, and the sum of the integrals of the function \(1\) over the pieces is \(1/2 + 1/2 = 1\ \text{mm}^3\), the volume of the cube.

On the right take the boxes \(V_1 = [0, 2/3] \times [0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) and \(V_2 = [1/3, 1] \times [0, 1] \times [0, 1]\). Their union is again \(K\). But the point \(P = (1/2, 1/2, 1/2)\) is an interior point of the box \(V_1\), because the ball of radius \(1/10\) mm around it lies in \(V_1\), and it also lies in \(V_2\). The condition is violated. The sum of the integrals of the function \(1\) over the pieces is \(2/3 + 2/3 = 4/3\ \text{mm}^3\) instead of \(1\ \text{mm}^3\), because the slab \(1/3 \le x \le 2/3\) with volume \(1/3\ \text{mm}^3\) is counted twice, in \(V_1\) and in \(V_2\).

The definition agrees with the ones we already have. A box is a body between the graphs of constant functions, and then (4.14) is equation (4.7). A body made of boxes is cut into pieces that are its cells, and definition 4.21 gives the sum of definition 4.11, item 1. Two things remain open, however. Would another order of integration give the same number, for example with the inner integral over \(y\) instead of over the chord along \(z\), and would another cut of the same body, with two other cuts, give the same sum? For a box and for a body made of boxes we proved both (theorem 4.9 and lemma 4.12). For a body between graphs and for a body cut into pieces both questions are answered by sections 4.2.9 and 4.2.10, in which we define the integral without iterated integrals and without a cut. The proof of the divergence theorem does not need these answers. Its inner integral always runs along the chord between the covers, it exchanges the order of the two outer ones only on the rectangle \(R\), where theorem 4.9 allows it, and it uses only the given cut. Whenever we compute the integral over a body cut into pieces, we will say which cut we use.

For computing we need linearity and monotonicity.

For a nonnegative function the inner integral along the chord on the axis \(z\) is the area under the graph. The figure shows nonnegative functions and \(\alpha = 2\). On the left is the area under \(f_1\) and on it the area under \(f_2\), together the area under \(f_1 + f_2\), which is their sum. The area under \(\alpha f_1\) is \(\alpha\) times the area under \(f_1\). On the right the smaller area under \(f_1\) lies inside the larger one under \(f_2\), so the first is not larger than the second.

The lemma that follows, however, holds for functions of any sign and for every \(\alpha\). What the integral means then is shown in figure 4.68. On the left is the graph of the function \(f(z) = z - 1\) over the chord from \(0\) to \(3\). In the lower and upper sums of definition 3.49 a rectangle below the axis has a negative height, so the sum counts it negatively. The integral is therefore the area above the axis, \(2\), minus the area below the axis, \(1/2\), so \(\int_0^3 (z - 1)\,\mathrm{d}z = 3/2\). In the middle is the graph of the function \(-f\), so \(\alpha = -1\). It is the mirror image of the graph of \(f\) across the axis, the two areas change sign, and the integral is \(-3/2 = (-1) \cdot 3/2\), as linearity says. On the right are \(f_1(z) = z - 2\) and \(f_2(z) = (z - 1)/2\). We have \(f_1 \le f_2\), because \(f_2(z) - f_1(z) = (3 - z)/2 \ge 0\) for \(z \le 3\). Both are partly below the axis, so the picture of a nested area no longer applies. Monotonicity holds all the same: by linearity the difference of the integrals is the integral of the nonnegative function \(f_2 - f_1\), the area of the band between the graphs. In numbers, \(\int_0^3 f_1\,\mathrm{d}z = -3/2\), \(\int_0^3 f_2\,\mathrm{d}z = 3/4\) and the difference is \(3/4 - (-3/2) = 9/4 \ge 0\).

Lemma 4.22 Properties of the integral over a body between two graphs (lastnosti integrala po telesu med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between graphs or a body cut into pieces (definition 4.21), \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) continuous functions on \(V\) and \(\alpha\) a number.

  1. Linearity: \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} (f_1 + f_2)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_1\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_2\,\mathrm{d}V\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \alpha f_1\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_1\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. Monotonicity: if \(f_1(P) \le f_2(P)\) for every point \(P \in V\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f_1\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_2\,\mathrm{d}V\).
Proof

We must show both items. The proof is the proof of lemma 4.10, items 1 and 4.

  1. For a body between graphs we use, on each of the three iterated integrals, the linearity or the monotonicity of the integral over an interval (lemma 3.54, items 1 and 4), first on the inner one, over the chord, then on the middle and on the outer one, over the shadow \(R\). We may do so because by lemma 4.18 and by lemma 4.7, item 2, all the intermediate integrals are continuous functions. Where \(g(x, y) = h(x, y)\), as for the piece \(D\) of the round bar at the corners of the cuts, the chord has length zero. There the inner integrals are zero by the convention of definition 3.49, and the equality or inequality holds as \(0 = 0\) or \(0 \le 0\).
  2. For a body cut into pieces we add the equalities or inequalities of step 1 over the pieces, for the round bar over the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\).

Source: LEBL2 Propositions 10.1.10 and 10.1.11 (PDF p. 96) for integrable functions on a rectangle. The proof by iterated integrals is not from the sources.

We call the integral of the constant function \(1\) over a body its volume. For a box this is the school volume by lemma 4.10, item 2. Let us compute the volume of the round bar with the cut into the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\) of section 4.2.6 (figure 4.57, right), given by the cuts \(y = \pm 3\), with the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) in millimetres.

  1. The piece \(C\). The inner integral, along a vertical chord, is \(\int_{-\mathrm{q}(\mathrm{y})}^{q(y)} 1\,\mathrm{d}z = 2\,q(y)\), the middle one \(A_{\mathrm{C}} = \int_{-3}^{3} 2\,q(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\), and the outer one \(\int_0^L A_{\mathrm{C}}\,\mathrm{d}x = L\,A_{\mathrm{C}}\).
  2. The piece \(D\). The inner integral, now over \(y\), along a horizontal chord, is \(\int_3^{q(z)} 1\,\mathrm{d}y = q(z) - 3\), the middle one \(A_{\mathrm{D}} = \int_{-4}^{4} \big(q(z) - 3\big)\,\mathrm{d}z\), the outer one \(L\,A_{\mathrm{D}}\).
  3. The piece \(E\). The inner integral is \(-3 - (-q(z)) = q(z) - 3\), so the middle one is again \(A_{\mathrm{D}}\).

We call the numbers \(A_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{D}}\) the areas of the cross sections of the pieces. Section 4.2.10 shows that they do not depend on the cut. We cannot compute them with the tools of the book, because the function whose derivative is \(\sqrt{25 - t^2}\) needs the inverse sine function, which we have not defined. SymPy gives \(A_{\mathrm{C}} = 56{,}18\ \text{mm}^2\) and \(A_{\mathrm{D}} = 11{,}18\ \text{mm}^2\). The area of the cross section is therefore \(A = A_{\mathrm{C}} + 2A_{\mathrm{D}} = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), which is the area of a disc \(\pi r^2\) of radius \(5\) mm from school geometry. The volume of the bar is

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} 1\,\mathrm{d}V = L\,(A_{\mathrm{C}} + 2A_{\mathrm{D}}) = L\,A = 10\,000\ \text{mm} \cdot 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 785\,400\ \text{mm}^3 .\]

For a constant function \(\alpha\), by linearity \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \alpha\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha\,L\,A\). For a function \(f\) that depends only on \(x\), \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = A \int_0^L f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\). On each piece the inner and the middle integral give \(f(x)\) times the area of the cross section of the piece, and the areas add up to \(A\). We will use this for the equilibrium of the whole bar in section 4.2.13.

4.2.9 Sets with volume

So far we have computed the integral over a body by a chosen recipe. For a box and for a body between graphs by iterated integrals in a chosen order, for the round bar by a cut into the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\). The questions from the end of section 4.2.8 remain. Would another order of integration give the same number? Would another cut? We could also cut the round bar by the planes \(y = 4\) mm and \(y = -4\) mm, and the pieces would have cross sections with other areas. If two cuts gave different sums, the words volume of the bar and weight of the bar would have no meaning, because the numbers would depend on our computation, not only on the bar.

We get the answer by defining the integral over a body as KREYSZIG does (§10.7, PDF p. 478). We cover the body by a grid of small boxes and add up the values of the function times the volumes of those cells that lie entirely in the body (figure 4.69 shows this in the plane, on the cross section of the bar). Such a sum knows neither an order of integration nor a cut. If we show that for ever finer grids it approaches one single number, and that for a body between graphs this number equals the iterated integral in every order, both questions are settled.

The trouble comes from cells that lie in the body only partly. The sum leaves them out, so their total volume must be small for a fine grid. This is a property of the border between the body and its surroundings. In this section we describe this border precisely, name the sets that are covered by boxes of arbitrarily small total volume and the sets whose border is such, and show that the cells along the border have a small total volume for a fine grid. We define the integral in section 4.2.10.

Let us look at the cells along the boundary on the cross section of the round hanging bar, a disc of radius \(r = 5\) mm with its centre on the axis of the bar (figure 4.69). We write the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) in the plane of the cross section in millimetres. We cut the square \([-5, 5] \times [-5, 5]\), which contains the disc, by equally spaced lines parallel to the axes into square cells of side \(h\) (\(h = 1\) mm in the left picture, \(h = 0{,}5\) mm in the right one). A cell \([y_0, y_1] \times [z_0, z_1]\) lies in the disc exactly when its corner farthest from the centre lies in the disc. For a point of the cell we have \(|y| \le |y_0|\) when \(y < 0\), and \(|y| \le |y_1|\) when \(y \ge 0\), because \(y\) lies between \(y_0\) and \(y_1\). By lemma 1.29, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(y^2\) is therefore not larger than the larger of the numbers \(y_0^2\) and \(y_1^2\), and the same holds for \(z\). The cell \([3, 4] \times [2, 3]\) has the corner \((4, 3)\) farthest from the centre, at the distance \(\sqrt{16 + 9} = 5\) mm from it, so this corner still lies in the disc, and therefore the whole cell lies in the disc. The cell \([-5, -4] \times [0, 1]\) has its farthest corner \((-5, 1)\) at the distance \(\sqrt{26}\) mm, which is more than \(5\) mm, so it does not lie entirely in the disc, although its corner \((-4, 0)\) does lie in the disc. Cells that have a point in the disc and a point outside it are grey in the figure. NumPy counted the cells:

side of the cell \(h\) cells in the disc their area grey cells their area
1 mm 60 60 mm² 36 36 mm²
0,5 mm 276 69 mm² 76 19 mm²
0,25 mm 1176 73,5 mm² 156 9,75 mm²
0,1 mm 7644 76,44 mm² 396 3,96 mm²

The area of the cells that lie in the disc grows toward the area \(A = 78{,}54\) mm², which we computed in section 4.2.8 by a cut into pieces. The area of the grey cells falls. Why does it roughly halve when the side is halved? The grey cells form a staircase along the circle. A quarter of the circle from the point \((5, 0)\) to the point \((0, 5)\) crosses \(5/h\) columns and \(5/h\) rows of cells, so there are about \(10/h\) grey cells along it, and about \(40/h\) along the whole circle. For \(h = 1\) mm the estimate gives \(10\) cells along the quarter, and in the left picture we count \(9\) along it. For \(h = 0{,}1\) mm the estimate gives \(400\) cells along the whole circle, NumPy counted \(396\). Each has the area \(h^2\), so their total area is about \(40/h \cdot h^2 = 40\,h\), proportional to the side. The cells that lie in the disc therefore cover almost the whole disc. That this is so for every body we will meet has to be shown. The grey cells stay close to the circle, so let us start with the border between a set and its surroundings.

A grey cell contains a point in the disc and a point outside it. On the segment between them there is a point where the segment leaves the disc, a point of the circle. Every disc around this point, however small, reaches into the cross section and out of it (figure 4.70, the point \(B\)). Recall that the ball with centre \(P\) and radius \(r\) is the set of all points that are closer to \(P\) than \(r\) (section 1.12.6), and that \(P\) is an interior point of a set if some ball around it lies entirely in the set (section 1.15.6).

Definition 4.23 Boundary point and boundary of a set (robna točka in rob množice)

Let \(W\) be a set of points of space. A point \(P\), which may or may not lie in \(W\), is a boundary point (robna točka) of the set \(W\) if for every \(r > 0\) the ball with centre \(P\) and radius \(r\) contains a point of the set \(W\) and a point that is not in \(W\). The set of all boundary points of the set \(W\) is the boundary (rob množice) of \(W\).

We define boundary points and the boundary of a set of points of the plane in the same way, with discs in place of balls.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.3, footnote 2 (PDF p. 452), for regions in the plane: a point, of the region or not, such that every disc with centre at it contains points of the region and points not of the region. LEBL1 Def. 7.2.23 (PDF p. 270), for sets in which a distance is given, defines the boundary by the closure and the interior, and Proposition 7.2.27 (PDF p. 271) shows that this is the same property as ours.

The definition looks only at the balls around the point, so it is the same for points of the set and for points outside it (figure 4.70, where the set is a disc in a plane with the axes \(y\) and \(z\)). An interior point is not a boundary point, because some ball around it has no point outside the set. A point around which some ball has no point of the set is not a boundary point either. Are all other points boundary points? Yes. If such a point lies in the set, every ball around it contains the point itself and, since the point is not interior, a point outside the set. If it does not lie in the set, every ball around it contains the point itself, which is not in the set, and, since no ball around it is free of points of the set, a point of the set. For closed sets, like our bodies, even more holds: the boundary points lie in the set. Let us write this, and two more properties of the boundary that we will need, in a lemma.
