The third property is about a union, because we will build bodies from pieces (figure 4.71). Take a disc \(W_1\) and a rectangle \(W_2\) that overlap, and their union \(W\). The point \(A\) is a boundary point of the union, and it is also a boundary point of the disc \(W_1\). The lemma will say that this is always so: the boundary of a union lies in the boundaries of the pieces. The converse does not hold. The point \(S\) lies on the circle, the boundary of the disc \(W_1\), but a disc around it lies entirely in \(W_2\), so it is an interior point of the union. The boundary of a union can thus be smaller than the union of the boundaries, but not larger, and this will be enough for us, because we only look for an upper bound for the volume of the boundary.

Lemma 4.24 Boundary of a closed set and of a union (rob zaprte množice in rob unije)
  1. Let \(W\) be a closed set of points (definition 1.75) and \(P\) a point such that every ball with centre \(P\) contains a point of the set \(W\). Then \(P\) lies in \(W\) and not outside it. Hence every boundary point of the set \(W\) lies in \(W\), and for every point \(P\) that is not in \(W\) there is a ball with centre \(P\) that has no point of the set \(W\).
  2. Every point of the set \(W\) is an interior point of the set \(W\) or a boundary point of the set \(W\).
  3. Let \(W\) be the union of the sets of points \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\). Every boundary point of the set \(W\) is a boundary point of at least one of the sets \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\). If all of them are closed and bounded, so is \(W\).

The same holds for sets of points of the plane, with discs in place of balls. A set of points of the plane is then called closed and bounded if the set of the corresponding points \((x, y, 0)\) of space is.

Proof

We must show all three items. For the first we build, from points in ever smaller balls, a sequence that converges to \(P\).

1. A closed set.

  1. For every natural number \(n\) the ball with centre \(P\) and radius \(1/n\) contains a point of the set \(W\). We choose one and call it \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\). Then \(0 \le |P_{\mathrm{n}} P| < 1/n\). In figure 4.70 such a point is \(B\) on the circle, and in the two discs around it the points \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) of the set are chosen.
  2. The sequence \((1/n)\) converges to \(0\) (lemma 1.40). By the squeeze lemma 1.47 with the lower sequence \(0, 0, \dots\) the sequence of distances \((|P_{\mathrm{n}} P|)\) also converges to \(0\), so by definition 1.66 the sequence of points \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(P\).
  3. All points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) lie in \(W\), and \(W\) is closed, so \(P\) lies in \(W\).
  4. For a boundary point \(P\) of the set \(W\) every ball with centre \(P\) contains a point of the set \(W\) (definition 4.23). By steps 1 to 3, \(P\) therefore lies in \(W\).
  5. Let \(P\) not lie in \(W\). By steps 1 to 3 it is then not true that every ball with centre \(P\) contains a point of the set \(W\). So there is a ball with centre \(P\) that has no point of the set \(W\).

2. Points of the set.

  1. Let the point \(P\) lie in \(W\) and not be an interior point of the set \(W\). Then no ball with centre \(P\) lies entirely in \(W\) (section 1.15.6), so every one contains a point that is not in \(W\). Every one also contains the point \(P\), which is in \(W\). By definition 4.23, \(P\) is a boundary point.

3. The union.

  1. Let \(P\) be a boundary point of the set \(W\). We argue by contradiction: suppose that \(P\) is a boundary point of none of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  2. Then for every \(k\) there is a radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\) such that the ball with centre \(P\) and radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) does not contain both a point of \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) and a point outside \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). It lies entirely in \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), or it has no point of \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3. If for some \(k\) the ball of radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) lies entirely in \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), it lies entirely in \(W\), because every point of the set \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) is in the union. This contradicts the fact that a ball around the boundary point \(P\) of the set \(W\) contains a point that is not in \(W\). This is the case of the point \(S\) in figure 4.71, where the disc lies entirely in \(W_2\).
  4. Otherwise none of the balls of radii \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) has a point of its set \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). Let \(r\) be the smallest of the numbers \(r_1, \dots, r_{\mathrm{m}}\). A point that is closer to \(P\) than \(r\) is closer than every \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\), so it lies in none of the \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) and therefore not in \(W\). So the ball of radius \(r\) has no point of the set \(W\), which contradicts the fact that \(P\) is a boundary point. In figure 4.71 the disc of radius \(r_1\) around the point \(P\) has no point of \(W_1\), but it reaches into \(W_2\), so it is not enough by itself. The disc of radius \(r_2\) has no point of \(W_2\) and, being smaller than the first, none of \(W_1\) either.
  5. Closedness. Let a sequence of points \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) from \(W\) converge to a point \(P\), and suppose that \(P\) is not in \(W\). The point \(P\) is in no \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), since it is not in \(W\). By the fifth step of the first item, used on each closed \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), there is a radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\) such that the ball with centre \(P\) and radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) has no point of \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). Let \(r\) be the smallest of the numbers \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\). The distances \(|P_{\mathrm{n}} P|\) converge to \(0\), so there is a place \(N\) with \(|P_{\mathrm{N}} P| < r\). The point \(P_{\mathrm{N}}\) lies in some \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) and is closer to \(P\) than \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\), which contradicts the choice of the radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\). So \(P\) lies in \(W\).
  6. Boundedness. If \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R_{\mathrm{k}}\) for every point \(P \in W_{\mathrm{k}}\), then \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\) for every point \(P \in W\), where \(R\) is the largest of the numbers \(R_1, \dots, R_{\mathrm{m}}\).

4. The plane.

  1. The steps are the same, only the balls are discs in the plane.

Source: LEBL1 Propositions 7.2.22 and 7.2.19 (PDF p. 270): a point lies in the closure of a set exactly when every ball around it contains a point of the set, and a closed set equals its closure. Item 1 follows from both. Proposition 7.2.8 (iii) (PDF p. 266): a union of finitely many closed sets is closed. The source defines closedness by open sets. The proof by sequences and items 2 and 3 on the boundary are not from the source.

The lemma confirmed what figure 4.70 shows. The boundary point \(B\) of a closed set lies in the set, and the point \(Q\) outside it has a disc around it without points of the set. The key move was a sequence of points \(P_1, P_2, \dots\) from ever smaller balls, which converges to the centre of the balls. Closedness is necessary in the first item. A disc without its circle, the set of points with \(y^2 + z^2 < 25\), does not contain the point \((5, 0)\), yet this point is a boundary point of it. A disc of radius \(r\) around it contains the point itself, which is not in the set, and the point \((5 - t, 0)\) with \(0 < t < 5\) and \(t < r\), which is. For the union the smallest radius decided. Since there are finitely many sets, the smallest of the radii \(r_1, \dots, r_{\mathrm{m}}\) exists and is positive.

With infinitely many sets the conclusion fails (figure 4.73). On the \(y\) axis we take the points \((1, 0)\), \((\tfrac12, 0)\), \((\tfrac13, 0)\) and so on. Each of them, as a set with a single point, is closed and its own boundary. The point \(O = (0, 0)\) is not in their union, but every disc around it contains a point \((1/n, 0)\) once \(1/n\) is smaller than its radius, so \(O\) is a boundary point of the union. It is not a boundary point of the set made of the single point \((1/n, 0)\), since the disc around it of radius \(r_{\mathrm{n}} = 1/n\) does not contain that point, the point lies on its circle. Step 4 of the proof would therefore need the smallest of the numbers \(r_1, r_2, r_3, \dots\), but each is larger than the next, so there is no smallest one. Nor is the union closed, since the sequence of its points \((1/n, 0)\) converges to the point \(O\) outside it.

What is the boundary of the cross section of the round bar, a disc of radius \(5\) mm? We expect the circle. The cross section is the set of points \((y, z)\) with \(y^2 + z^2 \le 25\). Seen as the set of points \((0, y, z)\) of space, it is given by the equation \(x = 0\) and by a non-strict inequality with a polynomial, so by lemma 1.76 it is closed, like the bar in section 1.13.4.

  1. A point \((y, z)\) with \(y^2 + z^2 > 25\) is not a boundary point. It lies outside the closed cross section, so by lemma 4.24, item 1, there is a disc around it without points of the cross section, as for the point \(Q\) in figure 4.70.
  2. A point \(P = (y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) with \(y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{P}}^2 < 25\) is not a boundary point. The set of points with \(y^2 + z^2 \ge 25\) is closed by lemma 1.76, and \(P\) does not lie in it. By lemma 4.24, item 1, there is therefore a disc around \(P\) without its points, that is, a disc that lies entirely in the cross section. The point \(P\) is interior.
  3. A point \(P = (y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) with \(y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{P}}^2 = 25\) is a boundary point. It lies in the cross section. For \(r > 0\) and \(t\) with \(0 < t < r/5\) the point \(((1 + t)\,y_{\mathrm{P}},\ (1 + t)\,z_{\mathrm{P}})\) lies outside the cross section, because \((1 + t)^2 \cdot 25 > 25\), and its distance from \(P\) is \(\sqrt{t^2 y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + t^2 z_{\mathrm{P}}^2} = 5\,t < r\). In figure 4.70 such a point of the circle is \(B\). The point \(((1 + t)\,y_{\mathrm{P}},\ (1 + t)\,z_{\mathrm{P}})\) lies on the ray from the centre through the point of the circle, farther from the centre by \(5\,t\), so right behind the circle.

So the boundary of the cross section is the circle.

The staircase of grey cells in figure 4.69 covers the circle, and its area is about \(40\,h\) and goes to zero. The circle is thin. We can cover it by finitely many rectangles whose total area is as small as we like. Let us name this property.

Definition 4.25 Set of zero volume (množica s prostornino nič)

A set of points of space \(Z\) has zero volume (prostornina nič) if for every \(\eta > 0\) there are finitely many boxes with edges along the axes that cover \(Z\), that is, every point of the set \(Z\) lies in at least one of them, and the sum of their volumes is less than \(\eta\).

A set of points of the plane has zero area (ploščina nič) if for every \(\eta > 0\) it is covered by finitely many rectangles with edges along the axes with a total area less than \(\eta\).

Source: LEBL2 Def. 10.3.1 (PDF p. 108) allows a sequence of infinitely many rectangles and calls the notion measure zero. By Proposition 10.3.7 (PDF p. 112) a closed and bounded set of measure zero is already covered by finitely many rectangles of arbitrarily small total volume, so for such sets this is the same notion as ours.

A set of zero volume is thus a set of points that we can enclose in boxes of arbitrarily small total volume. A point has zero volume. It is covered by a cube of side \(t\) with its centre at the point, whose volume \(t^3\) is less than \(\eta\) when \(t\) is small enough. A rectangle in the plane \(z = c\) also has zero volume, for example a face of a box, made of the points \((x, y, c)\) with \(a_1 \le x \le b_1\) and \(a_2 \le y \le b_2\) (figure 4.74, left, where we look at it from the side, along the axis \(y\), so that it looks like a segment). It is covered by the box \([a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [c - t, c + t]\) of thickness \(2t\) with the volume \(2t\,(b_1 - a_1)(b_2 - a_2)\), which is less than \(\eta\) when \(t\) is less than \(\eta/(2(b_1 - a_1)(b_2 - a_2))\). A flat face has no thickness, so every thinner box encloses it too.

The faces of our bodies are not all flat. The top lid of a body between graphs is the graph of a continuous function, and the lateral surface of the round bar is made of such graphs. Let us show that graphs of continuous functions have zero volume, and write down two more rules that follow at once from the definition.

Let us show the idea on a function of one variable (figure 4.75). The interval \([a, b]\) on the axis \(x\) is cut into six equal pieces, over each stands a rectangle of height \(2\omega\) whose centre is the value of the function at the right end of the piece. Over a short piece a continuous function changes by less than \(\omega\), so the graph over it lies in a rectangle of height \(2\omega\). The total area of the rectangles is \(2\omega\,(b - a)\), and it goes to zero with \(\omega\). We must take care of one thing only: the same length of the pieces must work everywhere on the interval, which is what uniform continuity gives.

Lemma 4.26 Subsets, unions and graphs of zero volume (podmnožice, unije in grafi s prostornino nič)
  1. Every subset of a set of zero volume has zero volume.
  2. The union of finitely many sets of zero volume has zero volume.
  3. Let \(\varphi\) be a function that is continuous on the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\). Then the graph of the function \(\varphi\), the set of points \((x, y, \varphi(x, y))\) with \((x, y) \in R\), has zero volume (the figure shows the same for one variable). The same holds for another naming of the axes, for example for the set of points \((\varphi(y, z), y, z)\) with \((y, z)\) from a rectangle in the plane of the axes \(y\) and \(z\).

The same holds in the plane, with the area in place of the volume. The graph of a function \(\varphi\) that is continuous on the interval \([a, b]\), the set of points \((x, \varphi(x))\) with \(a \le x \le b\), has zero area, and so does the set of points \((\varphi(y), y)\).

Proof

We must show all three items. The first two follow from the definition, for the third we enclose the graph over each small rectangle in a low box.

1. A subset.

  1. Boxes that cover a set also cover each of its subsets, since every point of the subset is a point of the set.

2. A union.

  1. Let \(Z_1, \dots, Z_{\mathrm{m}}\) have zero volume and let \(\eta > 0\). For each \(k\) we choose finitely many boxes that cover \(Z_{\mathrm{k}}\) and have a total volume less than \(\eta/m\).
  2. There are finitely many of all these boxes. Every point of the union lies in some \(Z_{\mathrm{k}}\) and therefore in one of the boxes chosen for it. The total volume of all the boxes is less than \(m \cdot \eta/m = \eta\).

3. A graph.

  1. The rectangle \(R\), seen as the set of points \((x, y, 0)\), is closed and bounded (section 4.2.2). We choose \(\eta > 0\) and let \(\omega = \eta/(4(b - a)(d - c))\). We choose the number \(4\) so that the total volume in step 5 is \(\eta/2\), less than \(\eta\). By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|\varphi(P) - \varphi(Q)| < \omega\) for any points \(P, Q \in R\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\).
  2. By the Archimedean property 1.36 there is a natural number \(n\) such that \(n\,\delta/2\) is larger than \(b - a\) and than \(d - c\). We divide the intervals \([a, b]\) and \([c, d]\) into \(n\) equal pieces, which are shorter than \(\delta/2\), and get the rectangles \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = [x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}]\). Two points of the same rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are closer than \(\delta\). The differences of their coordinates are less than \(\delta/2\) in absolute value, by lemma 1.29 their squares are less than \(\delta^2/4\), the square of the distance is therefore less than \(\delta^2/2\), and by the same lemma the distance is less than \(\delta\).
  3. Let \(P_{\mathrm{ij}} = (x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}})\) be a corner of the rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By steps 1 and 2, for every point \((x, y) \in R_{\mathrm{ij}}\)
    \[\varphi(P_{\mathrm{ij}}) - \omega < \varphi(x, y) < \varphi(P_{\mathrm{ij}}) + \omega ,\]
    so the point \((x, y, \varphi(x, y))\) lies in the box \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = R_{\mathrm{ij}} \times [\varphi(P_{\mathrm{ij}}) - \omega,\ \varphi(P_{\mathrm{ij}}) + \omega]\). In figure 4.75, which shows the same for one variable, this is the rectangle that reaches \(\omega\) above and below the value at the end of the piece.
  4. Every point \((x, y)\) of the rectangle \(R\) lies in at least one of the rectangles \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), because \(x\) lies in one of the pieces of the interval \([a, b]\) and \(y\) in one of the pieces of the interval \([c, d]\). The boxes \(K_{\mathrm{ij}}\) therefore cover the graph.
  5. The box \(K_{\mathrm{ij}}\) has the volume \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}} \cdot 2\omega\). By distributivity and the telescoping sum, as in step 6 of the proof of theorem 4.9, the sum of the areas \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\) is \((b - a)(d - c)\). The total volume of the boxes is therefore \(2\omega\,(b - a)(d - c) = \eta/2 < \eta\).
  6. For another naming of the axes the steps are the same, only the coordinates exchange roles.

4. The plane.

  1. Items 1 and 2 are the same, with rectangles in place of boxes.
  2. For the graph of the function \(\varphi\) on \([a, b]\) we take \(\omega = \eta/(4(b - a))\) and the band \(\delta\) that theorem 3.52 on uniform continuity on a closed interval gives for the error \(\omega\). We divide the interval into pieces shorter than \(\delta\) and enclose the graph over the piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\) in the rectangle \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [\varphi(x_{\mathrm{i}}) - \omega,\ \varphi(x_{\mathrm{i}}) + \omega]\). The total area of the rectangles is \(2\omega\,(b - a) = \eta/2 < \eta\).

Source: LEBL2 (PDF p. 108) states that a subset of a set of measure zero is again such a set, and Proposition 10.3.4 (PDF p. 110) that a countable union of sets of measure zero is such a set. The proof for finitely many boxes and item 3 are not from the source.

The proof of item 3 carried the idea of figure 4.75 out for a function of two variables. The rectangles over the pieces of the interval became the boxes \(K_{\mathrm{ij}}\) over the small rectangles \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), with a total volume of \(2\omega\) times the area of the rectangle \(R\). Uniform continuity made sure that one single height \(2\omega\) worked for all the boxes at once. This is why the lemma requires continuity on a closed rectangle or interval, end points included. Where this is missing, the conclusion can fail.

The function \(1/x\) is continuous on the interval \((0, 1]\) without its left end point, but its graph over the \(x\) axis does not have zero area (figure 4.76). Take finitely many rectangles meant to cover it. Since there are finitely many, there is a number \(M \ge 1\) larger than the height of the top edge of each of them. The point \((x, 1/x)\) of the graph with \(0 < x < 1/M\) has \(1/x > M\), so it lies in none of the rectangles. Finitely many rectangles do not cover such a graph at all, however narrow or tall they are.

Now we can say which sets we will integrate over.

Definition 4.27 Set with volume (množica s prostornino)

A set of points of space \(W\) is a set with volume (množica s prostornino) if it is closed and bounded (definition 1.75) and its boundary (definition 4.23) has zero volume (definition 4.25).

A set of points of the plane \(M\) is a set with area (množica s ploščino) if it is closed and bounded when we view each of its points \((x, y)\) as the point \((x, y, 0)\) of space, and its boundary, determined in the plane with discs, has zero area.

Source: LEBL2 (PDF p. 123) calls a bounded set Jordan measurable if its characteristic function is integrable, and in Proposition 10.5.1 (PDF p. 123) shows that this is so exactly when its boundary has measure zero. The source does not require closedness.

The definition requires two things, and we will need both. Closedness and boundedness will give the largest value and uniform continuity of a continuous function on the set (theorems 1.79 and 4.6). A boundary of zero volume will make sure that the cells along the boundary have a small total volume. The source does not require closedness and also integrates functions that are not continuous, which we will not need. Our bodies together with their surfaces are closed sets (section 1.13.4), so the requirement does not restrict us.

Why this agreement in the plane? We defined closedness and boundedness only for sets of points of space, so we view the points of the plane as the points \((x, y, 0)\). The distance between the points \((x, y, 0)\) and \((x', y', 0)\) is \(\sqrt{(x' - x)^2 + (y' - y)^2}\), equal to the distance in the plane, so theorems 1.79 on the largest value and 4.6 on uniform continuity also hold for continuous functions on a closed and bounded set of the plane. This is how we already treated the rectangle in section 4.2.2 and, above, the cross section of the bar. The boundary, however, we determine in the plane. In space every ball around the point \((x, y, 0)\) contains points with \(z \neq 0\), which are not in \(M\), so in space every point of the set \(M\) would be a boundary point. A disc in the plane does not contain these points. We do the same in the plane of two other axes, for example with the cross section of the bar in the plane \(x = 0\).

Let us check the definition on two sets we know.

The box \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) is a set with volume (figure 4.78, left, where the box is drawn in the plane as a rectangle). It is closed and bounded by section 1.13.4.

  1. A point \(P\) with \(a_1 < x_{\mathrm{P}} < b_1\), \(a_2 < y_{\mathrm{P}} < b_2\) and \(a_3 < z_{\mathrm{P}} < b_3\) is not a boundary point. Let \(\rho\) be the smallest of the six distances \(x_{\mathrm{P}} - a_1\), \(b_1 - x_{\mathrm{P}}\), \(y_{\mathrm{P}} - a_2\), \(b_2 - y_{\mathrm{P}}\), \(z_{\mathrm{P}} - a_3\) and \(b_3 - z_{\mathrm{P}}\) to the faces (the drawing in the plane has four). A point that is closer to \(P\) than \(\rho\) differs from \(P\) by less than \(\rho\) in every coordinate (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.67), so it lies in \(K\). The ball of radius \(\rho\) has no points outside \(K\).
  2. A boundary point lies in \(K\) by lemma 4.24, item 1, so by step 1 at least one of its coordinates equals an end point. It lies on one of the six faces of the box.
  3. Every face is the graph of a constant function over a rectangle. The face \(x = a_1\), for example, is the set of points \((a_1, y, z)\) with \((y, z) \in [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\). By lemma 4.26, item 3, it has zero volume, by item 2 of the same lemma so does the union of the six faces, and by item 1 so does the boundary, which lies in it.

In the same way a rectangle with edges along the axes is a set with area.

What does the definition reject? Take the half-open box \(H = (0, 1] \times [0, 1] \times [0, 1]\), which differs from the unit cube only in that it lacks the face \(x = 0\) (figure 4.78, right). Its boundary is the same as the boundary of the cube. Points inside the cube and points outside it have the same ball around them as before, and every ball around a point of a face still contains points of the inside of the cube, which are in \(H\), and points outside the cube, which are not in \(H\). So the boundary is six faces of volume zero (step 3), and the second condition holds. The first does not: \(H\) is not closed. The point \(Q = (0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12)\) is not in \(H\), but every ball around it contains the point \((1/n, \tfrac12, \tfrac12)\) of \(H\) once \(1/n\) is smaller than the radius of the ball. If \(H\) were closed, then by lemma 4.24, item 1, the point \(Q\) would lie in \(H\). So \(H\) is not a set with a volume, because the requirement of closedness fails while the boundary is fine.

The cross section of the round bar, a disc of radius \(5\) mm, is also a set with area. It is closed and bounded, and its boundary is the circle. We cut the circle as we cut the bar in section 4.2.6, at \(y = \pm 3\) (figure 4.57, right). A point \((y, z)\) of the circle with \(|y| \le 3\) has \(z^2 = 25 - y^2\), so by theorem 1.37 on the existence of square roots \(|z| = q(y)\), where \(q(t) = \sqrt{25 - t^2}\), and the point lies on the graph of the function \(q\) or \(-q\) over \([-3, 3]\). A point with \(|y| > 3\) has \(z^2 < 16\), so \(|z| < 4\), and in the same way \(|y| = q(z)\), so it lies on the graph \(y = q(z)\) or \(y = -q(z)\) over \([-4, 4]\). By lemma 4.16 the function \(q\) is differentiable at every point of \((-5, 5)\), which contains \([-4, 4]\), so by lemma 1.80 it is continuous there. By lemma 4.26, item 3 in the plane, the four graphs have zero area, and by items 2 and 1 so does the circle. The four graphs are the upper and the lower arc between the cuts and the left and the right arc outside them, and they meet at the points \((\pm 3, \pm 4)\).

A disc without its circle, \(y^2 + z^2 < 25\), is not a set with an area, although its boundary has area zero. Steps 1 and 2 for the cross section hold for it as well: a disc around a point with \(y^2 + z^2 > 25\) that has no point of the cross section has none of the smaller set either, and a disc around a point with \(y^2 + z^2 < 25\) lies entirely in it. Its boundary therefore lies on the circle and by item 1 of lemma 4.26 has area zero. What fails is closedness, as for \(H\). The point \((5, 0)\) on the circle is a boundary point of it but does not lie in it, so by lemma 4.24, item 1, it is not closed.

Is the bar itself, a cylinder of length \(10\) m, a set with volume? Its surface is made of the lids of the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\), which are graphs, and of flat faces. We will show this in section 4.2.10 for every body between graphs and for every body cut into such bodies.

Let us return to the cells. Recall the words from section 4.2.3. A grid of the box \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) is given by partitions \(D_1 = \{x_0, \dots, x_{\mathrm{l}}\}\), \(D_2 = \{y_0, \dots, y_{\mathrm{m}}\}\) and \(D_3 = \{z_0, \dots, z_{\mathrm{n}}\}\) of its edges. Its cells are the boxes \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}} = [x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}] \times [z_{\mathrm{k}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}}]\) with the volumes \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} = \Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}}\). For a set of points \(W\) in the box \(K\) a cell lies in \(W\), written \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq W\), if all its points are in \(W\). A cell that has a point in \(W\) lies in \(W\) or else also has a point outside \(W\). Cells of the second kind are grey in figure 4.69. In the plane the cells are rectangles \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = [x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}]\) with the areas \(\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}} = \Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\).

We will compare cells with boxes that are not cells of the grid, for example with boxes that cover the boundary. We need a rule for how the volumes of the cells that lie in a given box add up.

Figure 4.79 shows the question in the plane. The grid of the rectangle \(K\) has unequal pieces. The box \(B\) does not lie on the lines of the grid. The cells that lie in \(B\) are light blue. The grey cell reaches across the edge of the box \(B\), so we do not count it. The pieces of the partition that lie in the horizontal edge of the box \(B\) follow each other without gaps and have the total length \(L_1\), which is not larger than the length of the edge \(\beta_1 - \alpha_1\). It is the same in the vertical direction with the length \(L_2\). The blue cells together form a rectangle with the sides \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) that lies in \(B\), so their total area is not larger than the area of the box \(B\). The lemma says this for three directions.

Lemma 4.28 Cells in a box (celice v kvadru)

Let a grid of a box \(K\) with the partitions \(D_1\), \(D_2\) and \(D_3\) be given, and a box \(B\) \(= [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) with edges along the axes.

  1. The cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) lies in \(B\) exactly when the piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\) lies in \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\), the piece \([y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}]\) in \([\alpha_2, \beta_2]\) and the piece \([z_{\mathrm{k}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}}]\) in \([\alpha_3, \beta_3]\).
  2. The cells of the grid that lie in \(B\) have a total volume of at most \(V_{\mathrm{B}}\).
  3. If the numbers \(\alpha_1\) and \(\beta_1\) are points of the partition \(D_1\), \(\alpha_2\) and \(\beta_2\) points of the partition \(D_2\), and \(\alpha_3\) and \(\beta_3\) points of the partition \(D_3\), this total volume equals \(V_{\mathrm{B}}\).

The same holds in the plane, with rectangles and areas.

Proof

We must show all three items. The cells in \(B\) are all combinations of the pieces that lie in the edges of the box \(B\), and the pieces in an edge add up to a telescoping sum.

  1. If every piece lies in the corresponding edge of the box \(B\), every point of the cell has all three coordinates in the edges of the box \(B\) and lies in \(B\). Conversely, let the cell lie in \(B\) and let \(x\) be a number from the piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\). The point \((x, y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}-1})\) lies in the cell, hence in \(B\), so \(\alpha_1 \le x \le \beta_1\). So the piece lies in \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\). The same for the other two pieces. In figure 4.79 the piece of the grey cell reaches to the left across \(\alpha_1\), so this cell does not lie in \(B\).
  2. The pieces of the partition \(D_1\) that lie in \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\) follow each other without gaps. If pieces with indices \(i_0 < i_1\) lie in it, then for every \(i\) between them \(x_{\mathrm{i}-1} \ge x_{\mathrm{i}_0 - 1} \ge \alpha_1\) and \(x_{\mathrm{i}} \le x_{\mathrm{i}_1} \le \beta_1\), because the points of a partition increase. Let \(i_0\) be the smallest and \(i_1\) the largest such index. The sum of the lengths of these pieces is a telescoping sum (section 3.5.2)
    \[L_1 = \sum_{\mathrm{i} = \mathrm{i}_0}^{i_1} \Delta x_{\mathrm{i}} = x_{\mathrm{i}_1} - x_{\mathrm{i}_0 - 1} \le \beta_1 - \alpha_1 .\]
    In figure 4.79 these are three pieces of length \(L_1\) inside the edge \(\beta_1 - \alpha_1\). If no piece lies in \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\), then \(L_1 = 0\). In the same way we define \(L_2 \le \beta_2 - \alpha_2\) and \(L_3 \le \beta_3 - \alpha_3\).
  3. By step 1 the cells in \(B\) are exactly the cells \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) for which all three pieces lie in the edges of the box \(B\). By distributivity, as in step 6 of the proof of theorem 4.9, the sum of their volumes is \(L_1 L_2 L_3\) (in figure 4.79, in the plane, the area \(L_1 L_2\) of the blue rectangle). All the numbers are nonnegative, so by step 2 this product is at most \((\beta_1 - \alpha_1)(\beta_2 - \alpha_2)(\beta_3 - \alpha_3) = V_{\mathrm{B}}\).
  4. Let \(\alpha_1 = x_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(\beta_1 = x_{\mathrm{q}}\) be points of the partition \(D_1\), with \(p < q\). Exactly the pieces with indices from \(p + 1\) to \(q\) lie in \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\), so \(L_1 = x_{\mathrm{q}} - x_{\mathrm{p}} = \beta_1 - \alpha_1\). In the same way \(L_2 = \beta_2 - \alpha_2\) and \(L_3 = \beta_3 - \alpha_3\), and the product from step 3 is \(V_{\mathrm{B}}\).
  5. In the plane the steps are the same, with two partitions and two lengths.

Source: The lemma is not from the sources.

The lemma also tells us what the definition of zero volume rejects. The slab \(P = [0, 1] \times [0, 1] \times [0, 0{,}001]\) differs from a rectangle in the plane \(z = 0\) only in the thickness \(0{,}001\), but it does not have zero volume (figure 4.74, right, seen from the side). For the error we take \(\eta = 0{,}0005\), half of the volume of the slab \(V_{\mathrm{P}} = 0{,}001\), and show that the sum of the volumes of any finitely many boxes \(B_1, \dots, B_{\mathrm{m}}\) that cover \(P\) is at least \(0{,}001\), so not smaller than \(\eta\). The figure has four boxes.

  1. For each axis we take a partition of the edge of the slab in that direction that contains, besides the endpoints of the edge, those endpoint coordinates of the boxes \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\) that lie in this edge. This is a grid of the box \(P\), and no piece of the partition contains in its interior an endpoint of the edge of any box \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\). In the figure the lines of the grid run through the slab where the edges of the boxes cut it.
  2. The centre of every cell of the grid lies in \(P\), so some \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\) covers it, in the figure the box \(B_4\). The centre of every piece of the cell lies in the edge of the box \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\) and is not its endpoint, and the piece has no endpoint of an edge of the box \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\) in its interior. If the piece reached past an endpoint of the edge of \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\), that endpoint would lie between an endpoint of the piece and its centre, so in the interior of the piece, which step 1 rules out. So the whole piece lies in this edge. By item 1 of lemma 4.28 the cell lies in \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\). Every cell therefore lies in at least one box.
  3. By item 3 of lemma 4.28, applied to \(B = P\), all the cells together have volume \(V_{\mathrm{P}} = 0{,}001\). By item 2 of the same lemma, the box \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\) has at most the volume \(V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{l}}\) among them. Since every cell lies in at least one box, we get \(0{,}001 \le V_{\mathrm{B}_1} + \dots + V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{m}}\).

A cover with total volume below \(0{,}0005\) therefore does not exist, so \(P\) does not have zero volume. For a rectangle of the plane \(z = 0\) it is different, because it has thickness zero: a box of thickness \(2t\) covers it for every \(t\). The slab fails the requirement that a cover exists for every \(\eta\), because of a thickness that we cannot make smaller.

Now let us show that the cells along the boundary have a small total volume for a fine grid. The idea has two steps (figure 4.80). A cell that has a point in \(W\) and a point outside \(W\) contains a boundary point, because the segment between them leaves \(W\) somewhere. The boundary, in turn, is covered by boxes of small total volume, and a small cell that has a point in one of them lies in this box, slightly enlarged.

Lemma 4.29 Boundary cells (robne celice)

A cell of a grid is a boundary cell (robna celica) of the set \(W\) if it contains a point of the set \(W\) and a point that is not in \(W\).

  1. Let the set of points \(Z\) have zero volume. For every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that for every grid of a box in which all pieces of the partitions are shorter than \(\delta\), the cells that contain at least one point of the set \(Z\) have a total volume less than \(\eta\).
  2. If the set \(W\) is closed, every boundary cell of the set \(W\) contains a boundary point of the set \(W\).
  3. Let \(W\) be a set with volume. For every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that for every grid of a box that contains \(W\), in which all pieces of the partitions are shorter than \(\delta\), the boundary cells of the set \(W\) have a total volume less than \(\eta\).

The same holds in the plane, with rectangles and areas.

Proof

We must show all three items. In the first we enclose the cells in slightly enlarged boxes that cover \(Z\), in the second we find a boundary point by a supremum on a segment, and the third follows from the first two.

1. Cells along a set of zero volume.

  1. We choose \(\eta > 0\). If \(Z\) is empty, no cell has a point of \(Z\), and every \(\delta\) works. Let \(Z\) not be empty. Since it has zero volume, it is covered by \(p \ge 1\) boxes \(B_1, \dots, B_{\mathrm{p}}\) with a total volume less than \(\eta/2\). Figure 4.80, right, shows one of them along a piece of the set \(Z\).
  2. Let \(\Lambda\) be a number that is not smaller than any edge of any of the boxes \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\). For \(\delta\) we take a positive number that is less than \(1\) and than \(\eta/(12\,p\,(\Lambda + 2)^2)\). The condition \(\delta < 1\) makes the edges of the enlarged boxes shorter than \(\Lambda + 2\). The factor \(12 = 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 2\) comes from the three terms in step 6, from the enlargement by \(2\delta\) and from half the error, \(\eta/2\), shared among \(p\) boxes.
  3. For the box \(B_{\mathrm{l}} = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) let \(B_{\mathrm{l}}^\delta = [\alpha_1 - \delta, \beta_1 + \delta] \times [\alpha_2 - \delta, \beta_2 + \delta] \times [\alpha_3 - \delta, \beta_3 + \delta]\) be the box enlarged by \(\delta\) on all sides.
  4. Let all pieces of the partitions be shorter than \(\delta\) and let the cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) contain a point \(Q \in Z\). The point \(Q\) lies in some box \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\). For every point of the cell, its coordinate \(x\) and the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{Q}}\) are on the same piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\), so they differ by less than \(\delta\). Since \(\alpha_1 \le x_{\mathrm{Q}} \le \beta_1\), we have \(\alpha_1 - \delta < x < \beta_1 + \delta\). The same for \(y\) and \(z\). The cell therefore lies in \(B_{\mathrm{l}}^\delta\).
  5. By lemma 4.28, item 2, the cells that lie in \(B_{\mathrm{l}}^\delta\) have a total volume of at most \(V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{l}^\delta}\). By step 4 every cell with a point of \(Z\) lies in at least one of the boxes \(B_{\mathrm{l}}^\delta\), so the total volume of such cells is at most \(V_{\mathrm{B}_1^\delta} + \dots + V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{p}^\delta}\). A cell that lies in several boxes is counted several times on the right, which only makes the right side larger.
  1. Let us estimate by how much the enlargement increases the volume. Let \(s_1, s_2, s_3\) be the edges of the box \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{i}}' = s_{\mathrm{i}} + 2\delta\) the edges of the box \(B_{\mathrm{l}}^\delta\). The volume of a box depends only on the lengths of its edges, so in figure 4.81, top right, we may put the box with edges \(s_1, s_2, s_3\) into a corner of the box with edges \(s_1', s_2', s_3'\). We cut the rest into three slabs of thickness \(2\delta\): the right one with edges \(s_2'\) and \(s_3'\), the back one with edges \(s_1\) and \(s_3'\) and the top one with edges \(s_1\) and \(s_2\), which are taken out at the bottom right. Their volumes are the three terms on the right side of the equation
    \[s_1' s_2' s_3' - s_1 s_2 s_3 = (s_1' - s_1)\,s_2' s_3' + s_1\,(s_2' - s_2)\,s_3' + s_1 s_2\,(s_3' - s_3) ,\]
    which we also check by multiplying out the right side: the terms \(s_1 s_2' s_3'\) and \(s_1 s_2 s_3'\) cancel, and the left side remains. Each difference is \(2\delta\), each \(s_{\mathrm{i}}\) is at most \(\Lambda\), and each \(s_{\mathrm{i}}'\) is less than \(\Lambda + 2\), because \(\delta < 1\). Each slab therefore has a volume less than \(2\delta\,(\Lambda + 2)^2\), and \(V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{l}^\delta} - V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{l}} < 3 \cdot 2\delta\,(\Lambda + 2)^2 = 6\delta\,(\Lambda + 2)^2 < \eta/(2p)\).
  2. By steps 5 and 6 the total volume of the cells with a point of \(Z\) is less than \(V_{\mathrm{B}_1} + \dots + V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{p}} + p \cdot \eta/(2p) < \eta/2 + \eta/2 = \eta\).

2. A boundary cell contains a boundary point.

  1. Let the boundary cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) contain a point \(P \in W\) and a point \(Q\) that is not in \(W\) (figure 4.80, left). The points are different, so \(|PQ| > 0\). For \(t \in [0, 1]\) let \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) be the point with the coordinates \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{Q}} - x_{\mathrm{P}})\), \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,(y_{\mathrm{Q}} - y_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,(z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}})\). Since \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{Q}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}) = (1 - t)\,x_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,x_{\mathrm{Q}}\) and \(1 - t\) and \(t\) are nonnegative numbers with the sum \(1\), this coordinate lies between \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{Q}}\), hence on the piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\). The same for \(y\) and \(z\). All points \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) therefore lie in the cell, \(P_0 = P\) and \(P_1 = Q\).
  2. Let \(T\) be the set of all \(t \in [0, 1]\) for which \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) lies in \(W\). It contains \(0\) and is bounded above by \(1\). By the completeness axiom 1.33 it has a supremum \(t^*\), and \(0 \le t^* \le 1\). Let \(B = P_{\mathrm{t}^*}\).
  3. The point \(B\) lies in \(W\). By theorem 1.34, item 2, for every natural number \(n\) there is a \(t_{\mathrm{n}} \in T\) with \(t^* - 1/n < t_{\mathrm{n}} \le t^*\). The sequence \((t^* - 1/n)\) converges to \(t^*\) by lemmas 1.40 and 1.61, and so does the constant sequence \(t^*, t^*, \dots\), so by the squeeze lemma 1.47 the sequence \((t_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(t^*\). By lemma 1.61 on limit laws for sequences the coordinates of the points \(P_{\mathrm{t}_\mathrm{n}}\) converge to the coordinates of the point \(B\), so by lemma 1.67 the points \(P_{\mathrm{t}_\mathrm{n}}\) converge to \(B\). All of them lie in \(W\), which is closed, so \(B\) lies in \(W\).
  4. Hence \(t^* \in T\), and \(t^* < 1\), because \(P_1 = Q\) is not in \(W\).
  5. The point \(B\) is a boundary point. Let \(r > 0\). The ball with centre \(B\) and radius \(r\) contains the point \(B\) of \(W\). Let \(t\) be the smaller of the numbers \(1\) and \(t^* + r/(2|PQ|)\). Both are larger than \(t^*\) (step 4), so \(t > t^*\), so \(t\) is not in \(T\), and the point \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) is not in \(W\). The vector from \(B\) to \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) has the components \((t - t^*)(x_{\mathrm{Q}} - x_{\mathrm{P}})\), \((t - t^*)(y_{\mathrm{Q}} - y_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \((t - t^*)(z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}})\), so by (1.10) the square of its length is \((t - t^*)^2\,|PQ|^2\). The nonnegative number \((t - t^*)\,|PQ|\) has this square, so by theorem 1.37 the length is \((t - t^*)\,|PQ| \le r/2 < r\). So the ball also contains the point \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\), which is not in \(W\). By definition 4.23, \(B\) is a boundary point of the set \(W\), and by step 1 it lies in the cell.

3. Boundary cells of a set with volume.

  1. A set with volume \(W\) is closed, and its boundary has zero volume (definition 4.27). For \(\eta > 0\) we take the \(\delta\) that the first item gives for the boundary of the set \(W\) in place of \(Z\).
  2. For a grid with pieces shorter than \(\delta\), every boundary cell of the set \(W\) contains a boundary point by the second item. So the boundary cells are among the cells of the first item, which have a total volume less than \(\eta\).

4. The plane.

  1. The steps are the same, with two coordinates. In step 6 of the first item, instead of three slabs there are two strips of width \(2\delta\) (figure 4.81, left), \(s_1' s_2' - s_1 s_2 = (s_1' - s_1)\,s_2' + s_1\,(s_2' - s_2)\), so a \(\delta\) less than \(1\) and than \(\eta/(8\,p\,(\Lambda + 2))\) suffices. The factor \(8 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2\) comes from the two strips, from the width \(2\delta\) and from half the error, \(\eta/2\), shared among \(p\) rectangles.

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. LEBL2 in the proof of Proposition 10.5.3 (PDF pp. 124-125) likewise compares the rectangles of a partition that lie in the set with those that meet it.

The first item showed how a grid meets a cover. The grid does not know the boxes \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\) that cover the boundary, but since the cells are small, every cell that touches the boundary lies in a box enlarged by \(\delta\), and the enlargement increases the volume only a little. The second item found a boundary point by a supremum. The last point of the segment that still lies in \(W\) is a boundary point, because right after it there are points outside \(W\). We used the closedness of the set \(W\) only in step 3, so that the point \(B\) lies in \(W\). For a set that is not closed, \(B\) may lie outside it, but it is still a boundary point, because every ball around it contains the point itself and the points \(P_{\mathrm{t}_\mathrm{n}}\) of \(W\). So the requirement does not narrow the conclusion, it only shortens the proof, and our bodies are closed. On the cross section of the bar the table shows what the third item promises: for \(h = 0{,}1\) mm the grey cells have a total area of \(3{,}96\) mm², so below \(\eta = 4\) mm².

With this we have what we need for the definition of the integral. For a set with volume the cells along the boundary have an arbitrarily small total volume for a fine enough grid, so the sum may leave them out. The next section tells how.

4.2.10 The integral without an order

The weight of a bar is an integral over its body. So far we have always computed such an integral along some path: in a chosen order of the variables and with a chosen cut into pieces. If another path gave another number, the weight would not be a property of the bar but of our calculation. So in this section we define the integral without a path, as the number that the sums over the cells of a grid approach, and then show that every path leads to it. Figure 4.69 shows the idea: we add up over the blue cells that lie in the cross section, leave out the grey cells at the edge, and make the grid finer.

Recall what theorem 4.9 on the order of integration says in item 1. We cut a box by a grid into cells, choose a point in each cell and add up the values of the function at these points times the volumes of the cells. For ever finer grids these sums approach the iterated integral, in any order. For a set \(W\) that is not a box we do the same, except that we add up only the cells that lie in \(W\). We leave out the boundary cells. For a set with volume they have a small total volume for a fine grid by lemma 4.29, so with them we leave out only a small part of the set. We must also leave out the boundary cells because the function may not even be defined outside \(W\), and in a boundary cell we could choose a point outside \(W\).

Definition 4.30 Integral over a set with volume (integral po množici s prostornino)

Let \(W\) be a set with volume (definition 4.27) and \(f\) a function that is continuous on \(W\) (definition 1.68). A number \(I\) is the integral (integral) of the function \(f\) over the set \(W\) if for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) with the following property. For every box that contains \(W\), for every grid of it in which all pieces of the partitions are shorter than \(\delta\), and for every choice of a point \(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) in each cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) that lies in \(W\),

\[\Big| \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{W}} f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} - I \Big| < \eta . \tag{4.15}\]

The sum runs over the cells that lie in \(W\), and it is zero if there are no such cells. We write the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). The integral of the constant function \(1\) is the volume (prostornina) of the set \(W\), \(V_{\mathrm{W}} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} 1\,\mathrm{d}V\).

In the plane \(M\) is a set with area, the cells are rectangles \(K_{\mathrm{ij}}\) with the areas \(\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the sum in (4.15) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ij}} \subseteq \mathrm{M}} f(Q_{\mathrm{ij}})\,\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), we write the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{M}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\), and the area (ploščina) of the set \(M\) is \(A_{\mathrm{M}} = \int_{\mathrm{M}} 1\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF pp. 478-479) defines the triple integral as the limit of sums over the boxes of a grid that lie entirely in the body, and §10.3 (PDF pp. 452-453) the double integral likewise with rectangles that lie entirely in the region. LEBL2 Def. 10.5.4 (PDF pp. 124-125) extends the function by zero outside the set and integrates over a rectangle, and defines the volume of a set on PDF p. 123.

What goes in and what comes out? In go a set with volume \(W\) and a continuous function \(f\) on it, out comes one number. The definition mentions neither an order of integration nor a cut, only the cells of grids that lie in \(W\). The requirement holds for all grids of all boxes that contain \(W\), not only for some chosen sequence of grids. This is exactly why the number will belong to the set and not to our choice of grid. For the function \(1\) the sum (4.15) is the total volume of the cells that lie in \(W\). For the cross section of the round bar these are the areas of the blue cells from the table in section 4.2.9. For cells with the sides \(1\) mm, \(0{,}5\) mm, \(0{,}25\) mm and \(0{,}1\) mm they are \(60\), \(69\), \(73{,}5\) and \(76{,}44\) mm², and they approach \(78{,}54\) mm².

For a function that is not constant we must also choose a point in each cell. Let us see in numbers how much the choice matters. Take the function \(y^2 + z^2\), the square of the distance from the axis of the bar, on the same cross section and with the same grids. In each blue cell we choose once the corner nearest to the axis and once the corner farthest from it. NumPy gives the sums (4.15) in mm⁴:

side of the cell nearest corner farthest corner difference
1 mm 376 832 456
0,5 mm 628 904,5 276,5
0,25 mm 786,4 937,6 151,2
0,1 mm 898,3 962,3 64,0

The iterated integral over the disc gives \(625\pi/2 = 981{,}7\) mm⁴ (SymPy). That this really is the number the sums approach will be said only by theorem 4.33, but the table already shows it. It also shows both things the definition requires. The difference between the two choices of points falls, because a continuous function changes little on a small cell. And both sums grow towards the same number, because the grey boundary cells that we leave out take up less and less area, \(36\), \(19\), \(9{,}75\) and \(3{,}96\) mm². The function is not larger than \(25\) mm² on the cross section, so with them we leave out at most \(25 \cdot 3{,}96 = 99\) mm⁴ for the finest grid.

The definition has two assumptions, and the table shows what each one does. The first is the continuity of the function \(f\) on \(W\). Because of it the last column of the table falls. Without it the definition fails: a function that is \(1\) at the points with a rational \(y\) and \(0\) elsewhere takes both values in every cell, so one choice of points would give the sum \(0\) and another the area of all blue cells, however fine the grid. The second assumption is that \(W\) has volume, hence a thin boundary (definition 4.27). Because of it the area of the grey cells falls. For a set whose boundary has a thickness, as the slab from section 4.2.9 has, the total volume of the boundary cells does not fall below the volume of the boundary, and the sum would leave out a part that does not become small.

The symbol \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) already has a meaning for a box, for a body made of boxes, for a body between graphs and for a body cut into pieces. That the new definition gives the same number for all these bodies we show in the rest of this section. Until then we will say for every integral by which definition we take it.

The definition states that the number \(I\) is the integral if it has the property. Does such a number exist at all, and is there only one? For a general set we have no iterated integral that could be a candidate, so we find the number by a supremum, as we found the integral over an interval by the supremum of the lower sums in section 3.5.3. For a nonnegative function we take, in each cell that lies in \(W\), the smallest value of the function on the cell and add up the products with the volumes of the cells. This gives a lower sum. When we refine the grid, the lower sum does not decrease (figure 4.82). In the figure \(W\) is an ellipse, in the left grid the cells in \(W\) are light blue and the boundary cells grey, and in the right grid, twice as fine, the cells in \(W\) that came from old boundary cells are darker blue, the grid being twice as fine. Every old cell in \(W\) splits into new cells, which also lie in \(W\) and have smallest values at least as large, because each new cell is part of the old one and the function on it takes no value below the smallest on the whole old cell. New cells that lie in \(W\) can appear only in old boundary cells, and they contribute nonnegative terms. The supremum of the lower sums is the candidate for the integral. That the lower sum of every fine enough grid is close to it follows from two estimates. When a fine grid is refined, the values on the old cells change little, because the function is uniformly continuous, and the new cells lie in boundary cells, which have a small total volume.

In the proof we will have to compare grids of two different boxes, since the definition allows every box that contains \(W\) (figure 4.83). On the left is the set \(W\) in the box \(K\) with the grid \(G\). We take a larger box \(K'\) and draw the lines of the grid \(G\) on to its edge. This makes new cells. Each of them reaches over the edge of the box \(K\), so it has points outside \(W\), and the sum over the cells in \(W\) stays the same. On the right the same box \(K'\) has, besides the extended first grid, the grid \(G_*\) of a second box \(K_*\), extended in the same way. All lines together are the grid \(H\), a refinement of both. The cell \(C\) of the first grid, which lies in \(W\), splits in the grid \(H\) into four cells that together take up the same area.

The proof needs five auxiliary figures. The first (figure 4.84) shows why a cube contains the set \(W\). Drawn are the axes with the origin \(O\) and around them the set \(W\). A set with volume is closed and bounded (definition 4.27). Let \(W\) not be empty. The square of the distance from the origin \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\) is a polynomial, so it is continuous (corollary 1.70, item 2), and by theorem 1.79 it has a largest value on \(W\). By lemma 1.29 the same point also has the largest distance from the origin. This is the point \(P\), and the distance \(|\overrightarrow{OP}|\) is the number we call \(R\). So the set lies in the circle of radius \(R\), and that in the cube \(K_0\) with the side \(2R + 2\). Boundedness alone is not enough for the point \(P\): the circle of radius \(R\) without its circumference is bounded, but it has no farthest point, because for each of its points there is another on the same radius that is closer to the circumference. The grid \(G\) cuts the cube into cells.

The second figure (figure 4.85) is a number line on which all sums of the proof will lie. It starts at zero. Between zero and the bound \(M\,V_0\) lie the lower sums of all grids, and their supremum \(I\) is the least upper bound. Around \(I\) are three bands: the band with the error \(\eta\), the narrower band with the error \(\eta/2\) and the thirds \(\eta/3\). In them lies the sum \(\Sigma\) over cells, and also the number \(I'\), if there were another number with the property of the definition.

The third (figure 4.86) shows how a continuous function becomes nonnegative. Over a piece \(W\) of the axis and the axes lies the graph of the function \(f\), which has a smallest value \(m_0\). The difference \(f - m_0\) is nonnegative everywhere, and the strip under it, of height \(m_0\), is what we add back to the integral.

The fourth (figure 4.87) shows one cell. Over the axes stands the cell \(C\), whose piece is shorter than \(\delta\), and over it the graph of the function \(f\). On the cell \(f\) has the smallest value \(m_{\mathrm{C}}\), and all values lie in a band of width \(\eta/(3V_0)\). The point \(P\) and the point \(Q_{\mathrm{C}}\) are two points of the cell, closer than \(\delta_1\).

The fifth (figure 4.88) shows the main estimate of the proof on a number line. On it are the supremum \(I\), the number \(I - \eta/3\) and the number \(I - \eta\). The lower sum \(s(f, H)\) of the common refinement \(H\) lies between \(I - \eta/3\) and \(I\). The lower sum \(s(f, G)\) of the fine grid \(G\) is smaller, but not by much. The sum \(s(f, H)\) is at most \(s(f, G)\) plus two contributions. The old cells in \(W\) add at most \(\eta/3\), because the values of the function on each of them differ by less than \(\eta/(3V_0)\). The new cells in old boundary cells add at most \(M\,\eta/(3M + 3)\), which is less than \(\eta/3\), because the boundary cells have a small total volume. Together the two contributions are shorter than \(2\eta/3\). So \(s(f, G)\) lies to the right of the number that is \(2\eta/3\) to the left of \(I - \eta/3\), that is, to the right of \(I - \eta\).

Theorem 4.31 Existence of the integral over a set with volume (obstoj integrala po množici s prostornino)

Let \(W\) be a set with volume and \(f\) a function that is continuous on \(W\). Then the function \(f\) has exactly one integral over the set \(W\) (definition 4.30), the number \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). The same holds in the plane.

Proof

We must show that such a number exists and that there is only one. We show existence first for nonnegative functions, with lower sums and the completeness axiom, and then for all continuous functions. In the proof \(G\) denotes grids, \(C\) cells of the grid \(G\) and \(C'\) cells of a finer grid.

1. The empty set.

  1. If \(W\) is empty, no cell lies in it, and every sum (4.15) is zero. The number \(0\) then has the property of the definition. From now on let \(W\) not be empty.

2. A box that contains all the cells.

  1. The set \(W\) is bounded, so there is a number \(R\) with \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\) for every point \(P \in W\). No coordinate is larger in absolute value than the distance from the origin (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.67), so \(W\) lies in the cube \(K_0 = [-R - 1, R + 1] \times [-R - 1, R + 1] \times [-R - 1, R + 1]\) with the volume \(V_0 = (2R + 2)^3\).
  2. Let \(G\) be a grid of a box that contains \(W\). The cells of the grid \(G\) that lie in \(W\) lie in \(K_0\), so by lemma 4.28, item 2, their total volume is at most \(V_0\).

3. Lower sums of a nonnegative function. Up to the end of the sixth part let \(f(P) \ge 0\) for every point \(P \in W\). Then the new cells in \(W\) contribute nonnegative terms, so that the lower sum does not fall under refinement (step 3 of the fourth part). For a function with negative values a new cell could lower it. For \(f = -1\) on the cross section of the bar the lower sum is minus the area of the blue cells, \(-60\) mm² at \(h = 1\) mm and \(-69\) mm² after refining to \(h = 0{,}5\) mm, and it falls by \(9\) mm². The seventh part removes the restriction by shifting the function by its smallest value.

  1. Let \(G\) be a grid of a box that contains \(W\), and \(C\) a cell of it that lies in \(W\). The cell is nonempty, closed and bounded (section 1.13.4), and \(f\) is continuous on it, because continuity on a part of a set checks only a part of the points. By theorem 1.79, \(f\) has a smallest value \(m_{\mathrm{C}}\) on \(C\). The lower sum of the function \(f\) for the grid \(G\) is the number
    \[s(f, G) = \sum_{\mathrm{C} \subseteq \mathrm{W}} m_{\mathrm{C}}\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}} .\]
  2. By theorem 1.79, \(f\) has a largest value \(M\) on \(W\). Since \(0 \le m_{\mathrm{C}} \le M\), by step 2 of the second part \(0 \le s(f, G) \le M\,V_0\).
  3. The set of all lower sums for all grids of all boxes that contain \(W\) is nonempty, because the cube \(K_0\) has a grid with a single cell, and it is bounded above by \(M\,V_0\). By the completeness axiom 1.33 it has a supremum, which we call \(I\). For every grid \(G\), \(s(f, G) \le I\).

4. Extension and refinement of a grid.

  1. Extension (figure 4.83, left). Let \(G\) be a grid of a box \(K\) that contains \(W\), and \(K'\) a box that contains \(K\). We add the end points of the edges of the box \(K'\) to the partitions of the grid \(G\) and get a grid \(G'\) of the box \(K'\). The cells of the grid \(G\) are cells of the grid \(G'\). Every new cell has a piece outside the corresponding edge of the box \(K\), for example the piece \([a_1', a_1]\) to the left of the edge \([a_1, b_1]\). Every cell that lies in a new cell contains a point whose coordinate lies strictly inside this piece, and this point is not in \(K\), hence not in \(W\). So no new cell and no cell that lies in a new cell lies in \(W\). The lower sum and the sums (4.15) for the grid \(G'\) are the same as for \(G\).
  2. Refinement (figure 4.83, right). Let \(H\) be a grid of the same box as \(G'\) whose partitions contain all points of the partitions of the grid \(G'\). Between two consecutive points of a partition of the grid \(H\) there is no point of the partitions of the grid \(G'\), so a piece of the grid \(H\) lies in a piece of the grid \(G'\), and every cell \(C'\) of the grid \(H\) lies in a cell of the grid \(G'\). There is only one such cell, because two pieces of the same partition overlap at most in an end point. The cells \(C'\) that lie in a cell \(C\) of the grid \(G'\) have, by lemma 4.28, item 3, the total volume \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\), because the end points of the edges of the cell \(C\) are points of the partitions of the grid \(H\).
  3. The lower sum does not fall under refinement. If a cell \(C\) of the grid \(G'\) lies in \(W\), the cells \(C'\) in it also lie in \(W\), and their smallest values are at least \(m_{\mathrm{C}}\), because \(C'\) is a part of the cell \(C\). By step 2 their contribution to \(s(f, H)\) is at least \(m_{\mathrm{C}}\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\). The other cells of the grid \(H\) that lie in \(W\) contribute nonnegative terms, because \(f \ge 0\). Therefore \(s(f, G') \le s(f, H)\).

5. Fine grids have lower sums close to \(I\).

  1. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 1.34, item 2, there is a grid \(G_*\) of some box \(K_*\) that contains \(W\) with \(s(f, G_*) > I - \eta/3\).
  2. By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|f(P) - f(Q)| < \eta/(3V_0)\) for any points \(P, Q \in W\) with \(|PQ| < \delta_1\). By lemma 4.29, item 3, there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that for every grid of a box that contains \(W\), with pieces shorter than \(\delta_2\), the boundary cells of the set \(W\) have a total volume less than \(\eta/(3M + 3)\). Let \(\delta\) be less than the numbers \(\delta_1/2\) and \(\delta_2\).
  3. Let \(G\) be a grid of a box \(K\) that contains \(W\), with pieces shorter than \(\delta\). Two points of the same cell are closer than \(\delta_1\), as in step 2 of the proof of theorem 4.9. On a cell \(C\) that lies in \(W\) every value of the function \(f\) is therefore less than \(m_{\mathrm{C}} + \eta/(3V_0)\).
  4. Let \(K'\) be a box that contains \(K\) and \(K_*\): on each axis it reaches from the smaller to the larger end point of the two edges. By step 1 of the fourth part we extend the grids \(G\) and \(G_*\) to grids \(G'\) and \(G_*'\) of the box \(K'\) with the same lower sums. Let \(H\) be the grid of the box \(K'\) whose partitions are the unions of the partitions of the grids \(G'\) and \(G_*'\). By step 3 of the fourth part, \(s(f, H) \ge s(f, G_*') = s(f, G_*) > I - \eta/3\).
  5. Let us also estimate \(s(f, H)\) from above. We sort the cells of the grid \(H\) that lie in \(W\) by the cells of the grid \(G'\) in which they lie (step 2 of the fourth part). If a cell \(C\) of the grid \(G'\) lies in \(W\), it is by step 1 of the fourth part a cell of the grid \(G\), and by step 3 all values on it are less than \(m_{\mathrm{C}} + \eta/(3V_0)\). The cells \(C'\) in it therefore have smallest values less than this number, and by step 2 of the fourth part the total volume \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\). Their contribution is at most \(m_{\mathrm{C}}\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\), increased by \(\eta\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}/(3V_0)\).
  6. Let a cell \(C\) of the grid \(G'\) not lie in \(W\) but contain a cell \(C'\) of the grid \(H\) that lies in \(W\). Then \(C\) has points in \(W\) and a point outside \(W\), so it is a boundary cell. By step 1 of the fourth part it is not a new cell of the extension, so it is a boundary cell of the grid \(G\). The cells \(C'\) in it have, by lemma 4.28, item 2, a total volume of at most \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\), and their smallest values are at most \(M\). Their contribution is at most \(M\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\).
  7. We add up over the cells of the grid \(G'\). The total volume of the cells of the grid \(G\) that lie in \(W\) is at most \(V_0\) by step 2 of the second part, and the total volume of the boundary cells of the grid \(G\) is less than \(\eta/(3M + 3)\) by step 2 of this part. Therefore
    \[s(f, H) \le s(f, G) + \frac{\eta}{3V_0}\,V_0 + M\,\frac{\eta}{3M + 3} < s(f, G) + \frac{2\eta}{3} .\]
  8. From steps 4 and 7 it follows that \(s(f, G) > s(f, H) - 2\eta/3 > I - \eta\). By step 3 of the third part, \(s(f, G) \le I\).

6. Sums over cells of a nonnegative function.

  1. Let \(G\) be the grid of step 3 of the fifth part and \(Q_{\mathrm{C}}\) a point in a cell \(C\) that lies in \(W\). By the same step \(m_{\mathrm{C}} \le f(Q_{\mathrm{C}}) < m_{\mathrm{C}} + \eta/(3V_0)\). We multiply by \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\) and add up. By step 2 of the second part the sum (4.15), which we call \(\Sigma\), lies between \(s(f, G)\) and \(s(f, G) + \eta/3\).
  2. By step 8 of the fifth part therefore \(I - \eta < \Sigma < I + \eta/3\), so \(|\Sigma - I| < \eta\). The number \(I\) has the property of definition 4.30, with the \(\delta\) of step 2 of the fifth part.

7. Any continuous function.

  1. By theorem 1.79, \(f\) has a smallest value \(m_0\) on \(W\). The function \(f - m_0\) is continuous (corollary 1.70, item 1) and nonnegative, and so is the constant function \(1\). By parts 3 to 6 there are numbers \(I_1\) and \(V\) with the property of the definition, the first for the function \(f - m_0\), the second for the function \(1\).
  2. Let \(I = I_1 + m_0 V\). For the same grid and the same points, the sum (4.15) for \(f\) equals the sum for \(f - m_0\) plus \(m_0 \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{W}} \Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}}\), where the last sum is the sum (4.15) for the function \(1\).
  3. We choose \(\eta > 0\). Let \(\delta\) be less than the band that the property of the number \(I_1\) gives for the error \(\eta/2\), and less than the band that the property of the number \(V\) gives for the error \(\eta/(2|m_0| + 2)\). For a grid with pieces shorter than \(\delta\), by step 2 and by the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1), the sum for \(f\) differs from \(I\) by less than \(\eta/2 + |m_0|\,\eta/(2|m_0| + 2) < \eta\).

8. Only one number.

  1. Let the numbers \(I\) and \(I'\) have the property of the definition. We choose \(\eta > 0\) and take a \(\delta\) that is less than the bands that the properties of the numbers \(I\) and \(I'\) give for the error \(\eta/2\).
  2. By the Archimedean property 1.36 there is a grid of the cube \(K_0\) with equal pieces shorter than \(\delta\). We choose a point in each cell that lies in \(W\), and let \(\Sigma\) be the sum (4.15).
  3. By the triangle inequality, \(|I - I'| \le |I - \Sigma| + |\Sigma - I'| < \eta\). The error was arbitrary, so by lemma 1.35 \(|I - I'| = 0\).

9. The plane.

  1. The steps are the same, with rectangles in place of boxes and areas in place of volumes. In step 3 of the fifth part the square of the distance of two points of the same cell is less than \(2 \cdot \delta_1^2/4\).

Source: LEBL2 Proposition 10.5.5 (PDF p. 125): a bounded continuous function on a bounded Jordan measurable set is integrable. KREYSZIG (PDF pp. 453 and 478) states that the sums converge to a number that does not depend on the choice of the grids and the points, and leaves the proof to other books. The proof by lower sums over the cells that lie in the set is not from the sources.

The proof repeated the path by which we arrived at the integral over an interval in section 3.5.3, with two new moves: the extension of grids to a common box and the bound on the new cells by the boundary cells. Nowhere did we integrate over one variable at a time, so no order of integration appears in the proof. Both assumptions of the definition entered in step 2 of the fifth part. Continuity gives, by uniform continuity, values on each cell that differ by less than \(\eta/(3V_0)\). The thin boundary gives the boundary cells a total volume below \(\eta/(3M + 3)\). Without the first the middle term of the estimate in step 7 would not be small, without the second the last one.

For computing we need rules like those we know for the integral over a box. New is the rule for a set made of parts (figure 4.89). In the figure the disc, a cross section of the bar, is cut into the parts \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\) in a plane with the axes \(y\) and \(z\), and covered by a grid of cells. The grey cells are the boundary cells of the disc. In a cut the cells fall into three groups. A cell that lies in one part contributes to the sum of that part. A cell cannot lie in two parts at once. The disc around its centre \(S\) with a radius of half a side lies in the cell, so the centre would be an interior point of one part that lies in the other, which a cut does not allow. A cell that lies in the union but in no part crosses the cut and is a boundary cell of a part that it crosses. There are few such cells.

The rules of the lemma are shown by figure 4.90 in three columns, each on an axis with the piece \(W\). For linearity, the functions \(f\) and \(g\) add to \(f + g\) point by point. For monotonicity, the region under \(f\) is part of the region under \(g\). For the bound, the graph lies in the band between \(-c\) and \(c\).

The second sentence of item 2 compares the integrals of the same function over a set and over a part of it, and it requires \(f \ge 0\). Why is shown by figure 4.91 in the plane. The cross section of the bar \(W\) is a disc of radius \(5\) mm, its part \(W_1\) is the piece \(D\) with \(y \ge 3\) mm. With the same grid the sum (4.15) over the cells in \(W\) is the sum over the cells in \(D\) plus the terms of the cells that lie in \(W\) but not in \(D\). Each term has the sign of the function. We draw the integrals as columns along a vertical axis in square millimetres. For \(f = 1\) the integral over \(D\) is a column of height \(11{,}18\) mm², the other cells stack \(67{,}36\) mm² on it, and the integral over \(W\), \(78{,}54\) mm², is larger (areas by SymPy). For \(f = -1\) the column for \(D\) reaches down to \(-11{,}18\) mm², the other cells extend it downwards by \(67{,}36\) mm², and the integral over \(W\), \(-78{,}54\) mm², is smaller than the integral over \(D\). For a function with negative values the inequality can turn around, so item 2 requires \(f \ge 0\). For the volume, the mass and the weight the integrands are \(1\), the density and the weight per unit volume, which are not negative, so the condition holds there.

Item 6 has figure 4.92. On the left is the box \(K\), in which all cells of the grid lie, on the right the body made of boxes \(V\), composed of cells that have a common edge of zero volume.

Lemma 4.32 Properties of the integral over a set with volume (lastnosti integrala po množici s prostornino)

Let \(W\) be a set with volume, \(f\) and \(g\) functions that are continuous on \(W\), and \(\alpha\) a number. The integrals are integrals of definition 4.30.

  1. Linearity: \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} (f + g)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} \alpha f\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. Monotonicity: if \(f(P) \le g(P)\) for every point \(P \in W\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\). If \(W_1 \subseteq W\) is a set with volume and \(f(P) \ge 0\) for every point \(P \in W\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{W}_1} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). In particular \(V_{\mathrm{W}_1} \le V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  3. Bound: if \(|f(P)| \le c\) for every point \(P \in W\), for example with \(c = \max_{\mathrm{W}} |f|\), then \(\big|\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\big| \le c\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  4. Additivity: let \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\) be sets with volume, and let no interior point of any of them lie in another. Then their union \(W_1 \cup \dots \cup W_{\mathrm{m}}\) is a set with volume, and for every function \(f\) that is continuous on the union
    \[\int_{\mathrm{W}_1 \cup \dots \cup \mathrm{W}_\mathrm{m}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{W}_1} f\,\mathrm{d}V + \dots + \int_{\mathrm{W}_\mathrm{m}} f\,\mathrm{d}V . \tag{4.16}\]
  5. A set of zero volume: if \(W\) also has zero volume (definition 4.25), then \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\). In particular \(V_{\mathrm{W}} = 0\).
  6. A box and a body made of boxes: a box \(K\) and a body made of boxes \(V\) (definition 4.11) are sets with volume. For a function that is continuous on \(K\), the integral over \(K\) of definition 4.30 equals the integral over a box of definition 4.8, and \(V_{\mathrm{K}}\) is the product of the lengths of the edges. For a function that is continuous on \(V\), the integral over \(V\) of definition 4.30 equals the sum of definition 4.11, item 1.
  7. Estimate by cells: for every grid of a box that contains \(W\),
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{W}} \Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} \le V_{\mathrm{W}} \le \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{W}} \Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} + \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \text{ boundary}} \Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} ,\]
    where the last sum runs over the boundary cells of the set \(W\).

The same holds in the plane, with the area in place of the volume.

Proof

We must show seven items. In all of them we compare the sums (4.15) for the same grid and the same points and use that the integral is the only number with the property of the definition (theorem 4.31).

1. Linearity.

  1. The functions \(f + g\) and \(\alpha f\) are continuous on \(W\) (corollary 1.70, item 1), so their integrals exist.
  2. For the same grid and the same points, the sum (4.15) for \(f + g\) is the sum of the two sums for \(f\) and for \(g\).
  3. We choose \(\eta > 0\) and take a \(\delta\) that is less than the bands that the definition gives the integrals of the functions \(f\) and \(g\) for the error \(\eta/2\). For a grid with pieces shorter than \(\delta\), by step 2 and by the triangle inequality for numbers, the sum for \(f + g\) differs from the number \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\) by less than \(\eta\). So this number has the property of the definition for the function \(f + g\), and by theorem 4.31 it equals \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} (f + g)\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  4. The sum for \(\alpha f\) is \(\alpha\) times the sum for \(f\), so by lemma 1.6, item 2, its distance from \(\alpha \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) is \(|\alpha|\) times the distance of the sum for \(f\) from \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). The band that the definition gives for the error \(\eta/(|\alpha| + 1)\) therefore gives a distance less than \(\eta\).

2. Monotonicity.

  1. Let \(f \le g\) on \(W\) and \(\eta > 0\). A box that contains \(W\) exists, because \(W\) is bounded (step 1 of the second part of the proof of theorem 4.31). By the Archimedean property 1.36 there is a grid of it with pieces shorter than the bands that the definition gives both integrals for the error \(\eta\). With the same points the term \(f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) is not larger than the term \(g(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}}\), so the sum \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{f}}\) for \(f\) is not larger than the sum \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{g}}\) for \(g\), and
    \[\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V < \Sigma_{\mathrm{f}} + \eta \le \Sigma_{\mathrm{g}} + \eta < \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V + 2\eta .\]
  2. So the number \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\) is less than \(2\eta\) for every \(\eta > 0\), and by lemma 1.35 it is at most \(0\).
  3. Let \(W_1 \subseteq W\) be a set with volume and \(f \ge 0\) on \(W\). A box that contains \(W\) also contains \(W_1\), and a cell that lies in \(W_1\) also lies in \(W\). We choose points in the cells that lie in \(W\). The sum over the cells in \(W\) is the sum over the cells in \(W_1\) plus the nonnegative terms of the cells that lie in \(W\) but not in \(W_1\). As in steps 1 and 2 it follows that \(\int_{\mathrm{W}_1} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). For \(f = 1\) this is \(V_{\mathrm{W}_1} \le V_{\mathrm{W}}\). Here the condition \(f \ge 0\) enters: for \(f = -1\) and \(W_1 = D\) these terms are negative, and the integral over \(W\) is smaller than the integral over \(D\).

3. Bound.

  1. From \(|f(P)| \le c\) it follows that \(-c \le f(P) \le c\) for every point \(P \in W\).
  2. By item 1, \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} c\,\mathrm{d}V = c \int_{\mathrm{W}} 1\,\mathrm{d}V = c\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} (-c)\,\mathrm{d}V = -c\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\). By item 2, \(-c\,V_{\mathrm{W}} \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le c\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\), which written with the absolute value is \(\big|\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\big| \le c\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  3. If \(W\) is not empty, \(f\) has by theorem 1.79 a largest value \(M\) and a smallest value \(m\) on \(W\). The larger of the numbers \(|M|\) and \(|m|\) is the value of \(|f|\) at one of the points and a bound for \(|f(P)|\), because \(m \le f(P) \le M\). This is \(\max_{\mathrm{W}} |f|\).

4. Additivity.

  1. The union \(W = W_1 \cup \dots \cup W_{\mathrm{m}}\) is closed and bounded by lemma 4.24, item 3. By the same item every boundary point of the set \(W\) is a boundary point of one of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). The boundaries of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) have zero volume, so by lemma 4.26, item 2, so does their union, and by item 1 of the same lemma so does the boundary of the set \(W\), which lies in this union. The set \(W\) has volume.
  2. No cell lies in two of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). Suppose that a cell lies in \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) and in \(W_{\mathrm{l}}\) with \(k \ne l\). Let \(S\) be its centre and \(\rho\) half of its shortest edge. A point that is closer to \(S\) than \(\rho\) differs from \(S\) by less than \(\rho\) in every coordinate (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.67), so it lies in the cell. The ball with centre \(S\) and radius \(\rho\) therefore lies in \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), and \(S\) is an interior point of the set \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) that lies in \(W_{\mathrm{l}}\). This contradicts the assumption.
  3. A cell that lies in \(W\) but in none of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) is a boundary cell of one of them. Its point \(P\) lies in some \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), and since the cell does not lie in \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), it also has a point outside \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  4. Let \(c\) be the bound for \(|f|\) on \(W\) from item 3 (for an empty \(W\), \(c = 0\)). We choose \(\eta > 0\). We take a \(\delta\) that is less than the bands that the definition gives the integrals over \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\) for the error \(\eta/(3m)\), less than the band it gives the integral over \(W\) for the error \(\eta/3\), and less than the bands that lemma 4.29, item 3, gives the sets \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\) for the total volume \(\eta/(3m\,(c + 1))\).
  5. Let a grid of a box that contains \(W\), and hence every \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), have pieces shorter than \(\delta\). In each cell that lies in \(W\) we choose a point. By step 2 every cell that lies in one of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) lies in exactly one of them, and it lies in \(W\).
