The sum \(\Sigma\) over the cells in \(W\) is therefore the sum of the sums \(\Sigma_1, \dots, \Sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) over the cells in \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\) and of the sum over the cells that lie in \(W\) but in no \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). By step 3 these are boundary cells of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) with a total volume less than \(m \cdot \eta/(3m\,(c + 1))\), so the last sum is less than \(\eta/3\) in absolute value.
  6. By the triangle inequality for numbers
    \[\begin{aligned} & \Big| \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V - \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \int_{\mathrm{W}_\mathrm{k}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \Big| \\ & \quad \le \Big| \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V - \Sigma \Big| + \Big| \Sigma - \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \Sigma_{\mathrm{k}} \Big| \\ & \qquad + \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \Big| \Sigma_{\mathrm{k}} - \int_{\mathrm{W}_\mathrm{k}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \Big| \\ & \quad < \frac{\eta}{3} + \frac{\eta}{3} + m\,\frac{\eta}{3m} = \eta . \end{aligned}\]
    The error was arbitrary, so by lemma 1.35 the left side is zero.

5. A set of zero volume.

  1. Let \(W\) also have zero volume and let \(c\) be the bound for \(|f|\) from item 3. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By lemma 4.29, item 1, used for \(Z = W\), there is a \(\delta\) such that for a grid with pieces shorter than \(\delta\) the cells with a point of \(W\) have a total volume less than \(\eta/(c + 1)\).
  2. A cell that lies in \(W\) contains a point of \(W\). Since \(|f| \le c\), the sum (4.15) is therefore at most \(c\,\eta/(c + 1)\) in absolute value, which is less than \(\eta\). The number \(0\) has the property of the definition, and by theorem 4.31 \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\).

6. A box and a body made of boxes.

  1. The box \(K\) is a set with volume, as we showed in section 4.2.9. All cells of a grid of the box \(K\) lie in \(K\), so for a grid of the box \(K\) the sum (4.15) is the Riemann sum of theorem 4.9.
  2. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 4.9, item 1, with the error \(\eta/(2V_{\mathrm{K}})\), there is a \(\delta_1\) such that such a sum for pieces shorter than \(\delta_1\) differs from the integral over the box by at most \(\eta/2\). By definition 4.30 there is a \(\delta_2\) for the error \(\eta/2\). A grid of the box \(K\) with equal pieces shorter than both bands gives a sum that differs from both numbers by at most \(\eta/2\), so the numbers differ by at most \(\eta\). By lemma 1.35 they are equal. For \(f = 1\) the integral over the box equals the product of the lengths of the edges by lemma 4.10, item 2.
  3. A body made of boxes \(V\) is the union of cells of some grid. Two different cells differ in at least one piece, for example in the pieces \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\) and \([x_{\mathrm{i}'-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}'}]\) with \(i < i'\). An interior point of the first cell has an \(x\) coordinate less than \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\), because a ball around a point with the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) contains points with a larger coordinate \(x\), which are not in the cell. Points of the second cell have \(x \ge x_{\mathrm{i}'-1} \ge x_{\mathrm{i}}\). So no interior point of the first cell lies in the second, and likewise no interior point of the second lies in the first.
  4. By item 4, \(V\) is a set with volume and the integral over it is the sum of the integrals over the cells, and these are by step 2 the integrals over boxes of definition 4.8. This is the sum of definition 4.11, item 1.

7. Estimate by cells.

  1. Let \(G\) be a grid of a box \(K\) that contains \(W\), and \(\eta > 0\). Let \(\delta\) be the band that the definition gives the integral of the function \(1\) over \(W\) for the error \(\eta\). We add to the partitions of the grid \(G\) the points of partitions of the edges into equal pieces shorter than \(\delta\) (Archimedean property), and get a grid \(H\) of the same box with pieces shorter than \(\delta\) that contains all points of the partitions of the grid \(G\).
  2. The sum (4.15) for the function \(1\) and the grid \(H\) is the total volume of the cells of the grid \(H\) that lie in \(W\), and it differs from \(V_{\mathrm{W}}\) by less than \(\eta\).
  3. A cell of the grid \(G\) that lies in \(W\) is the union of the cells of the grid \(H\) that lie in it and therefore in \(W\). By lemma 4.28, item 3, these have a total volume equal to its volume. So the total volume of the cells of the grid \(G\) in \(W\) is not larger than the total volume of the cells of the grid \(H\) in \(W\), which is less than \(V_{\mathrm{W}} + \eta\).
  4. A cell of the grid \(H\) that lies in \(W\) lies in a cell of the grid \(G\) (step 2 of the fourth part of the proof of theorem 4.31), which has a point in \(W\), so it lies in \(W\) or is a boundary cell. The cells of the grid \(H\) in one cell of the grid \(G\) have, by lemma 4.28, item 2, a total volume of at most its volume. Therefore \(V_{\mathrm{W}} - \eta\) is less than the total volume of the cells of the grid \(G\) that lie in \(W\) or are boundary cells.
  5. The error was arbitrary, so by lemma 1.35 both inequalities follow from steps 3 and 4.

8. The plane.

  1. The steps are the same, with rectangles and areas.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.3, (1) (PDF p. 453), for double integrals: linearity and additivity for a region divided into two parts (Fig. 228). LEBL2 Proposition 10.5.2 (PDF p. 123) for unions, Proposition 10.5.7 (PDF p. 125) for additivity over disjoint sets. The proof is not from the sources.

Item 7 tells how to estimate a volume by a grid. For the cross section of the round bar, the grids of the table in section 4.2.9 give the estimates of the area \(A\) of the cross section

\[\begin{aligned} 60 &\le A \le 96 , & 69 &\le A \le 88 , \\ 73{,}5 &\le A \le 83{,}25 , & 76{,}44 &\le A \le 80{,}4 , \end{aligned}\]

in square millimetres. The lower bound is the area of the blue cells, the upper bound adds to it the area of the grey boundary cells, which is arbitrarily small for a fine grid by lemma 4.29. Item 4 is the rule for a cut. Its condition, that no interior point of one piece lies in another, allows two pieces to touch along the cut, because the cut has volume zero, but it forbids an overlap. If the piece \(D\) in figure 4.89 reached to \(y = 2\) mm, the sum of the integrals would count the orange strip \(2 \le y \le 3\) mm twice, and the sum of the areas would be larger than the area of the cross section by its \(8{,}634\) mm² (SymPy).

What remains is the link with the iterated integral. Let us take a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R\) and cut it by a grid whose partitions of the edges \([a, b]\) and \([c, d]\) cut \(R\) into rectangles \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Over each \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) stands a column of cells (figure 4.93). The figure shows a section in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(z\): the bottom lid \(g\) and the top lid \(h\) are curves, the grid has pieces of different lengths, the axes are drawn below and to the left, and the cells of the column over the piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\) that lie in the body are blue and run from the height \(\alpha\) to the height \(\beta\). The cells of the column that lie in the body fill almost the whole vertical chord from \(g\) to \(h\) over a chosen point \(p\) of the rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\). At each end at most as much is missing as \(g\) or \(h\) changes on \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), plus one cell. For a cell lies in the body only if all of it is above the largest value \(g_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of the bottom lid and below the smallest value \(h_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of the top lid on \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so the cell just below \(\alpha\) and the cell just above \(\beta\) are not blue. The sum over the column is therefore close to the inner integral \(F(p) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{p})}^{h(p)} f\,\mathrm{d}z\) times the area of the rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The sum over the columns is a Riemann sum of the continuous function \(F\) on the rectangle \(R\), which approaches the iterated integral by theorem 4.9. The right picture shows a column where the body is thinner than two cells. In its grid no cell lies in the body, because the two cells at it cross the lids. Then the sum over the column is zero, but the chord is short as well, and with it the inner integral.

Before the proof sums over columns, it must show that a body between two graphs has a thin boundary, since definition 4.30 requires a set with volume. Figure 4.94 shows how, again in a section by the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(z\). The body \(V\) lies between the lower lid \(g\) and the upper lid \(h\), over the piece from \(a\) to \(b\) on the axis \(x\). Take a point \(P\) that lies strictly between the lids and strictly between \(a\) and \(b\). The lids are continuous, so in the strip of width \(\rho\) on each side of \(x_0\) they move by less than \(\varepsilon/2\): \(g\) stays below the lower and \(h\) above the upper of the grey dashed bounds. The blue band of heights from \(z_0 - \varepsilon/2\) to \(z_0 + \varepsilon/2\) lies between the bounds, and the ball of radius \(r\) around \(P\) lies in the blue band. So every point \(Q\) of the ball lies in the body, and \(P\) is not on the boundary. Only the points on the lids and on the side pieces, where \(x = a\) or \(x = b\), remain on the boundary. A side piece is put into a grey box of thickness \(t\), whose volume is arbitrarily small for a small \(t\).

Theorem 4.33 Integral over a body between two graphs without an order (integral po telesu med grafoma brez vrstnega reda)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15), with any naming of the axes. Then \(V\) is a set with volume, and for every function \(f\) that is continuous on \(V\) the integral of definition 4.30 equals the iterated integral of definition 4.20:

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{4.17}\]

The same holds in the plane. If \(g\) and \(h\) are continuous functions on \([a, b]\) with \(g(x) \le h(x)\), the region \(M\) of the points \((x, y)\) with \(a \le x \le b\) and \(g(x) \le y \le h(x)\) is a set with area, and for every function \(f\) continuous on \(M\), \(\int_{\mathrm{M}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x})}^{h(x)} f(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x\). This also holds with the roles of the coordinates exchanged.

Proof

We must show that the boundary of the body has zero volume and that the sum (4.15) for a suitable fine grid is close to the iterated integral. We write the proof for a body in which the coordinate \(z\) runs between the graphs.

1. The body has volume.

  1. The body \(V\) is closed and bounded by lemma 4.17. The functions \(g\) and \(h\) are continuous on the open set \(U\) from the definition of the body, as in step 1 of the proof of that lemma.
  2. Interior points (figure 4.94). Let \(P = (x_0, y_0, z_0)\) be a point with \(a < x_0 < b\), \(c < y_0 < d\) and \(g(x_0, y_0) < z_0 < h(x_0, y_0)\). Let \(\varepsilon\) be a positive number less than the positive numbers \(z_0 - g(x_0, y_0)\) and \(h(x_0, y_0) - z_0\). By the continuity of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) at the point \((x_0, y_0)\) there is a \(\rho > 0\) such that at points of \(U\) closer to \((x_0, y_0)\) than \(\rho\), \(g\) and \(h\) differ from their values at \((x_0, y_0)\) by less than \(\varepsilon/2\). Let \(r\) be the smallest of the numbers \(\rho\), \(x_0 - a\), \(b - x_0\), \(y_0 - c\), \(d - y_0\) and \(\varepsilon/2\).
  3. Let \(Q = (x, y, z)\) be a point with \(|PQ| < r\). Every difference of coordinates is less than \(r\), so \(a < x < b\), \(c < y < d\) and \(|z - z_0| < \varepsilon/2\). Since \((x - x_0)^2 + (y - y_0)^2 \le |PQ|^2\), by lemma 1.29 the point \((x, y)\) is closer to \((x_0, y_0)\) than \(\rho\). Therefore
    \[g(x, y) < g(x_0, y_0) + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \le z_0 - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} < z < z_0 + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \le h(x_0, y_0) - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} < h(x, y) ,\]
    and \(Q\) lies in \(V\). The point \(P\) is an interior point of the body \(V\), so it is not a boundary point.
  4. The boundary. A boundary point of the body \(V\) lies in \(V\) by lemma 4.24, item 1, and by step 3 it has \(x_0 = a\) or \(x_0 = b\) or \(y_0 = c\) or \(y_0 = d\) or \(z_0 = g(x_0, y_0)\) or \(z_0 = h(x_0, y_0)\). The boundary therefore lies in the union of the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over \(R\) and of the four side pieces on which \(x = a\), \(x = b\), \(y = c\) or \(y = d\).
  5. The graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over \(R\) have zero volume by lemma 4.26, item 3.
  6. The side pieces. By theorem 1.79 there are numbers \(m\) and \(M'\) with \(m \le g\) and \(h \le M'\) on \(R\). The piece with \(x = a\) lies in the box \([a, a + t] \times [c, d] \times [m - 1, M' + 1]\) for every \(t > 0\). For every \(\eta > 0\) the volume of this box \(t\,(d - c)(M' - m + 2)\) is less than \(\eta\) when \(t < \eta/((d - c)(M' - m + 2))\), so by definition 4.25 the piece has zero volume. The same for the other three pieces.
  7. By lemma 4.26, items 2 and 1, the boundary has zero volume. The body \(V\) is a set with volume.

2. Choice of the numbers.

  1. Let \(f\) be continuous on \(V\). By theorem 4.31 the integral \(J = \int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) of definition 4.30 exists. We call the iterated integral on the right side of (4.17) \(I\), and the inner integral \(F(x, y) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\). By lemma 4.18, \(F\) has the property of item 1 of lemma 4.7, so it is continuous on \(R\).
  2. By theorem 1.79 there are numbers \(M > 0\) and \(H\) with \(|f| \le M\) on \(V\) and \(h - g \le H\) on \(R\). We need a positive \(M\) for the strict inequalities in the third part. Let \(A_{\mathrm{R}} = (b - a)(d - c)\) be the area of the rectangle \(R\).
  3. We choose \(\eta > 0\). Let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}} = \eta/(9\,(H + 1)\,A_{\mathrm{R}})\) and \(\omega = \eta/(18\,(M + 1)\,A_{\mathrm{R}})\). By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta_{\mathrm{f}} > 0\) such that \(|f(P) - f(Q)| < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}}\) for points \(P, Q \in V\) with \(|PQ| < \delta_{\mathrm{f}}\), and a \(\delta_{\mathrm{g}} > 0\) such that \(g\) and \(h\) differ by less than \(\omega\) at points of the rectangle \(R\) closer than \(\delta_{\mathrm{g}}\). By theorem 4.9, item 1, used for the rectangle, the function \(F\) and the error \(\eta/(3A_{\mathrm{R}})\), there is a \(\delta_{\mathrm{F}}\) such that a Riemann sum of the function \(F\) for a grid of the rectangle \(R\) with pieces shorter than \(\delta_{\mathrm{F}}\) differs from \(I\) by at most \(\eta/3\). By definition 4.30 there is a \(\delta_{\mathrm{J}}\) for the integral \(J\) and the error \(\eta/3\).
  4. Let \(\delta\) be a positive number less than \(\delta_{\mathrm{f}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{g}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{F}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{J}}\) and \(\omega\). The box \(K = [a, b] \times [c, d] \times [m - 1, M' + 1]\) contains \(V\). By the Archimedean property 1.36 we divide its edges into equal pieces shorter than \(\delta/2\). Two points of the same rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = [x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}]\) are then closer than \(\delta\), as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 4.26, item 3.

3. One column.

  1. Let \(p = (x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}})\) be a corner of the rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\). In each cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}} = R_{\mathrm{ij}} \times [z_{\mathrm{k}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}}]\) that lies in \(V\) we choose the point \(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}} = (x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z_{\mathrm{k}})\). We compare the sum over these cells \(S_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}}\) with the number \(F(p)\).
  2. Let \(g_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be the largest value of the function \(g\) and \(h_{\mathrm{ij}}\) the smallest value of the function \(h\) on \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (theorem 1.79). The cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) lies in \(V\) exactly when \(g_{\mathrm{ij}} \le z_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{k}} \le h_{\mathrm{ij}}\). If this holds, then for every point of the cell \(g(x, y) \le g_{\mathrm{ij}} \le z_{\mathrm{k}-1} \le z \le z_{\mathrm{k}} \le h_{\mathrm{ij}} \le h(x, y)\). Conversely, if the cell lies in \(V\), its point \((x, y, z_{\mathrm{k}-1})\), where \(g\) attains \(g_{\mathrm{ij}}\), also lies in \(V\), so \(g_{\mathrm{ij}} \le z_{\mathrm{k}-1}\), and likewise \(z_{\mathrm{k}} \le h_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  3. Since the point \(p\) and the point where \(g\) attains \(g_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are closer than \(\delta_{\mathrm{g}}\), we have \(g(p) \le g_{\mathrm{ij}} < g(p) + \omega\). Likewise \(h(p) - \omega < h_{\mathrm{ij}} \le h(p)\).
  4. The first case: no cell of the column lies in \(V\), and \(S_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\). Then \(h_{\mathrm{ij}} - g_{\mathrm{ij}} < \delta\). Indeed, suppose that \(h_{\mathrm{ij}} - g_{\mathrm{ij}} \ge \delta\). Let \(z_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the smallest point of the partition that is not less than \(g_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Since \(z_0 = m - 1 < g_{\mathrm{ij}}\), we have \(k \ge 1\) and \(z_{\mathrm{k}-1} < g_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so \(z_{\mathrm{k}} < g_{\mathrm{ij}} + \delta/2\), because the pieces are shorter than \(\delta/2\). Since \(z_{\mathrm{k}} < h_{\mathrm{ij}} \le M' < M' + 1\), there is a next point \(z_{\mathrm{k}+1} < z_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta/2 < g_{\mathrm{ij}} + \delta \le h_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By step 2 the cell with the piece \([z_{\mathrm{k}}, z_{\mathrm{k}+1}]\) would lie in \(V\), which contradicts the assumption of the case. By step 3 therefore \(h(p) - g(p) < h_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega - (g_{\mathrm{ij}} - \omega) < \delta + 2\omega\). By the bound (lemma 3.54, item 3), \(|S_{\mathrm{ij}} - F(p)| = |F(p)| \le M\,(h(p) - g(p)) < M\,(\delta + 2\omega)\).
  5. The second case: the cells of the column with indices from \(k_0\) to \(k_1\) lie in \(V\). The cells between them lie in \(V\) by step 2, because the points of the partition increase. Let \(\alpha = z_{\mathrm{k}_0 - 1}\) and \(\beta = z_{\mathrm{k}_1}\). Then \(g_{\mathrm{ij}} \le \alpha < g_{\mathrm{ij}} + \delta\). The first inequality follows from step 2. Since \(\alpha \ge g_{\mathrm{ij}} \ge m > m - 1 = z_0\), the cell with the piece \([z_{\mathrm{k}_0 - 1}, z_{\mathrm{k}_0}]\) has a predecessor with the piece \([z_{\mathrm{k}_0 - 2}, \alpha]\). It does not lie in \(V\), because \(k_0\) is the smallest index, and its upper end is \(\alpha \le \beta \le h_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By step 2 therefore \(z_{\mathrm{k}_0 - 2} < g_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and \(\alpha < z_{\mathrm{k}_0 - 2} + \delta/2 < g_{\mathrm{ij}} + \delta\). Likewise \(h_{\mathrm{ij}} - \delta < \beta \le h_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By step 3 therefore \(0 \le \alpha - g(p) < \omega + \delta\) and \(0 \le h(p) - \beta < \omega + \delta\).
  6. For \(z\) from the piece \([z_{\mathrm{k}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}}]\) with \(k_0 \le k \le k_1\) the point \((x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z)\) lies in \(V\), because \(g(p) \le \alpha \le z \le \beta \le h(p)\), and it is closer to \(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) than \(\delta < \delta_{\mathrm{f}}\). Therefore \(|f(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z) - f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})| < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}}\), and by the bound
    \[\Big| \int_{\mathrm{z}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{z_{\mathrm{k}}} f(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z)\,\mathrm{d}z - f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}} \Big| \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}}\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}} .\]
    We add up over \(k\) and use additivity (lemma 3.54, item 2) and the triangle inequality for numbers: \(\big|\int_\alpha^\beta f(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z)\,\mathrm{d}z - S_{\mathrm{ij}}\big| \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}}\,(\beta - \alpha) \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}} H\).
  7. By additivity \(F(p) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{p})}^{\alpha} + \int_\alpha^\beta + \int_\beta^{h(p)}\), all with the integrand \(f(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z)\). The first and the last part are less than \(M\,(\omega + \delta)\) in absolute value by the bound and step 5. By the triangle inequality, \(|S_{\mathrm{ij}} - F(p)| < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}} H + 2M\,(\omega + \delta)\).
  8. In both cases \(|S_{\mathrm{ij}} - F(p)| < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}} H + 2M\,(\omega + \delta)\), because \(M\,(\delta + 2\omega)\) is at most \(2M\,(\omega + \delta)\).

4. All columns.

  1. The partitions of the edges \([a, b]\) and \([c, d]\) cut \(R\) into the rectangles \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so every cell lies over exactly one of them. Since \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} = \Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}}\), where \(\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the area of the rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the sum (4.15) with the chosen points equals \(\Sigma = \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} S_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  2. By the third part and by the triangle inequality
    \[\Big| \Sigma - \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} F(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}} \Big| < \big( \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}} H + 2M\,(\omega + \delta) \big)\,A_{\mathrm{R}} < \frac{\eta}{9} + \frac{4M\,\eta}{18\,(M + 1)} < \frac{\eta}{3} ,\]
    because \(\delta < \omega\) and the areas \(\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\) add up to \(A_{\mathrm{R}}\).

5. Conclusion.

  1. The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} F(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is a Riemann sum of the function \(F\) for a grid of the rectangle \(R\) with pieces shorter than \(\delta_{\mathrm{F}}\), so it differs from \(I\) by at most \(\eta/3\) (step 3 of the second part).
  2. The grid is a grid of a box that contains \(V\), with pieces shorter than \(\delta_{\mathrm{J}}\), so \(|\Sigma - J| < \eta/3\).
  3. By the triangle inequality, \(|J - I| < \eta/3 + \eta/3 + \eta/3 = \eta\). The error was arbitrary, so by lemma 1.35 \(J = I\).

6. Other namings of the axes and the plane.

  1. For another naming of the axes the steps are the same, only the coordinates exchange roles. Definition 4.30 treats all three coordinates alike, so it does not change.
  2. In the plane the region \(M\) is closed and bounded by the proof of lemma 4.17 with one coordinate less. Its boundary lies in the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) and in the segments \(x = a\) and \(x = b\), which have zero area. The columns stand over the pieces \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\). The function \(F(x) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x})}^{h(x)} f(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}y\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) by the proof of lemma 4.18 in which the points \((x, y)\) of the rectangle are replaced by numbers \(x\), and in place of theorem 4.9 we use theorem 3.53, item 3.

Source: LEBL2 Proposition 10.5.8 (PDF p. 126) for a region between the graphs of continuous functions in the plane, with the proof left to the reader. KREYSZIG §10.3, (3) (PDF p. 453), and §10.7 (PDF p. 479) use the iterated integral for computing, without proof. The proof is not from the sources.

The proof used only the continuity of the functions \(g\) and \(h\), not their derivatives. We need the derivatives for the lids and for the divergence theorem, not for the integral over the body. Continuity entered in step 3 of the third part: on a small rectangle \(g\) and \(h\) change by less than \(\omega\), so the uncovered ends of the chord are shorter than \(\omega + \delta\). For a lid with a jump this estimate fails (figure 4.95). We draw the figure as figure 4.93, with the axes, the upper lid \(h\) and the grid of the column over the piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\). The lower lid \(g\), however, jumps by \(1\) mm in the middle of the piece. The largest value \(g_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is on the upper side of the jump, so the cells of the column that lie in the body start only above it. The chord over the point \(p\) lies on the lower side of the jump and starts at \(g(p)\), \(1\) mm lower. The uncovered piece of the chord is therefore at least \(1\) mm long, however fine the grid, and step 7 of the third part no longer has a small bound. For continuous lids, such as those of a body between two graphs, the theorem holds: the iterated integral by which we defined the integral in section 4.2.8 is indeed the limit of sums over cells.

The answer to both questions follows at once from the theorem.

Corollary 4.34 The integral does not depend on the order or the cut (integral ni odvisen od vrstnega reda in razreza)

Let \(f\) be a function that is continuous on a set of points \(V\).

  1. If \(V\) is a body between graphs for two namings of the axes, the iterated integrals of the function \(f\) over \(V\) (definition 4.20) for the two namings are equal.
  2. If \(V\) is cut into the pieces \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\) (definition 4.21), \(V\) is a set with volume, and the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \int_{\mathrm{V}_\mathrm{k}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) of definition 4.21 equals the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) of definition 4.30. Hence it is the same for all cuts of the same body.

The same holds in the plane for a region that is the union of regions between graphs, of which no interior point of one lies in another.

Proof

We must show both items. We compare both numbers with the integral of definition 4.30, which knows neither an order nor a cut.

  1. By theorem 4.33 each of the iterated integrals equals the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) of definition 4.30, so they are equal.
  2. By the same theorem every piece \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\) is a set with volume, and the iterated integral over it equals the integral over it of definition 4.30. By definition 4.21 no interior point of any piece lies in another. By lemma 4.32, item 4, \(V\) is therefore a set with volume, and \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) is the sum of the integrals over the pieces, that is, the sum of definition 4.21.
  3. Two cuts of the same body give sums that by step 2 both equal the same number \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  4. In the plane the steps are the same, with the plane form of the theorem and of the lemma.

Source: KREYSZIG (PDF pp. 453 and 478) states that the limit of the sums over cells does not depend on the choice of the grids and the points. The corollary and its proof are not from the sources.

Let us test the first item on a prism cut out of the round bar. Its cross section is the triangle with the vertices \((0, 0)\), \((3, 0)\) and \((3, 4)\) in millimetres, in the plane of the axes \(y\) and \(z\) (figure 4.96). The vertex \((3, 4)\) lies on the circle, because \(3^2 + 4^2 = 25\). The prism is the set of points with \(0 \le x \le L\), \(0 \le y \le 3\) and \(0 \le z \le 4y/3\). It lies in the bar. Indeed, for each of its points \(0 \le z \le 4y/3\), so \(z^2 \le 16y^2/9\) by lemma 1.29, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, and since \(0 \le y \le 3\), \(y^2 + z^2 \le y^2 + 16y^2/9 = 25y^2/9 \le 25\). The prism is a body between the graphs of the functions \(0\) and \(4y/3\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [0, 3]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(y\). But it is also a body between the graphs of the functions \(3z/4\) and \(3\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [0, 4]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(z\). Indeed, from \(0 \le z \le 4y/3\) and \(y \le 3\) it follows that \(z \le 4\) and \(y \ge 3z/4\), and conversely from \(3z/4 \le y \le 3\) and \(z \ge 0\) it follows that \(0 \le z \le 4y/3\). All four functions are linear and therefore continuously differentiable everywhere.

Let us integrate the function \(y^2 + z^2\), the square of the distance from the axis of the bar, which appears in the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) of the hanging bar in the term \(-0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\). In the first description the inner integral is over \(z\), along the vertical chords, in the second over \(y\), along the horizontal ones. SymPy gives

\[\int_0^3 \int_0^{4y/3} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y = \int_0^3 \frac{172}{81}\,y^3\,\mathrm{d}y = 43\ \text{mm}^4 ,\]
\[\int_0^4 \int_{3\mathrm{z}/4}^{3} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}z = \int_0^4 \Big( 9 + 3z^2 - \frac{57}{64}\,z^3 \Big)\,\mathrm{d}z = 43\ \text{mm}^4 .\]

The outer integral over \(x\) multiplies both numbers by \(L = 10\,000\) mm, and in both descriptions we get \(430\,000\ \text{mm}^5\). The inner integrals are different functions, the first depends on \(y\), the second on \(z\), but the final numbers are equal by corollary 4.34, item 1. For the function \(1\) both descriptions give the area of the triangle, \(6\) mm², half the product of the legs \(3\) and \(4\) mm.

Let us also test the second item on the round bar. In section 4.2.6 we cut it by the planes \(y = \pm 3\) mm. Now let us cut it by the planes \(y = \pm 4\) mm (figure 4.97, the old cut on the left, the new one on the right). The cross section of the bar is a disc in a plane with the axes \(y\) and \(z\). The middle piece consists of the points with \(-4 \le y \le 4\), between the graphs of the functions \(-q(y)\) and \(q(y)\), where \(q(t) = \sqrt{25 - t^2}\). The function \(q\) is continuously differentiable on \((-5, 5)\), which contains \([-4, 4]\), by lemma 4.16. The right piece consists of the points with \(y \ge 4\). For them \(z^2 \le 25 - 16 = 9\), so \(-3 \le z \le 3\), and the piece is a body between the graphs of the functions \(4\) and \(q(z)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-3, 3]\), like the piece \(D\) in section 4.2.6. The left piece is the same with \(-q(z)\) and \(-4\). SymPy gives the areas of the cross sections of the pieces

\[\int_{-4}^{4} 2\,q(y)\,\mathrm{d}y = 70{,}36\ \text{mm}^2 , \qquad \int_{-3}^{3} \big(q(z) - 4\big)\,\mathrm{d}z = 4{,}088\ \text{mm}^2 .\]

The middle piece with \(70{,}36\) mm² and the two side pieces with \(4{,}088\) mm² each give together \(70{,}36 + 2 \cdot 4{,}088 = 78{,}54\) mm², as for the cut by the planes \(y = \pm 3\) mm, where the middle piece with \(56{,}18\) mm² and the side pieces with \(11{,}18\) mm² each gave \(56{,}18 + 2 \cdot 11{,}18 = 78{,}54\) mm². The pieces are different, and so are their areas, but the sum is the same, as item 2 of corollary 4.34 predicts. So the area of the cross section is a property of the cross section, \(A = 78{,}54\) mm², and it lies between the bounds that item 7 of lemma 4.32 gave. Likewise the volume of the bar \(L\,A = 785\,400\ \text{mm}^3\) and its weight are properties of the bar.

With this the questions from the end of section 4.2.8 are answered. The integral over a body between graphs and over a body cut into pieces is a number that belongs to the body, not to a chosen order or cut. We still compute it by iterated integrals, because we know how to evaluate them, and the sum over cells tells what they mean. The next section moves from the body to its surface.

4.2.11 Integral over a curved surface

The surface of a body between graphs has six pieces (figure 4.55). The four side pieces are flat, in the planes \(x = a\), \(x = b\), \(y = c\) and \(y = d\), with the outward normals \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). Each is a region between graphs in its own plane. The piece in the plane \(x = a\) consists of the points \((a, y, z)\) with \(c \le y \le d\) and \(g(a, y) \le z \le h(a, y)\), and we will write the integral over it as an iterated integral, with the inner integral over \(z\). The two lids are new, and they are curved. How do we compute the area of a small patch on a curved lid, and where does the normal to it point?

Take the top lid, the graph of the function \(h\), and the patch on it above a small rectangle of the shadow with sides \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\) (figure 4.98). When we move from the point \((x, y)\) by \(\Delta x\) in the direction of the axis \(x\), the height of the lid changes by about \(\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\), by theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step, written for two variables. In the figure it looks like this: the level step \(\Delta x\) from the corner does not end on the lid but above it, by the size of the number \(\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\), which is negative here, because the drawn lid falls in the direction \(x\). The side of the patch above the side \(\Delta x\) is therefore about the vector \(\vek a\), which goes forward by \(\Delta x\) and down by that much. In the direction \(y\) the drawn lid rises, so the level step \(\Delta y\) ends below it by \(\frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,\Delta y\), and the side above the side \(\Delta y\) is about the vector \(\vek b\). Written out, they are

\[\vek a = \Big(\Delta x,\ 0,\ \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\Big) , \qquad \vek b = \Big(0,\ \Delta y,\ \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,\Delta y\Big) .\]

The patch is approximately the parallelogram spanned by \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\). By definition 2.33

\[\begin{aligned} \vek a\times\vek b &= \Big( 0 - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\,\Delta y,\ \ 0 - \Delta x\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,\Delta y,\ \ \Delta x\,\Delta y - 0 \Big) \\ &= \Big( -\frac{\partial h}{\partial x},\ -\frac{\partial h}{\partial y},\ 1 \Big)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y . \end{aligned}\]

By item 4 of lemma 2.34 this vector is perpendicular to both sides, hence to the patch, and its length is the area of the parallelogram (section 2.8.1). We write

\[\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = \Big( -\frac{\partial h}{\partial x},\ -\frac{\partial h}{\partial y},\ 1 \Big) .\]

The area of the patch is about \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\), and the unit normal to it is \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}/|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\) (definition 2.17). The component \(z\) of the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) is \(1\), so the normal points up, out of the body, which lies below the top lid. For the bottom lid we take the opposite vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = (\partial g/\partial x,\ \partial g/\partial y,\ -1)\), which points down, out of the body.

What did we assume here? We replaced the curved patch by a flat parallelogram. Let us see what that costs on a surface we know: the mantle of the round bar with the radius \(r = 5\) mm of section 4.2.6 (figure 4.99, all lengths in millimetres). The top lid of the middle piece \(C\) is the graph of the function \(q(y) = \sqrt{25 - y^2}\). It does not change in the direction \(x\), so we look at it in the cross section with the axes \(y\) and \(z\), where the patch is an arc and the parallelogram a straight segment. The small frame is enlarged on the left. Above the piece of the shadow from \(y = 2\) to \(y = 3\), of length \(\Delta y = 1\), lies an arc of the circle that starts at the point \(P = (2, \sqrt{21})\). By lemma 4.16 the slope at \(P\) is \(q'(2) = -2/\sqrt{21} = -0{,}436\). The level step \(1\) from \(P\) therefore ends \(0{,}436\) above the end of the side \(\vek b = (0,\ 1,\ -0{,}436)\), which is a piece of the tangent of length \(\sqrt{1 + 0{,}436^2} = 1{,}091\). The arc has the length \(1{,}160\) (computed by SymPy). The straight piece is thus \(5{,}9\ \%\) too short.

There are three things to know about this assumption.

  1. Why we may make it. The functions \(g\) and \(h\) are continuously differentiable by definition 4.15, so by theorem 1.89 the error of a step falls faster than the step. Figure 4.100 shows this with magnifications. Each panel is the frame of the one before, magnified ten times, so the level step from the point \(P\) is equally long in all three, although it measures \(1\), \(0{,}1\) and \(0{,}01\). At the step \(1\) the arc visibly parts from the piece of the tangent, at the step \(0{,}01\) we can no longer tell them apart. The lengths of the piece of the tangent and of the arc are \(1{,}091\) and \(1{,}160\) at the step \(1\), the difference is \(5{,}9\ \%\), \(0{,}10911\) and \(0{,}10964\) at the step \(0{,}1\), the difference is \(0{,}49\ \%\), and at the step \(0{,}01\) only \(0{,}05\ \%\). Here a step ten times shorter gives a relative error about ten times smaller. In general theorem 1.89 only guarantees that the relative error goes to zero.
  2. What it does to the result. Nothing. The top of figure 4.101 shows the lid of the piece \(C\) above the shadow, divided into \(6\) strips of width \(1\). Above each strip we draw the piece of the tangent from the left edge of the strip, the straight piece that the approximation uses. The sum of their lengths is \(6{,}473\), with \(60\) strips \(6{,}4354\) and with \(600\) strips \(6{,}43501\). The sums approach the length of the arc, \(6{,}43501\). The definition below takes the integral that such sums approach, not any single sum. The approximation by a parallelogram is only the way to the definition, and it is no longer in it.
  3. When it fails. Where the lid has no derivative. At the edge of the bar, at \(y = \pm 5\), the tangent is vertical, and the length \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| = r/q(y)\), which we compute below, grows beyond all bounds. The bottom of figure 4.101 shows its graph above the axis \(y\). At \(y = 4{,}9\) it is \(5{,}03\), at \(y = 4{,}99\) already \(15{,}8\). This is why we cut the bar at \(y = \pm 3\) into the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\). This way \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\) is, on the lids of the piece \(C\), between the cuts, at most \(5/4\), and on the lids of the pieces \(D\) and \(E\), where the variable \(z\) runs up to \(\pm 4\), at most \(5/3\).

The same figure gives a second view of the number \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\), the view of a roofer: a sloping roof has a larger area than the floor below it. The level step, the drop and the piece of the tangent are the sides of a right triangle. The piece of the tangent is the hypotenuse and is tilted from the level step by the angle \(\gamma\), so its length is \(\Delta y/\cos\gamma\). The normal \(\vek n\) is tilted from the vertical by the same angle, because the normal is perpendicular to the tangent and the vertical to the horizontal. At the point \(P\) we have \(\cos\gamma = 1/1{,}091 = 0{,}917\) and \(\gamma = 23{,}6^\circ\). On a lid that is tilted in one direction only, therefore,

\[|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\,\Delta x\,\Delta y = \frac{\Delta x\,\Delta y}{\cos\gamma} .\]

The area of the patch is the area of the shadow divided by the cosine of the tilt. This view shows two things. A roof is never smaller than its floor, \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| \ge 1\), also when the lid is tilted in both directions, because \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|^2 = 1 + (\partial h/\partial x)^2 + (\partial h/\partial y)^2\). We will use this in the proof of lemma 4.37. And for a vertical wall, \(\gamma = 90^\circ\), the shadow has no area, so such a surface cannot be described as a lid, and we describe it as a side piece.

The divergence theorem will add up the products \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\,\Delta A\) over the patches. In each of them the length of the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\), which has a root, cancels:

\[\vek v\cdot\frac{\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}}{|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|}\,|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\,\Delta x\,\Delta y = \vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\,\Delta x\,\Delta y = \Big( v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} \Big)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y .\]

This is what the divergence theorem will need. For the integral of a function that is not of the form \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\), however, the root remains.

The integrand on the lid is the value of a function at the point \((x, y, h(x, y))\), which depends on the point \((x, y)\) of the shadow through the function \(h\). Why do we care whether it is continuous? Because for a continuous integrand on a closed rectangle the iterated integral exists (step 3 of the proof of lemma 4.37), and for a discontinuous one we do not know that. The following lemma says that it is continuous. Its idea is the chain in figure 4.102. The points \(Q_1, Q_2, Q_3, \dots\) of the shadow approach the point \(Q_0\). The functions \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}}\) carry them to the points \(p(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) on the lid, which lie in the set \(W\), where \(f\) is continuous, and approach the point \(p(Q_0)\). The function \(f\) assigns to them numbers on the number line, which approach the number \(f(p(Q_0))\). The approach passes through both links of the chain.

Lemma 4.35 Continuity of a composite function (zveznost sestavljene funkcije)

Let \(f\) be a function that is continuous on a set of points of space \(W\). Let \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}}\) be functions defined on a set \(M\), which is an interval or a set of points of the plane, such that the point \(p(Q) = \big(p_{\mathrm{x}}(Q), p_{\mathrm{y}}(Q), p_{\mathrm{z}}(Q)\big)\) lies in \(W\) for every \(Q \in M\). If \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuous at the point \(Q_0 \in M\), the function \(Q \mapsto f(p(Q))\) is continuous at \(Q_0\).

Proof

We must show that the values \(f(p(Q_{\mathrm{n}}))\) converge to \(f(p(Q_0))\) for every sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(M\) that converges to \(Q_0\). We use the lemma on continuity through sequences twice.

  1. The first link of the chain. Let the sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(M\) converge to \(Q_0\). The function \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\) is continuous at \(Q_0\), so by lemma 1.69 on continuity through sequences of points (on an interval by lemma 1.62) \(p_{\mathrm{x}}(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) \to p_{\mathrm{x}}(Q_0)\). Likewise \(p_{\mathrm{y}}(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) \to p_{\mathrm{y}}(Q_0)\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}}(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) \to p_{\mathrm{z}}(Q_0)\).
  2. The second link of the chain. By lemma 1.67 on convergence coordinate by coordinate, the points \(p(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) therefore converge to \(p(Q_0)\). They all lie in \(W\), and \(f\) is continuous at \(p(Q_0)\), so by lemma 1.69 \(f(p(Q_{\mathrm{n}}))\) \(\to\) \(f(p(Q_0))\). The assumption that the points \(p(Q)\) lie in \(W\) enters here: outside \(W\) we know nothing about the function \(f\). On the lid it holds, because the lid is a piece of the surface \(S\) of the body \(V\), and so it also lies in \(V\).
  3. The sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) was arbitrary, so by the same lemma, in the other direction, the function \(Q \mapsto f(p(Q))\) is continuous at \(Q_0\).

Source: LEBL1 Proposition 3.2.7 (PDF p. 125) for functions of one variable. The proof with sequences for points is not from the sources.

Now we can write down how we integrate over the surface of a body between graphs.

Definition 4.36 Flux and integral over the surface of a body between two graphs (pretok in integral po površini telesa med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15). Its surface (površina) \(S\) consists of six pieces:

  • the top lid \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\), the points \((x, y, h(x, y))\) with \((x, y) \in R\), with the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) \(= \big(-\frac{\partial h}{\partial x},\ -\frac{\partial h}{\partial y},\ 1\big)\),
  • the bottom lid \(S_{\mathrm{g}}\), the points \((x, y, g(x, y))\) with \((x, y) \in R\), with the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = \big(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y},\ -1\big)\),
  • the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\), the points \((a, y, z)\) and \((b, y, z)\) with \(c \le y \le d\) and \(z\) between \(g\) and \(h\) at the point \((a, y)\) or \((b, y)\), with the vectors \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\),
  • the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\), the points \((x, c, z)\) and \((x, d, z)\) with \(a \le x \le b\) and \(z\) between \(g\) and \(h\) at the point \((x, c)\) or \((x, d)\), with the vectors \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\).

On every piece with the vector \(\vek N\) the outward unit normal (zunanja enotska normala) is \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\). The surface integral of a function \(f\) over the top lid is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d f\big(x, y, h(x, y)\big)\,\big|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}(x, y)\big|\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{4.18}\]

and over the bottom lid likewise, with \(g\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\). Over the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) it is the number \(\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(a, y)} f(a, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y\), over \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) the same with \(b\), over \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\) the number \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{c})}^{h(x, c)} f(x, c, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x\), over \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) the same with \(d\). The integral over the surface \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\) is the sum of these six numbers, when all the integrals exist. For a field \(\vek v\) the flux (pretok) of the field through the surface is the integral over the surface of the function \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\), \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\). For a body with exchanged roles of the coordinates we rename the coordinates in these formulas, so that the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) has the component \(1\) in the direction of the coordinate that runs between the graphs.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.6, (2) (PDF p. 469): \(\vek N = \vek r_{\mathrm{u}}\times\vek r_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\), (3) (PDF p. 469) for the flux and (6) (PDF p. 474): \(\iint_{\mathrm{S}} G\,\mathrm{d}A = \iint_{\mathrm{R}} G(\vek r(u, v))\,|\vek N(u, v)|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v\), and §10.5, Problem 13 (PDF p. 469), \(\vek N = (-f_{\mathrm{u}}, -f_{\mathrm{v}}, 1)\) for the surface \(z = f(x, y)\). The definition with the pieces of the surface of a body between graphs is not from the sources.

Lemma 4.37 Flux through the surface of a body between two graphs (pretok skozi površino telesa med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between graphs with the surface \(S\) of definition 4.36.

  1. If the function \(f\) is continuous on \(S\), the integrals over all six pieces of the surface exist.
  2. If \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuous on the body \(V\), then
    \[\begin{aligned} \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A = {} & \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big[ v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} \Big]_{\mathrm{h}} \mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big[ v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} \Big]_{\mathrm{g}} \mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x \\ & + \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(b, y)} v_{\mathrm{x}}(b, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(a, y)} v_{\mathrm{x}}(a, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y \\ & + \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{d})}^{h(x, d)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, d, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{c})}^{h(x, c)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, c, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x , \end{aligned} \tag{4.19}\]
    where the bracket with the index \(h\) means that \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) are taken at the point \((x, y, h(x, y))\) of the top lid and the partial derivatives at the point \((x, y)\), and likewise with the index \(g\) on the bottom lid.
Proof

We must show that the integrands are continuous and that on the lids the root cancels. We point at the pieces of the surface in figure 4.55.

1. Existence.

  1. The top lid. The function \((x, y) \mapsto f(x, y, h(x, y))\) is continuous on the shadow \(R\) by lemma 4.35, with the functions \(p_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y) = x\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y) = y\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}} = h\), which are continuous.
  2. The square of the length \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|^2 = 1 + (\partial h/\partial x)^2 + (\partial h/\partial y)^2\) is a sum of products of continuous functions, hence continuous by corollary 1.70, item 1. That the length is continuous too is shown by figure 4.103. The numbers \(A, B \ge 1\) are the sides of two squares with the same corner, in the figure \(A = 1{,}5\) and \(B = 1{,}2\), and both squares contain the square of side \(1\). The difference of the areas \(A^2 - B^2\) is an L-shaped band of width \(A - B\). Unfolded into a strip it is \(A + B\) long, so \(A^2 - B^2 = (A - B)(A + B)\), in the figure \(0{,}81 = 0{,}3 \cdot 2{,}7\). The strip is at least \(2\) long, because each side is at least \(1\), so its width is at most half its area, \(|A - B| = |A^2 - B^2|/(A + B) \le |A^2 - B^2|/2\), in the figure \(0{,}3 \le 0{,}405\). For \(B > A\) we swap the roles. We have \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| \ge 1\), since the square of the length is \(1\) plus two squares (a roof is not smaller than its floor). The difference of the lengths at two points is therefore at most half the difference of the squares, and \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\) is continuous.
  3. The integrand in (4.18) is a product of continuous functions and is continuous on \(R\). Since \(R\) is closed and bounded, it is uniformly continuous by theorem 4.6, so it has the property of item 1 of lemma 4.7, and by its item 2 the iterated integral exists. For the bottom lid it is the same.
  4. The side piece \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) is the intersection of the closed set \(V\) (lemma 4.17) with the plane \(x = a\), which is closed (lemma 1.76, item 1), so by item 2 of the same lemma it is closed, and it is bounded. The proof of lemma 4.18, in which the numbers \(y\) of the interval \([c, d]\) take the place of the points \((x, y)\) of the rectangle, shows that the function \(y \mapsto \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(a, y)} f(a, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\) is continuous on \([c, d]\), hence integrable. For the other three side pieces it is the same.

2. Flux.

  1. On the top lid \(\vek n = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}/|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\), so at every point \((\vek v\cdot\vek n)\,|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| = \vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}}\). The integrand in (4.18) with \(f = \vek v\cdot\vek n\) is thus the first bracket in (4.19). It is continuous on \(R\) by lemma 4.35 and corollary 1.70, so the integral exists as in step 3 of the first part.
  2. On the bottom lid likewise \((\vek v\cdot\vek n)\,|\vek N_{\mathrm{g}}| = \vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = -\big(v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}}\big)\), and by linearity (lemma 3.54, item 1), applied to both iterated integrals, we take the minus sign out.
  3. On \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) we have \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek v\cdot\vek n = v_{\mathrm{x}}\), on \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) \(\vek v\cdot\vek n = -v_{\mathrm{x}}\), and likewise on \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\) with \(\pm v_{\mathrm{y}}\). Since \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) are continuous on \(V\), by lemma 4.18 the inner integral is a continuous function of the point \((x, y) \in R\), hence also of the number \(y\) at \(x = a\) or \(x = b\) and of the number \(x\) at \(y = c\) or \(y = d\), and so it is integrable.
  4. The sum of the six integrals is the right side of (4.19).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.6, (3) and (3*) (PDF p. 469), \(\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A = \vek N\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v\), and (5″) (PDF p. 470) for the lid \(z = h(x, y)\). The proof is not from the sources.

The definition describes every piece of the surface in a single way, with the two variables given by the description of the body. The same surface can be described in other ways too. The part of the plane \(y = 3\) between the pieces \(C\) and \(D\) of the round bar is, for the piece \(C\), a side piece \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) above the edge \(y = 3\) of its shadow, and for the piece \(D\) the bottom lid. That two descriptions of the same surface give the same integral when a suitable map between their pairs of variables joins them, we will show in section 4.3.6, where we describe surfaces more generally. We do not need it for the divergence theorem of section 4.2.12, and for the bar we will check the agreement of the two descriptions directly.

Let us test the definition on the mantle of the round bar (figure 4.99, right). The top lid of the piece \(C\) is the graph of the function \(h(x, y) = q(y)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-3, 3]\). By lemma 4.16 \(\partial h/\partial y = q'(y) = -y/q(y)\), and the partial derivative with respect to \(x\) is zero. Hence

\[\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = \Big(0,\ \frac{y}{q(y)},\ 1\Big) , \qquad |\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|^2 = 1 + \frac{y^2}{q(y)^2} = \frac{q(y)^2 + y^2}{q(y)^2} = \frac{r^2}{q(y)^2} ,\]

and \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| = r/q(y)\). The outward unit normal is \(\vek n = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\,q(y)/r = (0,\ y/r,\ q(y)/r)\). On the lid \(z = q(y)\), so \(\vek n = (0, y/r, z/r)\). This is the vector from the axis of the bar to the point, divided by the radius: the normal at the point \((3, 4)\) is \((0,\ 3/5,\ 4/5)\) and points along the radius. We have obtained the normal of the mantle that we wrote at the beginning of section 4.2.6 (figure 4.54, right). The area of the lid is the integral of the function \(1\):

\[\int_0^L \int_{-3}^{3} \frac{r}{q(y)}\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = L \cdot 6{,}435\ \text{mm} ,\]

where \(\int_{-3}^{3} 5/q(y)\,\mathrm{d}y = 6{,}435\) mm was computed by SymPy, because it again needs the inverse sine. This is the length of the arc of the circle above the shadow from \(y = -3\) to \(y = 3\), of length \(6\) mm. The arc is \(7\ \%\) longer than the shadow, because the lid is tilted more and more towards the two edges. The bottom lid of the piece \(C\) has the same area. For the piece \(D\) the top lid is the graph of the function \(q(z)\) over \([0, L] \times [-4, 4]\), with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = (0,\ 1,\ z/q(z))\) and \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| = r/q(z)\), and its area is \(L \cdot 9{,}273\) mm. The same holds for the bottom lid of the piece \(E\). The mantle of the bar consists of these four lids, with the total area

\[L \cdot (2 \cdot 6{,}435 + 2 \cdot 9{,}273)\ \text{mm} = L \cdot 31{,}42\ \text{mm} ,\]

which is the length of the bar times the circumference of the circle \(2\pi r = 31{,}42\) mm, the area of the mantle of a cylinder from school geometry. The integral of a constant function over a flat side piece is its value times the area of the region between graphs in its plane. The top face of the bar, \(x = 0\), consists of the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) of all three pieces, with the total area \(A_{\mathrm{C}} + 2A_{\mathrm{D}} = A\).

4.2.12 Divergence theorem for curved bodies

Now we have all the parts. The proof will follow the proof for a box. Let us cut the body with a plane of constant \(x\) (figure 4.104). In the section we see the body between the bottom lid \(z = g\) and the top lid \(z = h\), over the interval from \(c\) to \(d\) on the \(y\) axis. The term with the derivative with respect to \(z\) is handled by the fundamental theorem of calculus along the chords from the bottom to the top lid. When we add up the derivative \(\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) along a chord, what remains is the difference of the values of \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) at its upper and at its lower end. The terms with the derivatives with respect to \(y\) and to \(x\) are brought out of the inner integral over \(z\) by lemma 4.19, item 2, at the price of terms on the lids, and then the fundamental theorem of calculus does its work along \(y\) or \(x\).

Where does the price on the lids come from? Let us compare the integral along the chord at \(y_0\) with the integral along the neighbouring chord at \(y_0 + \Delta y\). On the heights they share only the field changes from one chord to the other, which the derivative \(\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y\) measures. But the neighbouring chord is also longer. At the top it is longer by about \(\frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,\Delta y\), because the top lid rises there, and at the bottom by about \(-\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,\Delta y\), because the bottom lid descends. The added pieces bring in the values of the field on the lids, multiplied by the slopes of the lids. The slope with the opposite sign, \(-\partial h/\partial y\), is a component of the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\), which is perpendicular to the top lid. That is why the terms on the lids are exactly those of the flux. When we then add up the changes from chord to chord over the whole interval from \(c\) to \(d\), only the integrals along the first and the last chord remain, that is, over the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\).

Before that we must settle one more technical question. The lemma on differentiating an integral needs the function on a rectangle around the chord, while we know the field \(\vek v\) only on an open set \(D\) containing the body \(V\) (figure 4.105). Near the edge of the body the rectangle reaches a little out of the body, above the top lid and below the bottom one. The following lemma says that it stays in \(D\) if it is narrow enough and reaches little enough beyond the lids. For around the body there is a band of constant width \(\delta_0\) that lies wholly in \(D\).

Why does such a band exist? An open set has around each of its points a ball that still lies in it (a disc in the figures, which are drawn in the plane). But the radii of these balls differ from point to point, and near the edge they could shrink toward zero. The lemma says that for a closed and bounded set this does not happen (figure 4.107, left). Around the set \(K\), which lies in the open set \(D\), there is a band of width \(\delta\) that lies wholly in \(D\). Every point that is less than \(\delta\) away from some point of the set \(K\) lies in this band.

When does this fail? Let \(K\) and \(D\) be the same set, the points of space less than \(5\) mm away from the origin \(O\), the interior of a ball (figure 4.106). This set is bounded and open, and its surface, which we draw dashed, does not belong to it. The point \(T_1\), \(4\) mm away from \(O\), is \(1\) mm away from points outside \(D\). The point \(T_2\) at \(4{,}9\) mm is \(0{,}1\) mm away from them, the point \(T_3\) at \(4{,}99\) mm \(0{,}01\) mm and the point \(T_4\) at \(4{,}999\) mm only \(0{,}001\) mm. So that these distances can be seen at all, each next picture is magnified ten times. The largest balls around these points that still lie in \(D\) thus shrink toward zero, as we feared above. The same happens for every distance, however small, so no number \(\delta > 0\) will do. Which hypothesis of the lemma is missing? The set is not closed, since the points \(T_1, T_2, \dots\) approach the point \(B\) on the surface, which does not lie in \(K\) (definition 1.75).

Lemma 4.38 Neighbourhood of a closed bounded set (okolica zaprte omejene množice)

Let \(K\) be a closed and bounded set of points of space (definition 1.75) and \(D\) an open set of points that contains \(K\). Then there is a number \(\delta > 0\) such that every point that is less than \(\delta\) away from some point of the set \(K\) lies in \(D\).

Proof

We must show that a single radius \(\delta\) suffices for all points of \(K\). We argue by contradiction, with the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, as in the proof of theorem 4.6.

  1. Suppose that no such \(\delta\) exists. Then for every natural number \(n\) there are a point \(P_{\mathrm{n}} \in K\) and a point \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) that does not lie in \(D\), with \(|P_{\mathrm{n}} Q_{\mathrm{n}}| < 1/n\).
  2. The set \(K\) is bounded, so by lemma 1.78 the sequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) has a subsequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) that converges to some point \(C\). The set \(K\) is closed, so \(C\) lies in \(K\) and therefore in \(D\).
  3. The sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) also converges to \(C\). The proof is the same as in steps 5 and 6 of the proof of theorem 4.6.
  4. The set \(D\) is open, so there is an \(r > 0\) such that all points less than \(r\) away from \(C\) lie in \(D\). Since \((Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converges to \(C\), for large enough \(k\) the distance \(|C Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}|\) is smaller than \(r\) (definition 1.66), and \(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}\) lies in \(D\). This contradicts step 1, so the assumption is false.

Source: LEBL1 Lemma 7.4.10 (the Lebesgue covering lemma, PDF p. 282), with open covers instead of a single open set. The proof follows the source, with pairs of points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) instead of balls around \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\).

The fourth part of the proof also needs the rectangle \(R\) in the \(xy\) plane (figure 4.108).

Let us draw it. The rectangle \(R\) lies in the \(xy\) plane, the body is above it, and the axes \(x\) and \(y\) run along its sides. At constant \(y\) the horizontal strip is the segment from \(x = a\) to \(x = b\). In part 4 of the proof we will integrate along it the derivative with respect to \(x\) of the function \(\tilde F\), which assigns to the point \((x, y)\) the integral of the component \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) along the chord of the body above that point. By the fundamental theorem of calculus this integral is the difference of the values of \(\tilde F\) at the left and right end, \(\tilde F(b, y) - \tilde F(a, y)\). At constant \(x\) the vertical strip is the segment from \(y = c\) to \(y = d\). The iterated integral over \(R\) adds up all the strips, and for a rectangle it does not matter whether we add the horizontal or the vertical ones first.

Theorem 4.39 Divergence theorem for a body between two graphs (izrek o divergenci za telo med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15), with the surface \(S\) and the outward unit normal \(\vek n\) (definition 4.36). Let \(D\) be an open set of points that contains \(V\), and \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) a field that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.91). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.20}\]

The same holds for a body with exchanged roles of the coordinates.

Proof

We must show that the integral of each of the three partial derivatives equals the part of the right side of (4.19) in which the same component of the field appears.

1. Preparation.

  1. The body \(V\) is closed and bounded (lemma 4.17). By lemma 4.38 there is a \(\delta_0 > 0\) such that every point that is less than \(\delta_0\) away from some point of \(V\) lies in \(D\).
  2. The partial derivatives of the components of the field are continuous on \(D\) by definition 1.91, and the components themselves by lemma 1.92, that a continuously differentiable function is continuous. All of them are therefore continuous on \(V\). The integrals of the partial derivatives over \(V\) therefore exist (definition 4.20), and by linearity (lemma 4.22) the left side of (4.20) is the sum \(I_{\mathrm{x}} + I_{\mathrm{y}} + I_{\mathrm{z}}\) of the integrals of the functions \(\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\), \(\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y\) and \(\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) over \(V\).
  3. For a function \(w\) that is continuous on \(V\), the functions \((x, y) \mapsto w(x, y, h(x, y))\) and \((x, y) \mapsto w(x, y, g(x, y))\) the values on the upper and the lower lid, are continuous on \(R\) by lemma 4.35, and so are their products with the partial derivatives of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) by corollary 1.70, item 1. Since \(R\) is closed and bounded, these functions are uniformly continuous by theorem 4.6, and by lemma 4.7 their iterated integrals over \(R\) in both orders exist.

2. The derivative with respect to \(z\).

  1. Let \((x, y) \in R\) and \(g(x, y) < h(x, y)\). The points \((x, y, z)\) with \(g(x, y) \le z \le h(x, y)\), a chord of the body, lie in \(V\) and therefore in \(D\), where \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) has a continuous partial derivative with respect to \(z\). The function \(z \mapsto v_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z)\) is therefore differentiable at every point of this interval, and its derivative is continuous. It is continuous on this interval, because \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) is continuous on \(D\) (lemma 1.92) and the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x, y, z')\) is \(|z - z'|\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55, item 1,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z = v_{\mathrm{z}}\big(x, y, h(x, y)\big) - v_{\mathrm{z}}\big(x, y, g(x, y)\big) .\]
    On the right are the values of the field at the upper and at the lower end of the chord. If \(g(x, y) = h(x, y)\), both sides are zero.
  2. Both functions on the right, the values at the upper and the lower end of the chord, are continuous on \(R\) by step 3 of the preparation. We integrate the equality over \(y\) and over \(x\) and use linearity (lemma 3.54, item 1). The integral \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\) therefore equals the two terms with the component \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) in the first two lines of (4.19).

3. The derivative with respect to \(y\).

  1. Let \(x \in [a, b]\) be fixed. For \(y \in [c, d]\) let
    \[\begin{aligned} F(y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z , \\ E(y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z + v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial y} - v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial y} , \end{aligned}\]
    where \(g\), \(h\) and their derivatives are taken at the point \((x, y)\). The number \(F(y)\) is the integral of the field along the chord at \(y\). The number \(E(y)\) is the candidate for the derivative of the function \(F\): the change of the field on the part that neighbouring chords share and the contributions of the upper and the lower end, which move with \(y\). By lemma 4.18 and step 3 of the preparation, \(F\) and \(E\) are continuous on \([c, d]\).
  2. Let \(y_0 \in (c, d)\). Let us show that \(F'(y_0) = E(y_0)\). Let \(\alpha = g(x, y_0) - \delta_0/2\) and \(\beta = h(x, y_0) + \delta_0/2\). The functions \(y \mapsto g(x, y)\) and \(y \mapsto h(x, y)\) are continuous at \(y_0\), so there is a \(\delta_1\) with \(0 < \delta_1 \le \delta_0/2\) such that the interval \([y_0 - \delta_1, y_0 + \delta_1]\) lies in \((c, d)\) and \(\alpha \le g(x, y) \le h(x, y) \le \beta\) for every \(y\) with \(|y - y_0| \le \delta_1\).
  3. Every point \((x, y, z)\) with \(|y - y_0| \le \delta_1\) and \(\alpha \le z \le \beta\) lies in \(D\). Let \(z^*\) be the number of the interval \([g(x, y_0), h(x, y_0)]\) closest to \(z\): \(z\) itself if it lies in the interval, otherwise the nearer end. Then \(|z - z^*| \le \delta_0/2\), the point \((x, y_0, z^*)\) lies in \(V\), and the distance between the two points is \(\sqrt{(y - y_0)^2 + (z - z^*)^2} \le \sqrt{\delta_0^2/4 + \delta_0^2/4} < \delta_0\). By step 1 of the preparation the point lies in \(D\).
  4. On the rectangle \([\alpha, \beta] \times [y_0 - \delta_1, y_0 + \delta_1]\) with the variables \(t = z\) and \(s = y\) let \(f(z, y) = v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z)\). By step 3 the rectangle lies in \(D\), which is open, so \(f\) has the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial y = \partial v_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y\) at every point of it. At \(y = y_0 \pm \delta_1\) this is a limit on both sides, so it is also the one-sided derivative of the function \(y \mapsto f(z, y)\) on \([y_0 - \delta_1, y_0 + \delta_1]\) that lemma 4.19 requires (section 1.3.3). Both functions are continuous on the rectangle, because the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x, y', z')\) equals the distance between \((z, y)\) and \((z', y')\). The functions \(\varphi(y) = g(x, y)\) and \(\psi(y) = h(x, y)\) have values in \([\alpha, \beta]\) and are differentiable at \(y_0\), with the derivatives \(\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}(x, y_0)\) and \(\frac{\partial h}{\partial y}(x, y_0)\) (definition 1.26). By lemma 4.19, item 2, \(F'(y_0) = E(y_0)\).
  5. The function \(F\) is thus continuous on \([c, d]\) and differentiable at every point of \((c, d)\), and its derivative \(E\) is continuous on \([c, d]\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus, item 1, \(\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d E(y)\,\mathrm{d}y = F(d) - F(c)\). Of all the chords only the ones at the edge remain, in the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\). By the definition of the function \(E\) and by linearity, therefore,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y = F(d) - F(c) - \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big( v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial y} - v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial y} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  6. All three terms on the right are continuous functions of \(x\). For the two boundary chords with \(F(d) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{d})}^{h(x, d)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, d, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\) and \(F(c)\) this is lemma 4.18, for the last integral lemma 4.7, item 2, with step 3 of the preparation. We integrate the equality over \(x\) and use linearity. The integral \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) therefore equals the last two lines of (4.19), together with the two terms with the component \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) in the first two lines.

4. The derivative with respect to \(x\).

  1. For \((x, y) \in R\) let
    \[\begin{aligned} \tilde F(x, y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z , \\ \tilde E(x, y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z + v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial x} - v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} . \end{aligned}\]
    As in steps 2 to 5 of the third part, only with the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged and with the section in figures 4.104 and 4.105 taken at constant \(y\), for fixed \(y\) the function \(x \mapsto \tilde F(x, y)\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) and differentiable at every point of \((a, b)\) with the derivative \(\tilde E(x, y)\), and \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \tilde E(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}x = \tilde F(b, y) - \tilde F(a, y)\).
  2. The function \(\tilde E\) is continuous on the rectangle \(R\) by lemma 4.18 and step 3 of the preparation. By theorem 4.9 on the order of integration, for a rectangle,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \tilde E\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \tilde E\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y = \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \big(\tilde F(b, y) - \tilde F(a, y)\big)\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  3. By the definition of the function \(\tilde E\) and by linearity
    \[I_{\mathrm{x}} = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \tilde E\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big( v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial x} - v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
    By step 2 this equals the third and the fourth line of (4.19), together with the two terms with the component \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) in the first two lines.

5. The sum.

  1. We add \(I_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\) from the fourth, third and second part. We obtain the right side of (4.19), which by lemma 4.37, item 2, is the flux \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7, Theorem 1, (2*) (PDF p. 479), with a proof for bodies that lie between graphs in the direction of all three axes (PDF pp. 480-482). It treats the term with the derivative with respect to \(z\) as we do. The proof of the terms with the derivatives with respect to \(x\) and \(y\) by lemma 4.19 is not from the sources.

The proof has shown where the terms on the lids with the derivatives of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) come from. When we bring the derivative with respect to \(y\) out of the integral over \(z\), the limits move, and the lemma on differentiating an integral adds the values of the field on the lids, multiplied by the slope of the lid in the direction \(y\). These are exactly the components \(-\partial h/\partial y\) and \(\partial g/\partial y\) of the vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\). The normal to the lid, which we obtained geometrically in section 4.2.11, from the vector product of the sides of a patch, has thus also come out of the computation. The fundamental theorem of calculus appeared three times in the proof, once for each coordinate, as for the box. We exchanged the order of integration in \(x\) and in \(y\) only in step 2 of the fourth part, and there we used that \(R\) is a rectangle.

Where did the other two hypotheses of the theorem enter, and what happens without them?

  • The field is continuously differentiable on an open set \(D\) that contains the body. We used the openness in step 4 of the third part. The rectangle reaches out of the body, and the derivative with respect to \(y\) at a point on a lid needs the values of the field on both sides of that point, also outside the body. For the fields of our examples, which are polynomials, \(D\) is all of space and the condition excludes nothing. Without continuous differentiability, however, the theorem fails. For the field that jumps from \(0\) to \(1\) in the middle of a cube with side \(1\), the integral of the divergence is \(0\) and the flux is \(1\) (section 4.2.5, figure 4.52).
  • The lids are graphs of continuously differentiable functions \(g\) and \(h\) (definition 4.15). Their slopes appear in the contributions of the ends of the chord, so they must exist and be continuous. The whole disc of radius \(5\) mm as one body between the graphs of two semicircles does not satisfy this, because the tangent of the semicircle at \(\pm 5\) mm is vertical and the slope does not exist there. That is why we cut the cross section of the bar at \(y = \pm 3\) mm. On the piece \(C\) the slope of the lids is at most \(\tfrac34\) in size, on the pieces \(D\) and \(E\) at most \(\tfrac43\), and the theorem holds for each piece separately.

Let us test the theorem on the right piece \(D\) of the round hanging bar, with the displacement field of the hanging bar (1.19),

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \end{aligned}\]

with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), the length \(L = 10\) m and the radius of the cross section \(r = 5\) mm. The bar hangs under its own weight and is held in the idealized way of section 1.7.1. For a test of the theorem the idealization does not matter, since the theorem holds for every continuously differentiable field, not only for the displacements of a real bar. For a bar held differently the numbers would change, but not the equality of the two sides. The piece \(D\) consists of the points of the bar with \(y \ge 3\) mm, a body between the graphs of the constant function \(3\) mm and the function \(q(z)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-4, 4]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(z\) (section 4.2.6, figure 4.57, right). The components of the field are polynomials, so they are continuously differentiable in all of space, which we take as the open set of the theorem.

Let us draw what the field does to the piece \(D\) (figure 4.109). On the left we look at it from the side, in the plane \(z = 0\). The axis of the bar is to the left of the piece, the \(x\) axis points down and the \(y\) axis to the right, and the piece has the length \(L\). We draw the piece before loading grey and dashed and the piece after loading orange, with the displacements magnified until they can be seen. The lower end at \(x = L\) moves down by \(aL^2 = 19{,}52\) µm. The displacement toward the axis at \(x = 0\) is \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,aL\,y\). On the mantle at \(y = 5\) mm this is \(5{,}9\) nm toward the axis, on the cut at \(y = 3\) mm \(3{,}5\) nm toward the axis, and at \(x = L\) it is zero. On the right is the cross section of the piece at \(x = 0\), with the axis of the bar at the origin. After loading the cross section is smaller, because all its points move toward the axis. The blackwhite arrows in the left picture are the outward normals of the piece, and the numbers next to them are the fluxes in cubic millimetres, which we now compute.

The left side is the integral over the piece \(D\). In section 4.2.5 we computed the divergence \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\). It does not depend on \(y\) and \(z\), so the inner and the middle integral give \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\,A_{\mathrm{D}}\), with the area of the cross section of the piece \(A_{\mathrm{D}} = 11{,}18\ \text{mm}^2\) from section 4.2.8, and the outer one

\[0{,}8\,a\,\frac{L^2}{2}\,A_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}4\,a L^2 A_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}4 \cdot 0{,}01952\ \text{mm} \cdot 11{,}18\ \text{mm}^2 = 0{,}08731\ \text{mm}^3 ,\]

where \(a L^2 = 19{,}52\) µm \(= 0{,}01952\) mm is the displacement of the lower end of the bar.

The right side. The flux through the six pieces of the surface of the piece \(D\), by lemma 4.37 with \(y\) as the coordinate that runs between the graphs:

  1. The side piece \(x = L\), part of the bottom face of the bar, with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integral of the function \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, y, z) = aL^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\) over the cross section of the piece is \(aL^2 A_{\mathrm{D}} - 0{,}3\,a\,\Theta_{\mathrm{D}} =\) \(0{,}2183\ \text{mm}^3\), where \(\Theta_{\mathrm{D}} = \int_{-4}^{4}\int_3^{q(z)} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}z = 203{,}8\ \text{mm}^4\). The second term is very small, \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{mm}^3\).
  2. The side piece \(x = 0\), part of the top face of the bar, with the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{x}}(0, y, z) = 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\), the flux \(0{,}3\,a\,\Theta_{\mathrm{D}} =\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{mm}^3\).
  3. The top lid \(y = q(z)\), part of the mantle, with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = (0,\ 1,\ z/q(z))\). At a point of the lid \(\vek u\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = u_{\mathrm{y}} + u_{\mathrm{z}}\,z/q(z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,\big(q(z) + z^2/q(z)\big) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,r^2/q(z)\). The integral over \(z\) is \(r\) times the arc length \(9{,}273\) mm from section 4.2.11, and the integral over \(x\) gives \(L^2/2\). The flux is \(-0{,}6\,a\,\tfrac{L^2}{2} \cdot 5\ \text{mm} \cdot 9{,}273\ \text{mm} =\) \(-0{,}2715\ \text{mm}^3\).
  4. The bottom lid \(y = 3\), the cut toward the piece \(C\), with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = (0, -1, 0)\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 3, z) = 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) \cdot 3\ \text{mm}\). The integral over \(z\) from \(-4\) to \(4\) gives the factor \(8\) mm, the one over \(x\) the factor \(L^2/2\), together \(0{,}6\,a\,\tfrac{L^2}{2} \cdot 24\ \text{mm}^2 =\) \(0{,}1405\ \text{mm}^3\).
  5. The side pieces \(z = \pm 4\). There \(q(\pm 4) = 3\), so \(y\) runs from \(3\) to \(3\), and the integrals are zero by the convention of definition 3.49. The pieces are segments on the mantle that have no area. In the cross section they are the corners \((3, 4)\) and \((3, -4)\).

The sum is \(0{,}2183 + 0{,}0000 - 0{,}2715 + 0{,}1405 = 0{,}0873\ \text{mm}^3\), the same as the left side. We computed all the integrals with SymPy. What do they say? The lower end of the piece moves down and sweeps \(0{,}2183\ \text{mm}^3\) outward. The mantle moves toward the axis of the bar, because the bar gets thinner, and sweeps \(0{,}2715\ \text{mm}^3\) inward.
