The cut \(y = 3\) also moves toward the axis, in the direction \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), which for the piece \(D\) is the outward direction, so it contributes \(0{,}1405\ \text{mm}^3\).

Why does the mantle sweep almost twice as much as the cut? It is longer, \(9{,}273\) mm against \(8\) mm, and it moves farther (figure 4.110). Only the part of the displacement along the normal sweeps volume, the part along the surface only shifts the surface within itself. In the cross section of the piece at \(x = 0\) the displacement of the point \((y, z)\) is \(-k\,(y, z)\) with \(k = 0{,}6\,aL\). It points straight toward the axis of the bar and is \(k\) times the distance of the point from the axis. On the mantle the direction away from the axis is exactly the normal, so the displacement of the point \(M\) points along the normal, inward, and is \(5{,}9\) nm long, since every point of the mantle is \(5\) mm from the axis. The point \(Q\) on the cut is \(4{,}24\) mm from the axis and moves by \(5{,}0\) nm. We split this displacement into the part along the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), which is \(k\) times the coordinate \(y = 3\) mm, that is \(3{,}5\) nm outward, and the part along the cut, which sweeps nothing. The part along the normal is the same at every point of the cut, since all of them are \(3\) mm from the plane \(y = 0\) through the axis. So the displacement component along the normal is proportional to the distance of the surface from the axis, \(5\) mm for the mantle and \(3\) mm for the cut, in the ratio \(5\) to \(3\). The products are \(5 \cdot 9{,}273 = 46{,}4\) and \(3 \cdot 8 = 24\), in the ratio \(1{,}93\), like the fluxes \(0{,}2715\) and \(0{,}1405\). The piece \(D\) follows the thinning of the bar toward its axis.

The round bar itself is not one body between graphs but is cut into three pieces. We apply the theorem to each piece and add the equalities. On the left we get the integral over the bar (definition 4.21). On the right, however, we get the fluxes through all pieces of the surfaces of all three bodies, also through the cuts \(y = \pm 3\), which are not part of the surface of the bar. As with the cells of a body made of boxes, the contributions of each cut cancel, because the cut has the normal \(\vek n\) for the piece on one side and \(-\vek n\) for the piece on the other side (figure 4.111). On the mantle of the bar, which in the figure is an arc of the circle, the normals point away from the axis.

Corollary 4.40 Divergence theorem for a body cut into pieces (izrek o divergenci za telo, razrezano na kose)

Let \(V\) be cut into the pieces \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\), which are bodies between graphs (definition 4.21). Let the pieces of the surfaces of these bodies (definition 4.36) be divided into outer and inner ones, and the inner ones into pairs, so that each pair consists of pieces of the surfaces of two different bodies and the flux of every continuous field through one piece is the negative of the flux through the other. Let \(S\) be the union of the outer pieces, the surface of the body \(V\), and \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\) the sum of the fluxes through the outer pieces. Let \(D\) be an open set of points that contains \(V\), and \(\vek v\) a field that is continuously differentiable on \(D\). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.21}\]
Proof

We must show that the fluxes through the inner pieces cancel.

  1. Every body \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\) lies in \(V\), hence in \(D\). By theorem 4.39 the integral of the divergence of the field \(\vek v\) over \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\) equals the flux through its surface, that is, the sum of the fluxes through its six pieces.
  2. We add the equalities over the pieces, \(k\) from \(1\) to \(m\). The sum of the left sides is, by definition 4.21, the integral of the divergence over \(V\).
  3. The sum of the right sides is the sum of the fluxes through all pieces of the surfaces of all bodies \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\). The inner pieces come in pairs, and the two fluxes of each pair are opposite numbers that cancel. What remains is the sum of the fluxes through the outer pieces, which is \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF p. 482): for a body that auxiliary surfaces cut into finitely many pieces, the integrals over the auxiliary surfaces cancel in pairs. The proof follows the source.

The condition on the pairs has to be checked for every cut. For two flat pieces in the same plane that both descriptions give by the same iterated integral and with opposite normals, it holds by itself. So it is for the bar. The cut \(y = 3\) is, for the piece \(C\), the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) with the flux \(\int_0^L \int_{-\mathrm{q}(3)}^{q(3)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 3, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x\), and for the piece \(D\) the bottom lid with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = (0, -1, 0)\) and with the flux \(\int_0^L \int_{-4}^{4} \big(-v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 3, z)\big)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x\). Since \(q(3) = 4\), these are the same iterated integral with opposite signs, for every continuous field \(\vek v\). The same holds for the cut \(y = -3\) between the pieces \(C\) and \(E\). For pieces that the two descriptions give differently, we show the agreement in section 4.3.6.

Let us check the corollary on the whole bar, with the same displacement field. The fluxes through the pieces of the surfaces and the integrals of the divergence are in cubic millimetres, computed with SymPy:

\(C\) \(D\) \(E\) bar
bottom face \(x = L\) \(1{,}0965\) \(0{,}2183\) \(0{,}2183\) \(1{,}5331\)
top face \(x = 0\) \(3{,}4 \cdot 10^{-8}\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\) \(5{,}7 \cdot 10^{-8}\)
mantle \(-0{,}3768\) \(-0{,}2715\) \(-0{,}2715\) \(-0{,}9199\)
cut \(y = 3\) \(-0{,}1405\) \(0{,}1405\) \(0\)
cut \(y = -3\) \(-0{,}1405\) \(0{,}1405\) \(0\)
sum of the fluxes \(0{,}4386\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}6132\)
integral of the divergence \(0{,}4386\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}6132\)

For each piece the last two rows are equal, as theorem 4.39 says. In the column of the bar the cuts cancel, as the corollary says. What remains is the bottom face, which moves down by \(aL^2 = 19{,}52\) µm and sweeps \(aL^2 A = 1{,}5331\ \text{mm}^3\), the mantle, which moves toward the axis and sweeps \(0{,}6\,aL^2 A = 0{,}9199\ \text{mm}^3\) inward, and a very small contribution of the top face, which rises a little at the rim. The volume of the bar increases by \(0{,}4\,aL^2 A = 0{,}6132\ \text{mm}^3\). The relative change is \(0{,}6132/785\,400 = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\), the same as for the box in section 4.2.5. Why the same?

The divergence \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\) depends only on the depth \(x\). At the top of the bar it is \(0{,}8\,aL\), at the bottom zero. A part of the bar that has the same cross section at every \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) holds a quarter of its volume in each quarter of the length, and so equal volumes in layers of equal thickness. The relative change of volume is therefore the mean of this linear function over \(x\), which is its value at the middle, \(0{,}4\,aL\), whatever the shape of that cross section. Why at the middle? The excess of the upper half above the mean equals the shortfall of the lower half below it, since these are equal triangles. When does this fail? A cone with its base on the top face of the bar and its apex at the centre of the bottom face also spans the whole length, but at depth \(x\) its cross section has the area \(A\,(1 - x/L)^2\). Its quarters of the length hold, from the top down, \(57{,}8\) %, \(29{,}7\) %, \(10{,}9\) % and \(1{,}6\) % of its volume, the most at the top, where the divergence is large. The mean of the divergence weighted by volume is therefore \(0{,}6\,aL\), the value at the depth \(L/4\), and the relative change of volume of the cone is \(1{,}171 \cdot 10^{-6}\), half as much again as for the bar.

With this we have proved the divergence theorem for all bodies that can be cut into finitely many bodies between graphs so that the inner pieces of the surfaces pair up (figure 4.113). Such are the box, the body made of boxes and the round bar, that is, all the bodies of our examples so far. Three more things remain. The first are the bodies that we cannot cut in this way, for instance a ball. We prove the theorem for them in section 4.3.7, for all bodies that we cut into bodies between graphs and into bodies that we get by bending a box continuously. This covers all the bodies of our examples, the ball, the thick spherical shell and the tube included. KREYSZIG states the theorem also for bodies with an arbitrary surface made of smooth pieces (§10.7, Theorem 1, PDF p. 479) and only mentions that they would need a further limit process (PDF p. 482). The second, the independence of the integral of the order of integration and of the cut, is already proved. By corollary 4.34 the sum of definition 4.21 is the integral over a set with volume, which knows nothing of the cut. The third, the independence of the surface integral of the description of the surface, we show in section 4.3.6 for descriptions joined by a suitable map between their variables.

4.2.13 Equilibrium of a part of a body

Now we can keep the promise of section 2.7.9. We derived the equilibrium equations (2.38) from the equilibrium of small cubes. Do they also imply the equilibrium of every finite part of the body?

From the body let us cut out in thought a part \(V\), built of boxes like a wall of bricks (figure 4.114, left). We draw its surface \(S\) thick. Two kinds of forces act on such a part. The rest of the body acts on it across the surface \(S\), with the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) per unit area, where \(\vek n\) is the outward normal of the part (definition 2.20). The traction vector differs from point to point of the surface and in general does not point along the normal. On all its material acts the body force \(\vek b\) per unit volume, downward in the case of weight. The total force across the surface is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek t\,\mathrm{d}A\), the total body force the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V\), both by components, as we agreed in section 4.2.3.

Corollary 4.41 Equilibrium of a part of a body (ravnovesje dela telesa)

Let a body be in equilibrium and let \(V\) be a part of it that is a body made of boxes with the surface \(S\) and the outward normal \(\vek n\), and let every point of \(V\) be an interior point of the body. Let the stress components be continuously differentiable on an open set \(D\) that contains \(V\) (definition 1.91), let the body force \(\vek b\) be continuous on \(D\), let the equilibrium equations (2.38) hold at every point of \(V\), and let the assumption of Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.26) hold at every point of \(V\), that the average force per unit area on a plane face approaches the traction vector at the point when we shrink the face towards this point. Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek t(\vek n)\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V = \vek 0 , \tag{4.22}\]

where \(\vek t(\vek n)\) is the traction vector at a point of the surface \(S\) for the outward normal \(\vek n\) of the part \(V\).

Proof

We must show that each component of the left side is zero, that is, the sum of the forces across the surface and the body forces on the part \(V\). We integrate the equilibrium equations over \(V\) and use the divergence theorem and Cauchy's formula.

  1. At every point of the part \(V\) the first equation (2.38) holds, \(\dfrac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} + b_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\). The last term is a component of the body force. All four terms are continuous on \(V\).
  2. We add the equation up over the whole part \(V\). The integral of the zero function is zero (lemma 4.10, item 2, on each cell). By linearity (same lemma, item 1) therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{V}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 .\]
  3. By the divergence theorem 4.14, item 2, with the field \((v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}}) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}})\), which is continuously differentiable on \(D\), the first integral equals an integral over the surface \(S\) with the outward normal \(\vek n\). Nothing remains from the interior, because the contributions of two neighbouring cells on their shared face cancel. What remains is
    \[\int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
  4. Every point of the surface \(S\) is an interior point of the body at which the assumption of Cauchy's formula holds, so Cauchy's formula holds there. Theorem 2.26 does require that the only body force is the weight, but the remark after its proof says that any body force that is bounded near the point will do. A body force \(\vek b\) that is continuous on \(D\) is bounded near every point of the surface \(S\), also on the other side of the surface, where the small tetrahedra of the proof reach. By (2.27) the integrand of step 3 is the component \(t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n)\) of the traction vector. From step 2 we get \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} t_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{V}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\).
  5. For the component \(y\) we repeat steps 1 to 4 with the second equation (2.38) and the field \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}})\), for the component \(z\) with the third equation and the field \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})\). By (2.27) the integrands on the surface are the components \(t_{\mathrm{y}}(\vek n)\) and \(t_{\mathrm{z}}(\vek n)\) of the traction vector.

Source: SADD (3.7.1)-(3.7.3) (PDF pp. 77-78), where the argument runs the other way: the equilibrium equations follow from the equilibrium of every part.

The proof wrote out exactly the picture of a wall of bricks from section 2.7.9. In the proof of the divergence theorem for a body made of boxes the contributions of the inner faces cancelled. Let us see why on two neighbouring cells, which we draw apart (figure 4.114, right). The outward normal of their shared face is \(\vek n\) for one cell and \(-\vek n\) for the other. By lemma 2.21 the two forces across the shared face are therefore opposite too: the left cell pulls the right one with the same force with which the right one pulls the left, which is Newton's law of action and reaction. In the sum over all cells such a pair cancels. What remains are the forces on the surface of the part and the body forces.

For a body that moves with an acceleration, the right side of (4.22) would hold, instead of the zero vector, the integral of the density times the acceleration, as in the equations of motion of section 2.7.9. We did not use the symmetry of stress (theorem 2.41). We need it for the second condition of equilibrium of a part, that the sum of the moments of the forces across the surface and of the body forces is zero. That follows in the same way from the equilibrium equations, the divergence theorem and the symmetry of stress (SADD (3.7.6) onward, PDF pp. 78-79), which we do not write out here.

Where did the proof need the assumptions of the corollary, and what happens without them?

  1. The stress is continuously differentiable on \(D\). The divergence theorem in step 3 needs this. When the stress jumps on some face in the interior of the part \(V\), we may not use the divergence theorem over all of \(V\), as for the field with a jump in figure 4.52. When the traction vector on this face jumps, the forces with which the material on the two sides of the face pulls no longer cancel. We see why on a thin layer of material at the face of the jump (figure 4.115, left). The material above the layer pulls it up, the material below pulls it down, and because the traction vector on the face jumps, the two forces differ. The layer is in equilibrium. When we make it thinner, its weight, which is proportional to the thickness, goes to zero, while the forces on its faces hardly change. So the difference is carried by a force that acts on the face itself. Equation (4.22), which does not capture this force, misses exactly this force. Below we will see on the hanging bar that a force of \(5{,}50\) N is then missing from the sum. A jump of a component that does not act on the face does not spoil the equation (figure 4.115, right). When on a plane perpendicular to the \(x\) axis only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) jumps, which acts on faces perpendicular to the \(y\) axis, the traction vector on the plane, \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\), is the same on both sides, and the equation holds, as we see when we use the divergence theorem on each side of the plane separately.
  2. The body force is continuous on \(D\). Step 2 needs this, so that the integral of the body force over \(V\) exists, and step 4, so that the force is bounded near every point of the surface \(S\), as the remark after the proof of Cauchy's formula requires. Why on \(D\) and not only on \(V\), we see on a part with a curved surface, like the pieces between graphs below (figure 4.116, left). The part \(V\) in the interior of the body has the surface \(S\) and on it a point \(Q\) with the outward normal \(\vek n\). The small tetrahedra of the proof of Cauchy's formula have their vertex at \(Q\) and their oblique face with the normal \(\vek n\), so they lie beyond \(S\), outside \(V\). The body force acts on their material, so it must be bounded there too. The open set \(D\) reaches beyond \(S\) and contains small enough tetrahedra. The weight of a material of constant density satisfies it. A force gathered on one face or at one point does not, and the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V\) does not capture it. Such is the force of the load on the hanging bar below. It acts on one plane, so the same \(5{,}50\) N is missing from the sum.
  3. Every point of \(V\) is an interior point of the body. Step 4 needs this, because we proved Cauchy's formula only at interior points, where on the other side of the surface \(S\) is the material of the body, in which the tetrahedra of the proof lie. When the part reaches the surface of the body (figure 4.116, right), the surroundings are on the other side. The tetrahedron would lie in them, where there is no material of the body, and the force of the surroundings acts on the surface. Then Cauchy's formula must hold for the force of the surroundings as an additional requirement, which we will use below for the whole bar.
  4. The part \(V\) is a body made of boxes. Only for such bodies do we have theorem 4.14. The condition is not essential: below we replace it by a cut into pieces between graphs.

Let us test the corollary on the box \(K = [x_1, x_2] \times [-c, c] \times [-c, c]\) in the hanging bar, with \(x_1 = 3\) m, \(x_2 = 6\) m and \(c = 0{,}003\) m, as in section 4.2.3 (figure 4.117). The bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight, is held in the idealized way, and has the axis \(x\) pointing down from the centre \(O\) of the top face. A real holder, for example a weld to the ceiling, distributes the force over the top face differently, but with the same total force along the axis of the bar, the weight of the bar. By Saint-Venant's principle (section 2.2) the stress therefore changes only near the top face. BOWER (§5.1.5, PDF p. 280) gives as the limit in practice a distance of three sizes of the loaded region, here three diameters, that is \(30\) mm. The box begins 3 m below the top face, a hundred times farther, so the numbers below hold almost exactly for the real holder too. The only stress component that is not zero is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\) (section 2.7.9), a polynomial that is continuously differentiable in the whole space. All points of the box are interior points of the bar. We see this in the cross section of the bar, a circle of radius 5 mm, in which the cross section of the box is a square with half side 3 mm (figure 4.117, middle). Farthest from the axis is a corner of the square, at \(3\sqrt 2 = 4{,}243\) mm. So every point of the box is at least \(5 - 4{,}243 = 0{,}757\) mm from the mantle of the bar, at least 3 m from the top face and at least \(L - x_2 = 4\) m from the bottom face. By (2.27), \(\vek t(\vek n) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0)\).

  1. On the top face \(x = x_1\) we have \(\vek n = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek t = (-\rho g\,(L - x_1), 0, 0)\). The integrand is constant, so the integral over the face of area \(4c^2\) is \((-4c^2\rho g\,(L - x_1), 0, 0)\). The part of the bar above the box pulls it up with the force \(36 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2 \cdot 76\,518\ \text{N/m}^3 \cdot 7\ \text{m} = 19{,}28\) N.
  2. On the bottom face \(x = x_2\) we have \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek t = (\rho g\,(L - x_2), 0, 0)\). The part of the bar below the box pulls it down with the force \(4c^2\rho g\,(L - x_2) = 11{,}02\) N.
  3. On the four side faces \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), so \(\vek t = \vek 0\). The neighbouring material does not act on the side faces.
  4. The weight of the box is \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V = (4c^2\rho g\,(x_2 - x_1), 0, 0)\), that is \(8{,}264\) N down, as we computed in section 4.2.3.

The component \(x\) of the left side of (4.22) is \(4c^2\rho g\,\big({-(L - x_1)} + (L - x_2) + (x_2 - x_1)\big) = 0\), with the numbers rounded to hundredths of a newton \(-19{,}28 + 11{,}02 + 8{,}26 = 0\). The weight of the box is thus exactly the difference between the forces on its top and bottom faces, which is why the upper arrow in the figure is as long as the two lower ones together. This is the same reasoning as in section 2.1, where we got the axial force from the equilibrium of the part of the bar below a cross section, only the box does not reach the bottom.

And what if the stress is not continuously differentiable? In thought let us hang on the bar at the depth \(x_0 = 4\) m a load of weight \(P = 12\) N, idealized so that its force acts evenly over the whole cross section at this depth (figure 4.117, right). Such a load does not exist. A real load hangs from the mantle of the bar, for example on a collar, and no force acts on any face in the interior of the bar. Then the force of the load reaches the box, which lies at least \(0{,}757\) mm inside the mantle, only across its surface, through shear stresses on the side faces. The box is in equilibrium and only the forces across its surface and its weight act on it, so the left side of (4.22) is zero. The idealization gives us the simplest jump, on which we see how an assumption of the corollary fails, and it is exactly because of it that \(5{,}50\) N will be missing from the sum below. Above this depth the bar also carries the load, so there \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x) + P/A\) with the cross-section area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), and below it \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\) remains. On the plane \(x = x_0\) the stress jumps by \(P/A = 12\ \text{N} / 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 0{,}1528\) MPa and is not differentiable there. At all other points the equilibrium equations hold as before, because \(P/A\) is constant and the derivative does not see it. Let us add up the forces on the same box. The top face is pulled up by the force \(19{,}28\ \text{N} + 4c^2 P/A = 19{,}28\ \text{N} + 5{,}50\ \text{N} = 24{,}78\) N, the bottom face down by \(11{,}02\) N, and the weight is \(8{,}26\) N. The sum

\[-24{,}78 + 11{,}02 + 8{,}26 = -5{,}50\ \text{N}\]

is not zero. What is missing is the force of the load on the box, \(4c^2 P/A = \dfrac{36\ \text{mm}^2}{78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2} \cdot 12\ \text{N} = 5{,}50\) N down, which acts on the plane of the jump in the interior of the box. This force is not a force across the surface of the box and not a continuous body force, so the left side of (4.22) does not capture it. The box is in equilibrium here too, but the equation holds only once we add this force separately. So we use the corollary only on parts in which the stress is continuously differentiable.

What about the whole bar (figure 4.117, left)? It is a cylinder, not a body made of boxes, and its surface is not in the interior of the body. On the surface of a body the traction vector is the force of the surroundings per unit area. SADD requires on the surface that this force be related to the stresses at the points of the surface by Cauchy's formula (§5.2, PDF pp. 104-106). For the hanging bar this is so: the top face is pulled up by the force \(\rho g L\) per unit area, which is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(0)\), while the bottom face and the mantle are free, \(\vek t = \vek 0\), which agrees with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(L) = 0\) and with \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) on the mantle. The integrands are constant on each face, so we compute the integrals with the cross-section area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) and the volume \(AL\), which we computed with the cut of the bar into three pieces in sections 4.2.8 and 4.2.11. The force on the surface is \((-\rho g L A, 0, 0)\), a force of \(60{,}10\) N up, and the body force is \((\rho g A L, 0, 0)\), the weight of \(60{,}10\) N down. The sum is the zero vector, as (4.22) requires.

The divergence theorem for a body cut into pieces (corollary 4.40) tells us that the test is no accident. With it corollary 4.41 holds, with the same proof, also for a part of a body that is cut into pieces between graphs, like the round bar cut into the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\) (figure 4.111). In step 2 we use the linearity of lemma 4.22, and in step 3 corollary 4.40 in place of theorem 4.14, in which the contributions of two neighbouring pieces on a cut cancel, just as the contributions of neighbouring cells did. So it holds for round parts of the bar in its interior, which are not made of boxes. It holds also for the whole bar, although the points of its surface are not interior points. At the points of the surface step 4 needs only Cauchy's formula, which holds on the surface of the bar by the requirement of SADD. The equilibrium equations, which step 1 needs, hold at all points of the bar for the polynomial stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\).

SADD takes this road in the opposite direction. From the equilibrium of every part of the body it obtains, with the divergence theorem, that the integral of the left side of the equilibrium equations is zero over every part, and concludes from this that the integrand is zero at every point (SADD (3.7.3) and (3.7.4) with (1.8.12), PDF pp. 28-29 and 78). We will need a similar conclusion in the next sections: a continuous function is zero if every integral of it of a certain kind is zero.

With this we have, for a body in space, the integral over a body and over its surface and the theorem that connects them, for all bodies that we can cut into pieces between graphs. Before we write equilibrium in a new form, with the work of the forces, the next section shows how an integral changes when we describe the points of a body by other variables. With this we will extend the divergence theorem to bodies that we cannot cut into pieces between graphs, and say exactly how the volume of a small piece changes under loading.
